Under this repo's parallel agent-authoring workflow the preconditions recur routinely, and a recurrence in purge_account means silently incomplete account erasure (a GDPR erasure defect) that the harness only partially detects (see the cascade blind-spot finding). The failure mode is scriptable in a few lines: grep function names per migration in a PR's batch and fail on duplicates not accompanied by a union note.
findings.evidence: packages/supabase/supabase/migrations/20260731090000_purge_account_union.sql:1-18 (incident record); docs/decisions/log.md:376-380 ('the next likely collision'); markers at 20260731090000:144 and 20260730070347_mutual_connections.sql:320; grep of .github/workflows shows no detection step; root CLAUDE.md standing rule is instruction-only.
findings.remediation: Add a small CI script (runs on packages/supabase/supabase/migrations/** PRs) that lists 'create or replace function' names per changed migration plus the existing history, and fails when a PR batch introduces two or more emissions of the same function or re-emits a marker-carrying function (purge_account, remove_connection) without the harness file changing in the same PR.

verification.note: Re-verified every citation: the incident record (20260731090000_purge_account_union.sql:1-18), the decision-log forewarning naming M52/M53 as "the next likely collision" (log.md:378), both in-body append markers, and the total absence of automated detection (the four workflows never touch packages/supabase; no git/husky/.claude hooks; supabase lint is a placeholder echo). The process gap and likelihood 3 are honest. Impact 4 is overstated, however: the section-(4) append site holds only auth.users ON DELETE CASCADE tables by explicit convention (all five connections-era FKs verified cascade), and the sole production caller, the delete-account edge function, ends with auth.admin.deleteUser — so even the actual regressed body would have left zero residual rows after a successful deletion flow; the erasure gap exists only when deleteUser fails after purge succeeds. The finding also double-counts the harness blind spot: the cascade that masks verify-account-purge.ts's zero-row checks is the same cascade that erases the data in production (blind spot and harm are complementary, not compounding), and the harness additionally pins the purge RPC's own counts for pebble_drafts plus the connections trio, so an exact recurrence fails loudly whenever the harness runs. Realistic recurrence harms are wrong purge accounting, drift on un-pinned newer tables (achievement_unlocks), residue confined to the deleteUser-failure window, and (for remove_connection) an app-consistency defect rather than erasure. Adjusted severity 3 x 3 = 9.

findings.title: The web Supabase client is untyped: generated database types are not imported anywhere in apps/web, and 155 hand-written casts substitute for the schema contract
findings.detail: lib/supabase/client.ts:14 calls createBrowserClient(url, key) and lib/supabase/server.ts:16 createServerClient(url, key) without the Database generic, so every query returns untyped rows. The provider then maps rows as Record<string, unknown> with per-field 'as' casts (155 occurrences of ' as ' in supabase-provider.ts, e.g. rowToMark at :905-914, toDraftRecord at :52-64), and shared shapes are hand-retyped in lib/types.ts. The committed generated types (packages/supabase/types/database.ts) are imported by apps/admin but by zero files in apps/web (grep 'types/database' over apps/web returns nothing). Consequence: a schema or RPC-shape change compiles cleanly on web and surfaces only as a runtime undefined or a silently wrong value; the type system provides no proof that web still matches the contract, defeating the point of regenerating database.ts with every migration (root AGENTS.md rule). Admin proves the typed pattern already works in this repo.
findings.evidence: apps/web/lib/supabase/client.ts:14; apps/web/lib/supabase/server.ts:16; grep -rn 'types/database|Database' apps/web/lib/supabase apps/web/lib/data returns zero hits; grep -c ' as ' apps/web/lib/data/supabase-provider.ts = 155; counter-example apps/admin/lib/supabase/browser.ts imports the generated types
findings.remediation: Parameterize both client factories with Database from packages/supabase/types/database.ts, then progressively replace Record<string, unknown> row mapping with typed rows, starting with the provider's loadFromSupabase and the RPC return shapes.

findings.title: Privileged admin actions leave no durable audit trail, making breach scoping and operator attribution impossible
findings.detail: No audit or action-log table exists. admin_delete_glyph hard-deletes the glyph and, via cascade, the submission row that held reviewed_by/reviewed_at, destroying the only incidental trail the pipeline has. set_glyph_listed, set_glyph_price, admin_attribute_glyph, and admin_find_user (a privileged personal-data lookup over auth.users by email) record no actor and no timestamp. Lab log create/update/delete are plain table writes. If an operator account is compromised or misused, there is no way to enumerate what was read or changed, by whom, in what window, which directly defeats Art. 33's 72-hour scoping requirement and leaves moderation decisions undefendable.
findings.evidence: grep -n 'audit' over packages/supabase/supabase/migrations/*.sql matches only comments; 20260701102810_glyph_marketplace_curation.sql:102-161 (four admin RPCs with no logging); :119-129 (admin_delete_glyph, delete cascades submission per FK design at :117-118); apps/admin/app/(authed)/logs/actions.ts:151-162 (deleteLog); reviewed_by/reviewed_at exist only on glyph_submissions (20260630084718:69-74)
findings.remediation: Add an admin_actions audit table (actor, action, target ids, timestamp, payload digest) and insert into it from every is_admin-gated mutation RPC in the same transaction; for hard deletes, write the audit row before the cascade removes the evidence.

findings.title: Out-of-band data-subject rights requests have no operator runbook and no admin tooling, against a published 30-day promise
findings.detail: The privacy policy invites rights requests by email and commits to a 30-day response, plus parental access/erasure for minors with proof of authority. Nothing on the operator side backs this: no versioned runbook covering identity verification, response steps, or escalation; no admin tooling to trigger an erasure or produce an access/portability export for a verified requester; and portability is unimplemented product-wide, so an Art. 15/20 request would be hand-written SQL under a regulatory clock. The only documented manual path is a comment inside the delete-account edge function. The gap becomes acute for parental and post-lockout requests, which cannot use the self-serve deletion flow.
findings.evidence: apps/web/docs/privacy/en.md:258-264 (30-day commitment), :288-293 (parental rights); grep -rilE 'runbook|out.of.band|rights request|subject access' over docs/, apps/admin, packages/supabase returns nothing relevant; admin route inventory has no user-management surface; packages/supabase/supabase/functions/delete-account/index.ts:21-23 (manual path exists only as a comment); no export code anywhere in apps/web
findings.remediation: Write a versioned operator runbook (identity verification, Art. 12(3) clock, per-right procedure, escalation) in docs/; add a minimal admin flow that, for a verified user id, runs purge_account plus auth deletion, and a scripted export that walks the user-owned tables in database.ts.

findings.title: The privacy policy Android links to describes a different product and is contradicted by shipped data flows
findings.detail: The policy reachable from the Android auth and settings screens (last updated 2026-04-09) documents Google Gemma AI processing, therapist access permissions, HealthKit, 'Events/Moods/Decisions/Cairns' and a 7-point mood scale - none of which exist - while omitting what actually ships: Google OAuth sign-in, photo snap uploads, public share links, public profiles with handles, mutual connections, the glyph marketplace, and Play distribution. It affirms 'We do not share your memories anywhere' while the product's visibility grades expose pebbles to connections and to anyone with a /p link. An Art. 13 notice that misdescribes purposes and processors fails transparency outright, and the mismatch is store-declaration risk for the Play listing the CI pipeline publishes to. There is also no in-repo source of truth for the Play Data safety answers to reconcile against the manifest and payloads.
findings.evidence: apps/web/docs/privacy/en.md:7 (last_updated 2026-04-09), :22 ('do not share your memories anywhere'), :71,324-339 (Gemma), :131-158 (HealthKit, therapist), :48 (7-point moods); shipped contradictions: packages/supabase/supabase/migrations/20260817130000_pebble_visibility_grades.sql (public/private grades), apps/android features/connections + SharedPebbleLink.kt + SettingsScreen public profile; docs/android-play-deploy.md contains no Data safety section; opened from LegalDocs.kt:14-16
findings.remediation: Rewrite the policy (EN and authoritative FR) from a code-derived data inventory of the current product, remove nonexistent processing, disclose the real sharing/marketplace/OAuth/media flows, and commit the Play Data safety answers next to the deploy runbook with a PR-checklist tie to schema changes.

findings.title: allowBackup=true with no backup rules ships the session token and intimate composer drafts to Google Auto Backup, outside the erasure story
findings.detail: The manifest enables Android Auto Backup with no dataExtractionRules or fullBackupContent filter, so the app's SharedPreferences - including supabase-kt's persisted session (a live refresh token) and the pebbles_prefs composer snapshot holding unpublished pebble content (name, description, valence, emotion, souls) - are periodically copied to the user's Google account backup. That is personal and special-category-adjacent data leaving the device to a processor the policy never names, with retention governed by Google's backup lifecycle rather than the product: account deletion purges Supabase and storage but no device backup, so intimate drafts and a credential can outlive the account. The fix is one manifest attribute or a small rules file excluding both prefs files.
findings.evidence: apps/android/app/src/main/AndroidManifest.xml:12 (android:allowBackup="true"); res/xml/ contains only locales_config.xml (no backup rules, grep dataExtractionRules|fullBackupContent over src/main returns nothing); services/ComposerSnapshotStore.kt:33,58-69 (draft content into pebbles_prefs); supabase-kt session persisted via its default Android settings storage (services/SupabaseService.kt install(Auth)); policy processor list omits Google backup (apps/web/docs/privacy/en.md:161-176)
findings.remediation: Set android:allowBackup="false", or add dataExtractionRules (and legacy fullBackupContent) excluding pebbles_prefs and the supabase-kt settings file from cloud backup and device transfer; document the decision.

findings.title: No data export or portability entry point exists on Android, and the account email is not rectifiable
findings.detail: The Android settings surface offers deletion and partial rectification but nothing for Art. 15/20: there is no export control anywhere in the client, while the policy promises machine-readable portability - fulfillable only via an email request for which no operator runbook (identity verification, Art. 12(3) window) exists in the repo. The account email is displayed read-only with no change path on this surface, leaving a core personal field uneditable. As the schema grows every milestone (souls, collections, glyphs, connections, drafts, achievements), the absent export also has no mechanism to track breadth, so the gap compounds silently.
findings.evidence: grep -rin 'export' apps/android/app/src/main/kotlin returns only a comment in features/path/render/wobble/WobbleOutlineBuilder.kt:28; apps/android/app/src/main/kotlin/app/pbbls/android/features/profile/SettingsScreen.kt:301-316 (read-only email row); apps/web/docs/privacy/en.md:246-248 (portability promised); grep -rlin 'runbook|rights request' docs/ finds no DSR procedure (only Kritik criteria files and the Play deploy runbook)
findings.remediation: Build a schema-driven export (edge function walking user-owned tables plus media references) with an entry point in Android settings; add email change behind confirmation; write the out-of-band DSR operator runbook and version it in docs/.

findings.title: No data-export entry point exists on iOS (or anywhere), while the terms urge users to export regularly
findings.detail: Art. 15/20 access and portability have no workflow: the iOS settings surface offers deletion, rectification of some fields, and legal links, but no way to obtain a copy of the user's pebbles, cards, souls, snaps, or profile. No export endpoint exists server-side either, and the published terms explicitly tell users 'We strongly encourage regular export of your data (see Section 11)', promising a capability the product does not have. An access request today would be improvised manual database work with no documented operator procedure, against the Art. 12(3) one-month clock. Secondary gap: the email address is not rectifiable from iOS (read-only row).
findings.evidence: grep -i 'export' over apps/ios/Pebbles matches only WobbleOutlineBuilder/LossyLogArray internals; grep -rn 'export_account|data_export' over apps/web and packages/supabase: no hits; apps/web/docs/terms/en.md:309 (export encouragement); apps/ios/Pebbles/Features/Profile/Sheets/SettingsSheet.swift:264-271 (email read-only); grep -rli 'runbook' docs/ matches only the quality framework
findings.remediation: Build a schema-driven export RPC or edge function (JSON covering all user-owned tables plus signed media URLs), add an Export entry to iOS settings (and the other clients), and write the operator runbook for out-of-band requests including identity verification. Diff export coverage against the schema's user-owned tables in the purge harness so breadth cannot rot.

findings.title: No DPIA exists despite shipped features that enlarged special-category processing
findings.detail: Systematic recording of emotional states with intensity and valence is at minimum health-adjacent, and Art. 35(3)(b) makes large-scale special-category processing an explicit DPIA trigger. The 2026 milestones materially enlarged that processing: photo attachments, mutual connections, connection-visible 'private' pebbles, public share-by-link, and public profiles all shipped with no impact assessment on record anywhere in the repo. The signup consent copy also never names the sensitive nature of what will be collected; it is two generic document checkboxes. The engineering posture on iOS is genuinely careful (no telemetry SDKs, privacy-annotated logs), but the accountability artifact the regulation requires before such features ship simply does not exist.
findings.evidence: grep -rni 'dpia|impact assessment|art. 9|special categor' over docs/ and apps/web/docs matches only docs/quality framework files; feature enlargement: packages/supabase/supabase/migrations/20260426000001_pebbles_pictures.sql, 20260730070347_mutual_connections.sql, 20260817130000_pebble_visibility_grades.sql, 20260730120000_public_profiles.sql; consent copy: apps/ios/Pebbles/Features/Auth/AuthView.swift:74-85
findings.remediation: Write and date a DPIA against the current feature set (data inventory, risks, mitigations, household-exemption reasoning for souls), add explicit consent copy at signup naming the emotional data, and add a PR-checklist rule that migrations touching emotion/valence/intensity columns require a DPIA touch.

findings.title: The privacy policy iOS links to describes a different product generation than the one shipping
findings.detail: The policy iOS presents from signup and settings is frozen at version 1.0.0, 2026-04-09. It documents a therapist-sharing relationship and Google Gemma AI processing that do not exist in the codebase, and it predates and never mentions the features that do exist and change the privacy picture: photo attachments, mutual connections and blocks, connection-visible pebbles, public profiles with handles, and anonymous public share-by-link. Its claim 'We do not share your memories anywhere' is now conditionally false (the user can share, and the policy should explain the grades). A user consenting on this document is consenting to a materially different description of processing, which undermines the Art. 13 transparency duty and the quality of the consent the checkboxes capture.
findings.evidence: apps/web/docs/privacy/en.md:5-7 (version 1.0.0, last_updated 2026-04-09), section 2.1 (Therapist Relationship), 6.2/7.2 (Google Gemma transfers; grep -rn 'gemma' over apps/ and packages/: no code hits), line 21 ('We do not share your memories anywhere'); shipped features postdating it: migrations 20260426000001, 20260730070347, 20260730120000, 20260817130000; iOS links: apps/ios/Pebbles/Features/Auth/LegalDocumentSheet.swift:12-17
findings.remediation: Rewrite the policy against the current data model (remove Gemma and therapist sections, add snaps, connections, blocks, visibility grades, public profiles and share links, the WhatsApp community link), bump version and last_updated, and add a release-checklist rule tying schema or feature changes to a disclosure review.

findings.title: Systematic emotional-state recording has no DPIA, no Art.9 consent naming, and no sensitive-column annotation
findings.detail: pebbles.intensity/positiveness/emotion_id/description are stored as ordinary NOT NULL columns (20260411000001:56-60) with no sensitive-field inventory, column comments, or type wrapper distinguishing them from ordinary content, so the l4 automation (fail CI when an annotated field enters a log/analytics/export sink) is impossible to build. Large-scale processing of emotional/health-adjacent signals is an explicit Art.35(3)(b) DPIA trigger, yet no DPIA or Art.9 memo exists (grep -rni dpia/'art. 9'/'special category' docs/ finds only the quality framework), and the signup consent copy names no sensitive data (register/page.tsx:186-221). Failure scenario: a regulator requests the DPIA for the emotional-recording feature set and evidence that users gave explicit Art.9 consent naming the sensitive nature; neither exists, and there is no machine boundary preventing a future migration from piping these columns into a new sink. Mitigating today: operator analytics are aggregate and is_admin-gated and sensitive fields do not reach logs/third-party telemetry.
findings.evidence: 20260411000001_core_tables.sql:56-60; grep dpia/'art. 9' docs/ -> quality framework only; apps/web/app/register/page.tsx:186-221; v_analytics_user_averages_weekly aggregate 20260501000002:82-100
findings.remediation: Write and date a DPIA against the current feature set, add explicit-consent copy naming the emotional/health-adjacent data at signup/capture, and commit a machine-readable sensitive-column inventory (or column comments) so a CI grep can flag any log/analytics/export addition of an annotated field.

findings.title: No machine-readable data export/portability endpoint (Art.15/20) on any surface
findings.detail: Erasure and rectification are self-serve, but there is no export path: grep of migrations and edge functions for export_/data_export/takeout returns nothing, so a user cannot obtain a machine-readable copy of everything held about them, and export breadth cannot be diffed against the schema's user-owned tables (so it would silently rot as milestones add tables). Failure scenario: a user exercises the right to access/portability; the controller has no in-product workflow and must hand-assemble an export by ad-hoc SQL, missing tables like pebble_drafts, connections, achievement_unlocks, or media references, and cannot demonstrate completeness. Also no operator runbook for out-of-band Art.12(3) requests exists.
findings.evidence: grep export_/data_export/takeout over supabase/migrations and supabase/functions -> none; purge exists (20260729201326:40) but no export counterpart
findings.remediation: Build a schema-driven export RPC/edge function covering all user-owned tables plus media references so breadth cannot silently rot, expose an entry point on each client, and write the operator runbook for out-of-band rights requests.

findings.title: No code-derived processor inventory, DPA references, or committed region pinning
findings.detail: No processor inventory or DPA reference is committed (grep -rnil processor/DPA/subprocessor docs/ outside quality/ returns nothing), and region is not pinned in the repo: config.toml declares no region and disables network restrictions with allowed_cidrs 0.0.0.0/0. The processor chain (Supabase backend/storage, Vercel hosting, Apple/Google OAuth federation, Deno edge runtime) is derivable from code but nowhere mapped to a DPA, data category, or contracted region, so a post-Schrems II transfer of intimate data cannot be shown to ride a documented Chapter V mechanism. Failure scenario: a data-subject or regulator asks where the emotional-content data is processed and under what safeguards; the answer is not derivable from any committed artifact and no automated check would catch a new SDK or egress being added. Positive: edge functions add no unlisted egress (no external fetch).
findings.evidence: grep processor/DPA docs/ -> none; supabase/config.toml (no region key; network_restrictions allowed_cidrs 0.0.0.0/0); no fetch to external hosts in supabase/functions
findings.remediation: Write a processor inventory from a code-derived dependency/endpoint sweep with a DPA reference and region per processor, pin EU regions where the platforms offer it, and add a dependency-review check that flags new SDKs/endpoints for inventory classification.

findings.title: No data-export capability exists although the policy promises Art. 20 portability
findings.detail: The policy grants users the right to 'a copy of your data in a structured, commonly used, and machine-readable format', but no export entry point exists in web settings or profile, no export edge function exists, and there is no operator runbook for fulfilling an out-of-band request within the Art. 12(3) one-month window. A portability or access request today would require improvised manual database work by the sole operator, with no identity-verification procedure written down. Since the schema now spans pebbles, cards, souls, snaps, collections, connections, achievements, karma, and drafts, an accurate manual export is error-prone and likely incomplete.
findings.evidence: grep -ri 'export|download|portability' over apps/web/components/settings and components/profile: no data-export UI; packages/supabase/supabase/functions/ contains only _shared, backfill-pebble-render, compose-pebble, compose-pebble-update, delete-account; apps/web/docs/privacy/en.md:246-248 (the promise); grep 'runbook|subject access|rights request' docs/: nothing
findings.remediation: Ship an export edge function that walks the user-owned tables (diffable against the schema so new tables fail a check) plus a settings entry point; write a short versioned operator runbook covering identity verification and the one-month window.

findings.title: Consent records carry no document version and no re-consent trigger exists for policy changes
findings.detail: profiles stores bare terms_accepted_at/privacy_accepted_at timestamps with no column identifying which version of the terms or policy was accepted, while the legal documents carry a version (1.0.0) and are due a substantial rewrite the roadmap already schedules. When the rewritten policy ships, nothing can distinguish users who accepted the old text from the new, and no mechanism forces re-acceptance, so the product cannot demonstrate version-bound consent as Art. 7(1) accountability expects. The settings surface also offers no consent withdrawal short of full account deletion, contradicting the policy's 'withdraw at any time via your profile'.
findings.evidence: packages/supabase/supabase/migrations/20260411000001_core_tables.sql:26-27 (timestamptz only); apps/web/docs/privacy/en.md:5,128 (version + withdrawal claim); apps/web/app/settings/page.tsx:141-181 (no consent section); docs/superpowers/specs/2026-07-28-store-launch-roadmap.md:139 (re-consent surface still future)
findings.remediation: Add terms_version/privacy_version columns written at acceptance, a version constant shared by clients, a login-time gate that requests re-acceptance when the current version exceeds the stored one, and a withdrawal control in settings.

findings.title: Processor inventory omits Vercel and the OAuth identity providers while declaring an unimplemented US transfer
findings.detail: The policy's Art. 28 sub-processor list names only Supabase and Google Gemma. Vercel, which hosts and serves the entire web app (and admin) and therefore processes every visitor's IP and request metadata, is absent, as are Apple and Google in their live role as sign-in identity providers. Meanwhile Google Gemma, presented with a Chapter V Data Privacy Framework justification for US transfers, has no implementation anywhere in the code, so the declared transfer both misinforms users and obscures which transfers actually occur (Vercel's edge network is not EEA-pinned: apps/web/vercel.json pins no region). The inventory therefore fails to match code-derived reality in both directions.
findings.evidence: apps/web/docs/privacy/en.md:159-193 (inventory + transfers); root CLAUDE.md ('Web and admin deploy to Vercel'); apps/web/lib/data/useSupabaseAuth.ts:159-177 (Apple/Google OAuth live); grep -ri gemma over apps/ (non-docs) and packages/supabase/supabase/functions: zero; apps/web/vercel.json (schema key only, no regions)
findings.remediation: Add Vercel (with its DPA and region posture) and the OAuth providers to the inventory; remove or clearly future-mark Gemma; pin Vercel function regions to an EEA region via the regions key in vercel.json.

findings.title: No report intake queue exists in the admin while cross-user content is live without any in-product reporting mechanism
findings.detail: Cross-user content already ships: mutual connections expose profile data between users (migrations/20260730070347) and the glyph marketplace publishes user-created glyphs to everyone. The admin has a pre-publication moderation queue for glyphs, but there is no reporting pillar anywhere in the stack: no report table in any migration, no report UI on any client, and consequently no operator queue in the admin for abuse reports. Connected users who encounter an abusive display name or avatar have no in-product path to report it, and operators have no intake to respond from. The decisions log defers reporting to M56, so the gap is known but unshipped; until it lands, the UGC apparatus required by Apple 1.2 and Play's UGC policy is incomplete on every surface, and the admin lacks the respond-to-reports half of its operator role.
findings.evidence: rg -in 'create table.*report|content_report|user_report|report_' packages/supabase/supabase/migrations/ returns zero hits; rg -il 'report' over apps/web/components, apps/ios/Pebbles, apps/android/app/src yields only incidental matches (e.g. apps/web/components/settings/PublicProfileSection.tsx:72 is a comment); docs/decisions/log.md:356 ('revisit if abuse appears (M56 adds reporting)'); admin queue covers only glyph submissions (apps/admin/app/(authed)/pebblestore/glyphs/page.tsx:7-19)
findings.remediation: Stand up a content_reports table with an is_admin-gated listing RPC, add an admin queue page mirroring the glyph moderation pattern, and wire client report affordances into it; the client-side controls belong to the web/ios/android cells but the schema and operator queue are the admin-plus-supabase slice.

findings.title: Apple sign-in absent on Android while iOS and web offer it, breaking cross-surface provider parity
findings.detail: iOS ships native Sign in with Apple and the web app ships Apple OAuth, but Android offers only Google and email, recorded in code comments as a settled non-goal. A user who created their account with Apple on iPhone and switches to Android has no matching provider; with Apple's hide-my-email relay they must discover the password-reset path against a relay address to get in at all. This is the exact l1 anchor of the criterion (provider sets differ so an account created on one client cannot sign in on another). The production provider list and redirect allowlist also have no repo-tracked record (local config.toml has apple disabled; production is dashboard-only state).
findings.evidence: apps/android/app/src/main/kotlin/app/pbbls/android/components/GoogleSignInButton.kt:32 and features/welcome/WelcomeScreen.kt:52 ('No Apple sign-in on Android (settled non-goal)'); apps/web/lib/i18n/messages/en.json:425-437 (Sign in with Apple strings); apps/web/lib/types.ts:269 (providers include 'apple'); packages/supabase/supabase/config.toml:305-306 (apple enabled = false locally, prod untracked)
findings.remediation: Add Apple via Supabase hosted OAuth on Android (supabase-kt signInWith(Apple) through the existing pebbles://auth-callback PKCE flow, no native SDK needed), or record the account-portability escape hatch (password set flow) as the documented decision and track the prod provider list in the repo.

findings.title: No repo-tracked inventory backing the Play Data safety declarations
findings.detail: Nothing in the repository records what has been or will be declared in the Play Data safety form for app.pbbls.android: no inventory maps collected data types (emotional entries, photos with EXIF-derived dates, email, display name, connections) or the SDK list to declaration answers, and the Play deploy runbook does not mention the form. The app collects Art. 9-adjacent intimate data, so a wrong or stale Data safety answer at production submission is a policy violation with removal exposure, and with no repo record a future dependency addition (for example a crash reporter) would silently invalidate the declaration with nothing in review to catch it. Today the dependency set is provably tracker-free and the manifest holds a single INTERNET permission, so writing the inventory now is cheap and locks in the clean posture.
findings.evidence: rg -i 'data safety|play console|privacy' over docs/android-play-deploy.md and docs/ returns no declaration record; gradle/libs.versions.toml (no analytics/ad SDKs); apps/android/app/src/main/AndroidManifest.xml:5 (INTERNET only)
findings.remediation: Add a docs/store/play-data-safety.md (or section in the deploy runbook) enumerating collected data types, purposes, sharing (none), and the deletion URL, and add a PR-review rule that dependency or permission changes update it.

findings.title: Apple-SSO accounts created on iOS cannot sign in on Android (provider set parity broken)
findings.detail: iOS offers Sign in with Apple, Google, and email; the web offers Apple and Google; Android offers only Google and email - no Apple provider exists anywhere in the Android client. A user who creates their account with Apple on iOS (the flow Apple 4.8 pushes them toward) has no way to authenticate on Android, which the store-launch roadmap itself concedes ('iOS-created Apple accounts are locked out of Android today'). The identity-provider set being inconsistent across surfaces is exactly the l1 condition of this criterion; it turns the platform-equity feature on iOS into a cross-device lock-in bug. Additionally, the production provider list and redirect allowlist exist only in the Supabase dashboard (local config.toml has apple disabled), so there is no reviewable record to keep the surfaces honest.
findings.evidence: apps/ios/Pebbles/Features/Auth/AuthView.swift:106-110; grep 'Apple|apple' over apps/android/app/src/main/kotlin auth/service files = 0 hits; apps/web/lib/data/useSupabaseAuth.ts:162-173 (apple+google); docs/superpowers/specs/2026-07-28-store-launch-roadmap.md:149; packages/supabase/supabase/config.toml:305 (enabled = false, local only)
findings.remediation: Implement Apple sign-in in the Android client via supabase-kt (~100-150 LOC per the roadmap estimate) and commit a versioned doc of the production provider set and redirect allowlist next to the auth code.

findings.title: Apple-created accounts are stranded on Android: the provider set differs across surfaces and no password-recovery escape hatch exists on any client
findings.detail: Web and iOS offer Sign in with Apple; Android deliberately does not (recorded as a settled non-goal in the component doc comment). A user who signs up with Apple has no password on the shared auth backend, and no client implements a password reset or magic-link flow, so that account has zero authentication paths on Android. Because all four surfaces share one database and one auth backend, this is a contract asymmetry, not a client styling choice: the same identity is portable web to iOS but dead on Android. Failure scenario: an iPhone user who signed up with Apple (the most prominent option on iOS) moves to an Android phone or installs the Play build on a tablet; login offers only email+password (which they never set) and Google (a different identity that would create a second account), so they are locked out of their history and likely churn or create a duplicate account. The deliberate-non-goal decision never addressed the stranding consequence.
findings.evidence: apps/android/app/src/main/kotlin/app/pbbls/android/components/GoogleSignInButton.kt:32 ('No Apple sign-in on Android, settled non-goal'); apps/web/lib/data/useSupabaseAuth.ts:159-176 and apps/ios/Pebbles/Services/SupabaseService.swift:92-138 (Apple offered on web and iOS); grep 'resetPassword|recover|forgot' across apps/web, apps/ios, apps/android returned zero code hits (no recovery flow anywhere)
findings.remediation: Either add Apple sign-in on Android through Supabase's hosted OAuth flow (no native Apple SDK required, mirroring the iOS Google approach), or ship a password-recovery / magic-link flow on Android and web so an OAuth-only account can establish a password; record the chosen portability story in docs/decisions/log.md.

findings.title: No in-product content reporting mechanism exists on web pages that render other users' content to anonymous visitors
findings.detail: Shared pebbles (/p/[id], granted to anon), public profiles (/u/[handle]) and the community glyph market all show one user's content (photos, titles, display names, carved glyphs) to other people, but the product offers no report affordance anywhere on web; the only channel is the contact email inside the terms document. Blocking exists (server-backed) and glyphs are pre-moderated, but a visitor who encounters abusive content in a shared pebble or an offensive display name/handle on a public profile has no in-product way to flag it and no moderation queue exists to receive such flags. This is the l1 anchor of the criterion verbatim and, because the store apps mirror the same product surface, it is also the class of gap Apple 1.2 and Play UGC review reject; for the web property itself it is a notice-and-action gap for an EU-facing service.
findings.evidence: app/p/[id]/page.tsx:8-12 (anonymous access by construction); app/u/[handle]/page.tsx; rg -i 'report' over apps/web/components returns no report UI (only the block flow at components/connections/ConnectionRow.tsx:51); rg -i 'report' over packages/supabase/supabase/migrations matches only achievements/purge files, so no report table or RPC exists; contact email only at apps/web/docs/terms/en.md:454.
findings.remediation: Add a content_reports table plus a create_report RPC feeding the existing admin back-office, and surface a report control on SharedPebbleView, PublicProfileView, and glyph market cards on every client surface; wire the admin queue to the existing moderation patterns from admin_glyph_moderation.

findings.title: Session caches are neither purged on sign-out nor reloaded on sign-in, leaking one account's data into the next and starving fresh sign-ins
findings.detail: RootView's sign-out handler invalidates only SnapURLCache; ReferenceDataService (souls and collections, private user data), PathStatsService (karma, ripple, assiduity), and PebbleDraftsService.count all keep the previous account's data in memory. Because refs/palettes load exactly once per app lifetime from RootView's .task and both services latch on hasLoaded/didFinishLoading, a sign-out followed by a different account's sign-in on the same install shows the previous user's souls and collections inside the record flow and composer pickers and their karma in the stats bar until the process restarts. The inverse failure hits the common case: on a fresh install, refs.load() fires before any session exists, RLS returns empty souls/collections under the anon key, and after the user signs in the arrays are never refetched, so an existing user signing in on a new device gets empty soul and collection pickers until they relaunch or mutate their profile lists.
findings.evidence: apps/ios/Pebbles/RootView.swift:134-135 (one-shot .task { await palettes.load() } / { await refs.load() }, racing the auth restore started at :127-129), RootView.swift:161-166 (sign-out purge touches only snapURLs.invalidateAll()); apps/ios/Pebbles/Services/ReferenceDataService.swift:41-81 (no session-change hook, no reset API); apps/ios/Pebbles/Features/Path/Services/PathStatsService.swift:29-32 (hasLoaded latch makes load() a no-op forever after); consumers: Features/Record/Steps/RecordSoulsStep.swift:17, Features/Path/CreatePebbleSheet.swift:124-126.
findings.remediation: Key the session caches to the auth identity: on supabase.session?.user.id change, reset ReferenceDataService, PathStatsService, PebbleDraftsService, and ConnectionsService state and re-run load() for a non-nil user; alternatively add a reset() on each service and call it from the existing RootView onChange handlers.

findings.title: All 77 RLS policies evaluate auth.uid() bare, per row; none use the (select auth.uid()) initplan form the repo's own skill prescribes
findings.detail: Every policy in the schema, from the original core tables to the newest visibility-grade rewrite, uses bare auth.uid() in its USING/WITH CHECK predicate. On plans where the predicate cannot become an index condition (the OR-disjunct policies pebbles_select and glyphs_select, and the junction-table parent-join EXISTS policies applied as filters), the function is re-evaluated per candidate row and the EXISTS subqueries re-executed per row. pebbles_select is the worst case: since 20260817 it runs least/greatest(auth.uid(), ...) plus a connections EXISTS probe per non-owner row on the hottest table in the product. Supabase's performance advisor flags exactly this shape (auth_rls_initplan), and the repo vendored a best-practices skill that documents the wrapped form, yet zero policies apply it. The degradation hits all four clients simultaneously and only becomes visible once real data volume arrives, which is the most expensive moment to discover it.
findings.evidence: packages/supabase/supabase/migrations/20260411000001_core_tables.sql:155-290 (all core policies bare); 20260817130000_pebble_visibility_grades.sql:64-77 (pebbles_select OR-chain with per-row auth.uid() in least/greatest plus connections EXISTS); 20260630003348_glyph_marketplace.sql:70-105 (glyphs policies with two EXISTS probes per row); grep '(select auth.uid())' over migrations = 0 matches vs 157 bare occurrences; prescribed form present in-repo at .agents/skills/supabase-postgres-best-practices/references/security-rls-performance.md:25
findings.remediation: One corrective migration re-emitting every policy with (select auth.uid()) (and (select public.is_admin(auth.uid())) where applicable), verified by running the Supabase performance advisor against the linked project and committing the clean report; add the advisor run as a scripted harness so new bare occurrences are caught.

findings.title: Unindexed foreign keys and hot filter columns concentrate on the delete, edit, and purge paths, including the karma ledger scanned on every pebble edit and delete
findings.detail: karma_events.ref_id is filtered on every update_pebble (karma recompute) and delete_pebble call but has no index; karma_events is the append-only ledger, so this seq scan grows monotonically with product usage. collection_pebbles.pebble_id trails its composite PK, so every pebble deletion's cascade scans the whole table. Additional unindexed FK columns sit exactly where purge_account and the auth.users cascades read: snaps.user_id (also an RLS predicate column), pebble_souls.soul_id, glyph_entitlements.karma_event_id (FK-checked per deleted karma event during purge), connection_blocks.blocked_id, glyph_submissions.submitter_id and reviewed_by, and the per-glyph kept-predicate probes on pebbles.glyph_id and souls.glyph_id. purge_account, the GDPR erasure path, therefore degrades superlinearly with ledger and content size while running under the platform's default statement_timeout with no override, so a large account's erasure aborting on timeout is the plausible end state. The Supabase advisor's unindexed_foreign_keys check would flag most of these today; no advisor report or EXPLAIN artifact exists in the repo.
findings.evidence: ref_id filters: packages/supabase/supabase/migrations/20260411000003_rpc_functions.sql:336,368 and 20260729140000_media_quota_profile_lookup.sql:424; full index inventory: 20260411000001_core_tables.sql:296-305, 20260629192621_karma_events_type_axis.sql:28-31 (no ref_id index anywhere); collection_pebbles PK (collection_id, pebble_id) at 20260411000001:117-121 with cascade from pebbles:119; snaps.user_id policy at 20260411000001:217-224 with only pebble_id indexed (:304); glyph_entitlements.karma_event_id at 20260630003348:34; connection_blocks at 20260730070347:68-74; purge scans at 20260731090000_purge_account_union.sql:57-71,88-96,108,152-160
findings.remediation: Single migration adding: karma_events(ref_id), collection_pebbles(pebble_id), pebble_souls(soul_id), snaps(user_id), glyph_entitlements(karma_event_id), connection_blocks(blocked_id), glyph_submissions(submitter_id) and (reviewed_by), pebbles(glyph_id), souls(glyph_id). Then run the database advisor against the linked project and commit the clean unindexed_foreign_keys result as the baseline.

findings.title: The entire pebble history is fetched unbounded on every app open and re-fetched after every mutation
findings.detail: loadFromSupabase selects the user's full v_pebbles_full history with no limit, plus a second full-table fetch of render_svg/render_version for every pebble (each row carrying a complete inline SVG document), plus all souls, collections, junction rows and glyphs, and then batch-signs a URL for every snap the user has ever attached. This entire sequence re-runs after every single mutation: createPebble, updatePebble, deletePebble, deletePebbleMedia and buyGlyph all call loadFromSupabase() again. For a journaling product whose core loop is accumulating entries for years, payload size and signing-batch size grow without bound; a heavy user pays a multi-megabyte, multi-second reload for every pebble they record, and the /path LCP degrades linearly with account age. listConnectionSharedPebbles similarly reads a peer's full pebble list unbounded. The DB already demonstrates the alternative shape (wallet history is keyset-paginated with a tie-broken composite cursor), so the pattern is known but unapplied to the main store.
findings.evidence: apps/web/lib/data/supabase-provider.ts:113-126 (unbounded parallel loads), 160-179 (signs every original), 475, 511, 554, 775, 1038 (full reload per mutation), 661-666 (unbounded peer read); contrast keyset pagination at 399-426; grep: 41 .select( sites in lib/data, 4 with .limit
findings.remediation: Bound the store: paginate pebbles by keyset on (happened_at, id) with lazy week-window loading behind the existing week-roll UI, apply targeted store patches after mutations instead of full reloads (the mutation responses already return the affected row), and add a limit to listConnectionSharedPebbles. Coordinate with iOS/Android since they mirror the read shape.

findings.title: Composer snapshot is not user-scoped and survives sign-out and account deletion
findings.detail: ComposerSnapshotStore writes the in-progress pebble (name, free-text description, emotion, soul ids) under a single constant key in pebbles_prefs with no user id in the key or payload guard. Sign-out clears only the SDK session and the signed-URL cache (RootScreen), and the account-deletion path calls only the delete-account function plus signOut (SettingsScreen), so the snapshot persists. Failure scenario: user A drafts an intimate entry, the app is killed, A signs out (or deletes their account); user B signs in on the same device, opens the composer, and is offered A's draft verbatim via the crash-recovery resume path. It also means account erasure leaves personal content on the device after the user exercised deletion.
findings.evidence: apps/android/app/src/main/kotlin/app/pbbls/android/services/ComposerSnapshotStore.kt:32-36 (constant PREFS_NAME/KEY_SNAPSHOT, no user scoping), 46-55 (load with no owner check); RootScreen.kt:113-123 (sign-out path clears only snapUrls); features/profile/SettingsScreen.kt:196-207 (deleteAccount performs no local store clearing); PebbleDraftPayload.kt:30-49 (fields held)
findings.remediation: Clear the composer snapshot (and stage) when the session drops to null in RootScreen's userId effect, and additionally key the stored entry by user id so a foreign snapshot is never offered on resume; add a JVM test asserting the store is empty after the sign-out transition.

findings.title: Coil disk cache retains private snap photos past the signed-URL grant, sign-out, and account deletion
findings.detail: PebblesApp builds the singleton Coil ImageLoader with defaults: the disk cache is enabled in the app cache dir and entries are keyed by the full signed URL. Two consequences. First, cached JPEG bytes of private pebble photos remain readable locally after the 1h signed-URL TTL expires, after sign-out, and after account deletion; only LRU size pressure ever evicts them (the deliberate SnapURLCache flush on sign-out clears URLs, not image bytes). Second, because the signing token changes on each re-sign, the same object accumulates duplicate cache entries, extending residue lifetime. Failure scenario: a user signs out or deletes their account on a shared or later-inspected device; the photos attached to their emotional records are still present in the app's image_cache directory. This directly contradicts the criterion's cache-no-longer-than-grant contract that the URL-level cache otherwise implements carefully.
findings.evidence: apps/android/app/src/main/kotlin/app/pbbls/android/PebblesApp.kt:134-139 (default loader, no diskCache policy, no cache keying override); grep for diskCache|memoryCache|CachePolicy in app/src/main returns nothing; RootScreen.kt:120-122 (sign-out clears only SnapURLCache); SnapURLCache.kt:93-95 (invalidateAll touches URL entries only)
findings.remediation: Set an explicit Coil cache key (memoryCacheKey/diskCacheKey) to the object storage path so entries deduplicate and can be addressed, and clear imageLoader.diskCache and memoryCache alongside snapUrls.invalidateAll() when the session drops to null; document the residue window.

findings.title: Recents snapshot shows emotional content verbatim and no app lock exists
findings.detail: No shielding treatment exists anywhere on the surface: no FLAG_SECURE, no setRecentsScreenshotEnabled(false), and no resign-to-background redaction overlay, so the app switcher shows the last-viewed screen (a pebble's emotion, intensity, free text, attached photo) to anyone handling the device. There is also no optional biometric or passcode app lock, so a handed-over or shared device opens straight into the journal. For a mental-state journaling app these are the two ambient exposure paths RLS and TLS cannot touch, and MASVS-PLATFORM-3 treats them as a distinct control class. Failure scenario: a user lends their unlocked phone; the borrower swipes into recents or taps the app icon and reads the last entry with zero effort.
findings.evidence: grep for FLAG_SECURE|setRecentsScreenshotEnabled|BiometricPrompt|biometric across apps/android/app/src/main returns nothing (verified in this audit); MainActivity.kt:41-97 configures no window flags; no lock-related setting exists in features/profile/SettingsScreen.kt
findings.remediation: Add FLAG_SECURE (or a lifecycle-driven redaction overlay if screenshots should stay allowed) on the activity while entry content is visible, ship an optional BiometricPrompt app lock with an auto-lock timeout, and record the notification-copy invariant now so the first notification feature inherits it; mirror all three on iOS per the 1:1 rule.

findings.title: No PrivacyInfo.xcprivacy privacy manifest despite required-reason API use, and no recorded egress inventory
findings.detail: Neither the app target nor the widget target ships a privacy manifest, while the app uses UserDefaults through @AppStorage - a required-reason API for which Apple has enforced declarations at App Store submission since May 2024. A submission can be rejected or flagged (ITMS-91053) until the manifest exists, and the app's nutrition-label/data-collection story has no committed source of truth to check against. Separately, no written third-party egress inventory exists for the surface: the actual egress set is admirably small (Supabase backend, own web host, a WhatsApp invite link opened externally on tap, bundled fonts), but nothing records or enforces that state, so a new SDK or remote asset would land unreviewed.
findings.evidence: find /home/user/pbbls/apps/ios -iname '*.xcprivacy' returns nothing; required-reason API use at apps/ios/Pebbles/RootView.swift:25 (@AppStorage -> UserDefaults); egress set from grep -rhoE 'https://...' over app source: chat.whatsapp.com link at apps/ios/Pebbles/Features/Lab/LabConfig.swift:8, own-host links only otherwise; fonts bundled per apps/ios/Pebbles/Resources/Info.plist:44-49; no inventory doc under docs/ (grep -rliE 'inventory|PII|data map')
findings.remediation: Add PrivacyInfo.xcprivacy to both targets declaring the UserDefaults required-reason category (CA92.1) and the app's collected-data types; commit a short egress inventory (host, purpose, data carried) and reference it from the iOS CLAUDE.md so dependency changes re-review it.

findings.title: No PII inventory / ROPA exists in the repo, so no personal-data field is traceable to a documented purpose
findings.detail: There is no data inventory, ROPA, or personal-data map anywhere in docs/. The schema accumulates intimate personal-data columns (pebbles.name/description free text, emotion + positiveness/intensity valence, snaps.storage_path media pointers, happened_at timestamps of intimate events, souls names of third parties, connection graph) with no per-field purpose record, and new personal-data columns land in migrations without a stated purpose marker. Per the PRV-01 checklist this caps the criterion at level 1 outright. The consequence is not a live exploit but a compliance-accountability and minimization-review gap: no one can mechanically answer 'what personal data do we hold, why, and where does it flow', which is the precondition for the GDP domain's Art.9 special-category posture (this product records emotional state, a special category).
findings.evidence: grep over docs/ for 'inventory','PII','personal data','ROPA','data map' finds only incidental mentions in feature plans/specs, no inventory document; personal-data columns enumerable from packages/supabase/types/database.ts and 20260411000001_core_tables.sql:20-99 carry no purpose annotation.
findings.remediation: Author a committed data inventory / ROPA (docs/) mapping each personal-data column and each cross-surface payload to a purpose and lawful basis, flag the special-category fields (emotion/valence), and add a review step (or a CI diff of generated database types against the inventory) so new personal-data columns must be listed with a purpose in the same change.

findings.title: Intimate composer draft (pebble name + free-text description) is written to localStorage and never cleared on sign-out
findings.detail: useComposerAutosave persists the whole draft payload — pebble name, free-text description, emotion, souls, domains — to localStorage under `pbbls-composer-draft`, and usePendingInvite stores an invite token under `pbbls-pending-invite`. On sign-out the app resets React state only; the SIGNED_OUT handler and the logout helper clear no localStorage, so on a shared, borrowed, or public browser the next person can read the previous user's unsaved journal draft straight from DevTools or a script on the origin. This is special-category-adjacent content (emotional state, named third parties) sitting in the most exposed client store. The draft is cleared on publish/server-save by design, but not on the identity boundary (sign-out), which is where the exposure matters.
findings.evidence: apps/web/lib/hooks/useComposerAutosave.ts:6,89,101; apps/web/components/record/draft-payload.ts:16-29,60-84; apps/web/lib/hooks/usePendingInvite.ts:5,62; sign-out path apps/web/lib/data/useSupabaseAuth.ts:81-87,179-184 (no store clear)
findings.remediation: Add a single clear-all-local-stores routine that removes pbbls-composer-draft, pbbls-pending-invite, and any other content keys, and invoke it from both the SIGNED_OUT branch of onAuthStateChange and from deleteAccount. Add a test asserting localStorage holds only convenience keys (theme/locale/haptics) after sign-out.

findings.title: Admin production failures reach no monitored destination
findings.detail: Every failure path in the surface ends at console.error: 51 call sites across 24 files terminate in Vercel function logs (server components and actions) or in the admin's own browser console (client components like CoverImageInput). There is no error-reporting SDK, no log drain, no alert rule, and no documented routine for checking hosting logs. Because the admin is also the moderation and publishing surface, a persistent failure (e.g. the moderation queue RPC failing after a migration, or createLog failing) manifests only as the admin noticing odd UI, and there is no signal at all for failures the admin does not personally trigger. The same gap means the crash-page failures from the missing error.tsx finding are invisible after the fact.
findings.evidence: apps/admin/package.json:11-38 (no sentry/bugsnag/datadog/etc.; repo-wide grep confirms only 'scrollbar' false positives); grep count: 51 console.error sites in apps/admin; no vercel.json for admin (ls: No such file or directory); grep for 'log drain', 'triage', 'error monitor', 'observability' in docs/ and apps/admin: no relevant hits; no alerting config in .github/workflows (android-release.yml, android.yml, arkaik.yml, lab-note-reminder.yml, lab-note.yml only).
findings.remediation: Add a lightweight error-reporting integration (e.g. Sentry for Next.js with beforeSend scrubbing) or at minimum a Vercel log drain plus a documented weekly check routine; wire server-action failures through one shared reporting helper instead of bare console.error.

findings.title: Edge-function and database failures terminate in unmonitored Supabase logs with no alerting, including failures of the account-erasure path
findings.detail: All four edge functions handle errors correctly and log labeled context, but the destination is the Supabase function-log dashboard, which no document, routine, or alert rule connects to a human. A sustained run of delete-account 500s (storage outage mid-sweep, purge exception) would go unnoticed until a user complains, and failed erasure carries legal exposure with deadlines. Compose failures are designed as soft-success (pebble exists, render null) with backfill-renders.ts as the recovery tool, but nothing surfaces the failure rate that would prompt anyone to run it, so text-only pebbles can accumulate silently. No error-reporting SDK, log drain, or alert configuration exists anywhere in the repo, and the admin surface reads product logs (changelog), not error logs.
findings.evidence: Terminal console.error handlers: packages/supabase/supabase/functions/delete-account/index.ts:54,65,87,97; compose-pebble/index.ts:45,60,71; compose-pebble-update/index.ts:51,67,78; backfill-pebble-render/index.ts:32,48,61; soft-success contract at compose-pebble/index.ts:70-81; zero SDK hits: grep sentry|crashlytics|bugsnag|posthog|datadog|rollbar over all dependency manifests; no alert or triage statement in docs/ (grep 'alert' in docs/decisions/log.md returns unrelated UI text)
findings.remediation: Pick one destination (Supabase log drain to a watched channel, or a Sentry project wired into the four functions) with PII scrubbing configured before first deploy; add an error-rate alert for delete-account and compose-pebble; document who triages and on what cadence; fire one deliberate test error per function to prove the loop closes.

findings.title: Anonymously served UGC (public pebbles, public profiles) has no moderation state and no admin takedown tooling
findings.detail: get_shared_pebble serves user-authored name, description, and render_svg to anonymous callers filtered only on visibility='public'; get_public_profile serves display_name, handle, and the owner's arbitrary self-drawn avatar glyph geometry to anon. Neither content type carries a moderation status column, there is no report intake anywhere in the schema or clients, and the admin app has no route or RPC for pebbles or profiles, so removing an abusive public pebble, profile, or avatar today is manual SQL under time pressure. The glyph moderation pipeline covers only marketplace submissions, not the avatar path: a user can carve any image as a glyph, set it as their profile avatar, flip public_profile, and it is served to the open web with no review state and no operator kill switch. This is also the enforcement depth Apple's UGC guideline (1.2) expects behind the report control.
findings.evidence: packages/supabase/supabase/migrations/20260817130000_pebble_visibility_grades.sql:99-131 (get_shared_pebble, anon grant at :131); 20260730120000_public_profiles.sql:197-282 (get_public_profile projects glyph strokes at :245-249, anon grant at :285); admin route inventory (apps/admin/app/(authed)/: logs, analytics, pebblestore/glyphs, achievements, domains, emotions only); grep -rniE 'report(ed|ing)?[_ ](content|user|abuse)|report_' across migrations and clients returns zero hits
findings.remediation: Add a moderation status (or at minimum an admin-settable hidden flag) checked inside get_shared_pebble, get_public_profile, and pebbles_select; add is_admin RPCs to hide a pebble, unpublish a profile, and clear an avatar; surface them in an admin queue; wire a report intake table so user reports become operator-actionable rows.

findings.title: The emotion_first achievement family conditions rewards on the emotion column and Android celebrates each first-time emotional disclosure
findings.detail: The achievement catalog generates one badge per emotion, granted when a pebble with that emotion_id first exists for the user, with an optional karma reward per badge - an engagement mechanic keyed directly on emotional content and disclosure breadth, the exact boundary SAF-02 draws. The Android client completes the loop: it fires check_achievements after mutations and presents a chained full-screen 'Achievement unlocked - First [emotion]' celebration, and the edit screen is even documented as qualifying emotion_first badges. The incentive structure nudges users to record across the full emotional palette (including negative states) to complete a badge collection in an intimate journal. The root lives in the shared schema (contract territory), but the surface's celebration presentation and RPC firing are Android code.
findings.evidence: packages/supabase/supabase/migrations/20260730090000_achievements.sql:112-117 (per-emotion catalog rows), :219-221 (grant when p.emotion_id = a.emotion_id); apps/android/app/src/main/kotlin/app/pbbls/android/features/shared/achievements/AchievementCopy.kt:41,59 with res/values/strings.xml:485-486 ('First %1$s' / 'Record your first pebble carrying %1$s'); features/karma/AchievementNotificationService.kt:26-37 (mutation-path celebration); features/path/EditPebbleScreen.kt:202 (comment: qualifying an emotion_first badge); no written decoupling rule found in docs/ or CLAUDE.md files
findings.remediation: Retire the emotion_first family (is_active = false keeps existing unlocks per the design) or rekey it to neutral activity; state the reward/emotion decoupling rule in the decision log and encode it as a check that fails when a grant condition references emotion/valence/intensity columns.

findings.title: Display names and public/shared pebble text are served cross-user and anonymously with no moderation state and no report or takedown path
findings.detail: Only glyphs have a moderation state machine. display_name is free text projected to connections (get_connections 20260730070347:349) and anonymously on public profiles (get_public_profile 20260730120000:243), and public pebble name+description are served to anonymous visitors via get_shared_pebble (20260817130000:107-109) and to connections via v_pebbles_full, all with no status/review column and no server-side gating on a moderation state. No report queue or takedown RPC exists for these types (no reports table; grep confirms). Failure scenario: a user sets display_name to a slur or an impersonation of a real person and enables a public profile, or writes abusive text in a pebble shared by public link; another user or operator has no in-schema way to flag it, and an operator can only remove it by manual SQL, so a DSA notice-and-action or store UGC-moderation obligation cannot be met for the majority of cross-user content.
findings.evidence: 20260730070347_mutual_connections.sql:347-362; 20260730120000_public_profiles.sql:242-281; 20260817130000_pebble_visibility_grades.sql:106-128; no reports/moderation_queue table (grep)
findings.remediation: Add a moderation status to cross-user-served content (display_name, publicly shared pebble text) with server-side status-gated serving, a report table feeding an operator queue, and admin-checked security-definer takedown RPCs that write an audit row; encode the reachability rule as a DB harness.

findings.title: Block oracle: preview returns 'valid' while accept returns 'expired', letting a blocked user confirm the block
findings.detail: The mutual-connections design documents an accepted residual (20260730070347:228-233): preview_connection_invite is block-unaware and returns status 'valid', while accept_connection_invite masks a block as 'invite_expired'. A signed-in blocked peer who previews an invite (valid) and then accepts (expired) can distinguish this from a genuinely expired invite (which previews as 'expired' too), inferring that they were specifically blocked. The rationale for this criterion stresses that in an intimate-journal product the abuser may be a named person in the victim's entries, so a block oracle that confirms the block to the abuser is a real escalation risk for users leaving abusive relationships. Failure scenario: an abuser holding the victim's old multi-use invite token probes preview+accept, receives valid-then-expired, and confirms the victim blocked them, prompting retaliation.
findings.evidence: 20260730070347_mutual_connections.sql:228-233 (accepted-residual comment), 168-198 (preview valid path), 218-240 (accept expired masking)
findings.remediation: Make preview_connection_invite block-aware for authenticated callers so a blocked caller receives the same dark shape as an expired invite, normalizing the preview/accept pair so a block cannot be inferred; add a block-matrix contract harness covering both directions and all read/contact paths.

findings.title: Publicly served pebbles and profile names have no moderation state, no report path, and no takedown tooling
findings.detail: get_shared_pebble serves a pebble's user-authored name and description to anonymous visitors, and get_public_profile serves display names and user-drawn glyph geometry to anyone, with no moderation status column and no status filter in either body. There is no report control anywhere on the web surface, so abusive public content (harassment in a shared pebble's text, an offensive display name or avatar drawing) has no user-initiated path into review, and an operator takedown would be manual SQL because admin RPCs exist only for glyph marketplace submissions. As the public surface grows this leaves the product unable to demonstrate any takedown capability for its most visible UGC.
findings.evidence: packages/supabase/supabase/migrations/20260817130000_pebble_visibility_grades.sql:99-128 (no status filter); 20260730120000_public_profiles.sql:197-284 (same); pebbles table has no moderation column (20260411000001:51-64); grep 'report' over apps/web/components: no report UI; admin moderation RPCs cover only glyph_submissions (20260630084718)
findings.remediation: Add a moderation status column to pebbles/profiles (or a takedown flag checked inside the public projections), a minimal report RPC + table feeding the existing admin surface, and takedown RPCs that flip the flag and reach storage; mirror report entry points on all clients.

findings.title: A block does not sever the blocked user's authenticated access to the blocker's public content, and the invite flow leaks a block oracle
findings.detail: Blocks are enforced on connection and invite paths, but the pebbles_select 'public' branch and get_public_profile contain no block predicate, so a blocked harasser who is logged in retains full, first-class read access to the victim's public pebbles and public profile including the assiduity grid (a 28-day activity pattern), enabling continued monitoring after the victim blocked them. Anonymous access makes perfect severance impossible, but the authenticated paths could and do not check. Additionally the migration documents an accepted block oracle: preview_connection_invite stays 'valid' while accept returns invite_expired, letting a blocked peer confirm the block by comparing the two. No test or harness covers any block behavior, so regressions in the paths that do check would go unnoticed.
findings.evidence: packages/supabase/supabase/migrations/20260817130000_pebble_visibility_grades.sql:64-77 (no block predicate in the public branch); 20260730120000_public_profiles.sql:197-284 (none); 20260730070347_mutual_connections.sql:226-233 (documented 'accepted residual' oracle); grep connection_blocks over packages/supabase/scripts: only the purge script
findings.remediation: Add a both-directions connection_blocks predicate to the authenticated branches of pebbles_select and get_public_profile (anon stays as-is); make preview block-aware for authenticated callers; add a block-matrix section to the verify-harness family.

findings.title: Achievement grants key on the chosen emotion and karma pays per unit of emotional disclosure
findings.detail: The emotion_first achievement family creates one badge per emotion in the catalog, granted when the user has recorded a pebble with that emotion_id. This is a grant condition referencing an emotion column and a collect-them-all incentive to record every emotion, including grief, shame, and despair, at least once for completeness. Separately, the karma formula pays +1 for a description, +1 per reflective card (the CBT-style free text), +1 for attaching people, and +1 for a photo, i.e. the reward scales with the volume of sensitive disclosure rather than with mere use. Both violate the criterion's boundary that no reward is conditioned on emotion choice or disclosure volume of sensitive fields, and no written rule stating that boundary exists in the repo. The rest of the mechanics (anti-streak copy, silent bounce decay, spend-only wallet, penalty-free exits) are genuinely well designed.
findings.evidence: packages/supabase/supabase/migrations/20260730090000_achievements.sql:112-117 and 219-221 (emotion_first generation and grant predicate on p.emotion_id); apps/web/lib/data/karma.ts:25-35 and 20260817130000:318-329 (disclosure-volume formula); no decoupling rule in docs/decisions/log.md (searched valence/emotion x reward/karma)
findings.remediation: Retire the emotion_first family (is_active=false, the schema's designed retirement path) or regenerate it on non-emotional axes; flatten karma to activity-based (base + capped enrichment count not tied to reflective text); write the decoupling rule into the decision log so future mechanics inherit it.

findings.title: No dependency vulnerability monitoring for the admin workspace (or any workspace)
findings.detail: The repo has no .github/dependabot.yml, no renovate config, and no CI job running npm audit or osv-scanner on any schedule. The admin app carries a substantial npm surface (next 16, react 19, @supabase/ssr, @uiw/react-md-editor, recharts, sonner and their transitive graphs) and is an authenticated operator tool, so a known-vulnerable transitive dependency would sit unnoticed until manually discovered. Lockfile pinning exists, which prevents drift but also freezes vulnerable versions in place indefinitely. Updates are demonstrably ad hoc (no bot PRs exist). Org-level GitHub alerting may exist but is not observable or enforced from the repo.
findings.evidence: ls .github/dependabot.yml -> absent; no renovate.json at root or .github/; grep of all four workflows (.github/workflows/android-release.yml, android.yml, arkaik.yml, lab-note-reminder.yml) for audit/osv/scanner returns nothing; apps/admin/package.json dependency list
findings.remediation: Commit a dependabot.yml covering npm (root workspaces), gradle, and swift, or a scheduled workflow running npm audit --audit-level=high / osv-scanner; triage cadence at milestone boundaries.

findings.title: No vulnerability monitoring or lockfile coverage for the Android dependency tree
findings.detail: The Android workspace has no Gradle dependency lockfiles and no dependency-verification metadata; the version catalog pins direct versions but nothing records or verifies resolved artifacts. No dependabot.yml, renovate config, or scheduled audit/osv-scanner job exists anywhere in .github, so a disclosed CVE in the network-facing stack (supabase-kt 3.1.4, Ktor 3.1.2, OkHttp via ktor-client-okhttp, Coil 3.3.0, AndroidSVG 1.4) would be discovered only by accident. For a client that ships session tokens and intimate content through these libraries, unmonitored known-vulnerable dependencies are the standing risk; the absence of process, not a current bug, is the finding. The wrapper checksum validation in CI is the only supply-chain gate present.
findings.evidence: apps/android: no gradle.lockfile or app/gradle.lockfile, no gradle/verification-metadata.xml (checked); .github/workflows contains only android.yml, android-release.yml, arkaik.yml, lab-note-reminder.yml with no audit job; no .github/dependabot.yml or renovate.json (checked); gradle/libs.versions.toml:24-39 (pinned network stack versions)
findings.remediation: Enable dependabot (gradle + github-actions + npm ecosystems) or renovate at the repo root, and enable Gradle dependency verification or lockfiles for the app module so resolved artifacts are recorded and drift is reviewable; optionally add an osv-scanner scheduled job that fails on high-severity findings.

findings.title: RLS/purge/cross-user verification harnesses exist but none run in CI, so no policy or purge regression is mechanically caught
findings.detail: The crown-jewel invariants of this surface are all proven only by harnesses that must be run by hand against the linked project: verify-account-purge.ts (zero rows + empty storage prefix after deletion), verify-pebble-visibility.ts (owner/connection/stranger/anon read matrix + owner-only writes), verify-public-profile.ts (exact cross-user key allowlist), verify-pebble-drafts.ts. baseline.md and the .github/workflows/ listing (android.yml, android-release.yml, arkaik.yml, lab-note-reminder.yml) show NO workflow runs any of these, and the packages/supabase lint script is a placeholder that exits 0 without checking anything. Failure scenario: a future migration adds a user-owned table and forgets the purge entry, or widens an RLS policy / a cross-user projection, or re-introduces the v_pebbles_full definer-view class — nothing fails the pipeline, because rowsecurity=true is never asserted in CI, the FK-vs-purge table set is never diffed mechanically, and the field-set harnesses are not gated. This is what holds SEC-02, SEC-03, PRV-07 and PRV-08 at level 3 instead of 4, and it is the exact mechanism by which the is_admin self-escalation (separate finding) went unnoticed. The primary defect belongs to Testing/CI, but it materially weakens the RLS default-deny guarantee here because 'a new unprotected table fails the pipeline' is the l4 promise and it does not hold.
findings.evidence: docs/quality/audits/2026-08/baseline.md (supabase lint = placeholder exits 0; no supabase test task); .github/workflows/ contains no job invoking packages/supabase/scripts/verify-*.ts (grep over .github returned nothing); harnesses at packages/supabase/scripts/verify-account-purge.ts, verify-pebble-visibility.ts, verify-public-profile.ts run against the REMOTE project via env vars only.
findings.remediation: Add a scheduled or PR CI job (against a disposable linked project or `supabase db start` ephemeral instance) that runs the four verify-*.ts harnesses plus a pg_tables assertion (rowsecurity=true for all public application tables) and an information_schema check that every table with a user-id FK appears in purge_account. Fail the build on any violation; this converts the existing manual proofs into the drift detection the framework's level-4 anchors require.

findings.title: Zero automated tests on the admin surface; 150-line hand-rolled YAML parser and 200-line SVG path math run unverified
findings.detail: The surface has no test files, no test script, and no framework, so every core path (log CRUD and publishing state machine, glyph moderation actions, achievements management) is verified only by lint, build, and manual checklists. The riskiest untested modules are pure logic with real edge-case density: lib/logs/parse-lab-note.ts (149 lines of custom YAML parsing with indent tracking, section state, and enum dropping) and lib/pebblestore/path.ts plus svg-to-strokes.ts plus transform-path.ts (SVG path tokenizing, relative-to-absolute normalization, affine transforms) whose output is baked into stored glyph geometry that web, iOS, and Android then render. A regression in the parser silently drops prefill fields (e.g. the FR title), producing a published Lab entry missing a language; a regression in the path math publishes corrupted market geometry. Both classes of module are trivially unit-testable today (no IO, no framework coupling), and the sibling web surface already runs 125 Vitest tests, so the pattern exists in-repo.
findings.evidence: find apps/admin -name '*.test.*' returns nothing; apps/admin/package.json:5-9 has no test script; lib/logs/parse-lab-note.ts:61-149 (parser logic); lib/pebblestore/path.ts:29+ (parsePath), lib/pebblestore/svg-to-strokes.ts, lib/pebblestore/transform-path.ts; docs/superpowers/specs/2026-06-30-issue-497-admin-glyph-moderation-design.md:279 ('No admin test runner (V1)')
findings.remediation: Add Vitest to apps/admin mirroring apps/web's setup, start with the pure modules (parse-lab-note, path/svg-to-strokes/transform-path, analytics date helpers, logs options guards), and wire the suite into the same CI job as the lint gate.

findings.title: Android emits seconds-less happened_at strings that iOS cannot parse, silently resetting cross-surface draft dates
findings.detail: OffsetDateTimeSerializer.serialize emits value.toString(), and Java's OffsetDateTime.toString() omits the seconds field entirely when second == 0 and nano == 0. WhenDateTime.combine builds happenedAt via date.atTime(hour, minute), so every pebble whose 'when' was set through the picker carries second 0 and serializes as e.g. '2026-07-30T01:23+02:00'. When that string lands in the shared pebble_drafts.payload jsonb and the draft is resumed on iOS, ISO8601Flexible.parse tries only the fractional and whole-second ISO8601DateFormatter forms, both of which require HH:mm:ss, returns nil, and iOS hydration silently falls back to 'now', which is exactly the #651 failure mode the standing CLAUDE.md rule ('emit at the narrowest precision every reader accepts, whole seconds') exists to prevent. The emit-side test knowingly avoids pinning the wire form (PebblePayloadTest comment: 'toString() trims :00 seconds'), so nothing detects this. The publish path to Postgres is unaffected (timestamptz accepts the form) and web's new Date() parses it, so the blast radius is Android-written drafts resumed on iOS, where the pebble's date is silently replaced and then lost on publish.
findings.evidence: apps/android/app/src/main/kotlin/app/pbbls/android/features/path/models/OffsetDateTimeSerializer.kt:25-30; apps/android/app/src/main/kotlin/app/pbbls/android/features/path/create/WhenDateTime.kt:29-37; apps/android/app/src/test/kotlin/app/pbbls/android/features/path/models/PebblePayloadTest.kt:115-120; apps/ios/Pebbles/Features/Path/Models/ISO8601Flexible.swift:27-48; apps/ios/Pebbles/Features/Path/Models/PebbleDraftPayload.swift:92-93; root CLAUDE.md 'Standing cross-surface rules' (timestamps bullet)
findings.remediation: In OffsetDateTimeSerializer.serialize, format with an explicit whole-second pattern (e.g. value.truncatedTo(ChronoUnit.SECONDS).format(DateTimeFormatter.ofPattern("uuuu-MM-dd'T'HH:mm:ssXXX"))) so seconds are always present and sub-second precision is dropped, then pin the emitted wire string as a literal in PebblePayloadTest and PebbleDraftPayloadTest (including a second==0 case). Optionally harden iOS ISO8601Flexible with a seconds-less fallback as defense in depth.

findings.title: Android CI is not a required check, never runs on shared-contract changes, and Play publishing is not gated on tests
findings.detail: Three gate holes compound. First, main has no required status checks (the branch ruleset carries only deletion and non-fast-forward rules), so a PR whose android.yml run is red, or a direct push to main, merges anyway; the conventional-commit discipline observed in history is convention, not enforcement. Second, android.yml's paths filter covers only apps/android/** and the workflow file, not packages/supabase/**, so a migration that changes an RPC or view contract Android consumes (path_pebbles, get_connections, buy_glyph, v_glyph_market, compose-pebble payloads) merges with zero Android checks executed, green by absence. Third, android-release.yml builds and publishes a signed AAB to the Play internal track on every push to main and on any PR labelled deploy-beta, running only bundleRelease with no dependency on the test job, so a commit whose unit tests fail (or never ran) still auto-ships to the maintainer's device.
