Today the exposure is bounded by the internal-testing-only track and a single-maintainer review culture, but nothing structural prevents a broken build from reaching the release channel.
findings.evidence: .github/workflows/android.yml (on.pull_request.paths: 'apps/android/**', '.github/workflows/android.yml'); .github/workflows/android-release.yml (on.push branches main, pull_request types labeled/synchronize, job runs only ./gradlew bundleRelease then publishes via r0adkll/upload-google-play); GET https://api.github.com/repos/alexisbohns/pbbls/rules/branches/main returning only deletion and non_fast_forward; GET .../branches/main showing required_status_checks enforcement_level 'off', contexts []
findings.remediation: Add a ruleset on main requiring the android.yml job (and each sibling surface's job) as a required status check and requiring PRs; add 'packages/supabase/**' to android.yml's pull_request paths; make android-release.yml's publish depend on the test job (needs: or workflow_run gating on android.yml success for the same SHA).

findings.title: Android emits timestamps via OffsetDateTime.toString(), producing seconds-less ISO strings that iOS silently drops on draft resume
findings.detail: The standing cross-surface rule (CLAUDE.md; decision 2026-07-30 #651) requires timestamps crossing a surface boundary to be emitted at whole-second precision, never left to an ambient strategy. Android's shared OffsetDateTimeSerializer serializes with value.toString(), which passes through whatever precision the value carries and, when seconds and nanos are zero, omits the seconds field entirely (e.g. 2026-08-26T14:23+02:00). Every picker-set date on Android is built as date.atTime(hour, minute) (seconds=0, nanos=0), so any draft whose 'when' the user adjusted stores a minute-precision happened_at in pebble_drafts.payload. iOS's ISO8601Flexible accepts only fractional or whole-second forms (both ISO8601DateFormatter variants require seconds), so an Android-written draft resumed on iOS decodes happened_at to nil and hydration silently falls back to 'now' — breaking the drafts design's 'restored verbatim' rule (D6) and corrupting the recorded moment, the core datum of the product. The Android test suite even documents the hazard ('toString() trims :00 seconds', PebblePayloadTest.kt:118) but works around it with a same-surface OffsetDateTime.parse round-trip, the exact oracle shape decision #651 identified as structurally blind. Postgres and web tolerate the form, so the break is invisible everywhere except the Android→iOS resume path.
findings.evidence: apps/android/app/src/main/kotlin/app/pbbls/android/features/path/models/OffsetDateTimeSerializer.kt:29 (encodeString(value.toString())); apps/android/app/src/main/kotlin/app/pbbls/android/features/path/create/WhenDateTime.kt:36 (date.atTime(hour, minute) — seconds/nanos zero); apps/android/app/src/main/kotlin/app/pbbls/android/features/path/models/PebbleDraftPayload.kt:32-34 (draft happened_at uses this serializer); apps/android/app/src/test/kotlin/app/pbbls/android/features/path/models/PebblePayloadTest.kt:118 ('toString() trims :00 seconds'); apps/ios/Pebbles/Features/Path/Models/ISO8601Flexible.swift:27-43 (fractional-then-whole-second only; neither accepts a seconds-less time); apps/ios/Pebbles/Features/Path/Models/PebbleDraftPayload.swift:88-93 + 203 (nil happenedAt falls back to defaults 'now')
findings.remediation: Give OffsetDateTimeSerializer.serialize a deliberate emission: truncate to whole seconds and format ISO-8601 with seconds always present (e.g. value.truncatedTo(ChronoUnit.SECONDS).format(ISO_OFFSET_DATE_TIME) — or convert to UTC and emit the same withInternetDateTime form iOS uses), mirroring iOS ISO8601Flexible.string. Add the seconds-less and nanosecond variants as decode fixtures to iOS DraftCrossSurfaceDecodingTests and to the Android encode tests as a pinned-output assertion (not a same-surface round-trip).

findings.title: Auth/session and destructive delete-pebble core paths have no behavior tests
findings.detail: The two classically highest-risk core paths on this surface are uncovered. Auth is tested only at the canSubmit form-validation level plus a trivial constructor assertion; signIn/signUp/signOut, the session stream handling in SupabaseService.start(), and the OAuth display-name patch have no tests and no SupabaseServicing fake exists to enable them (deferred by written YAGNI policy). The delete-pebble path (confirmation dialog, delete_pebble RPC call, timeline+stats refresh, error surfacing) is implemented inline in three views and asserted by nothing; a regression that silently fails deletes, or deletes the wrong pebble id, would reach users unnoticed, on a path that is irreversible by design ('This can't be undone.', PathView.swift:127). The gap is not tracked as an issue anywhere observable.
findings.evidence: grep -rln -i 'delete|purge' PebblesTests/ hits only PebbleDraftPayloadTests.swift and SnapUploadCoordinatorTests.swift (neither tests pebble deletion); delete paths at apps/ios/Pebbles/Features/Path/PathView.swift:263-276, Features/Profile/Views/CollectionDetailView.swift:186, Features/Profile/Views/SoulDetailView.swift:185; auth coverage limited to PebblesTests/Features/Auth/AuthViewLogicTests.swift (canSubmit only) and PebblesTests/SupabaseServiceTests.swift:8-12 (initial-state only); apps/ios/CLAUDE.md:23 defers the SupabaseServicing test seam.
findings.remediation: Extract the delete flow (confirm -> RPC -> refresh -> error mapping) into a testable helper mirroring PebblePublisher, add tests for it; introduce the SupabaseServicing protocol the CLAUDE.md already anticipates and cover signIn/signOut state transitions; track remaining path gaps as issues.

findings.title: verify-account-purge cannot detect a dropped delete line for 4 of the 8 auth.users-CASCADE tables, and log_reactions is asserted but never seeded
findings.detail: All section-(4) purge tables cascade from auth.users, so by the time the harness's zero-row assertions run (after deleteUser) the cascade would empty them even if purge_account lost the delete line — the harness authors identified this and pin the RPC's own counts, but only for pebble_drafts, connections, connection_invites, and connection_blocks. achievement_unlocks (seeded via check_achievements, seed guaranteed non-empty at :264-268), wallet_balances and bounces (seeded via the karma triggers) have counts printed but not asserted, and log_reactions is never seeded at all, making its zero-row check (:336) vacuous. Consequence: a future purge_account re-emission that silently drops any of those four delete lines — the exact #687 failure class this harness exists to make loud — passes the harness green. The practical harm is bounded (the auth cascade still removes the rows when deleteUser succeeds) but the 'all personal rows gone at RPC success' erasure guarantee and re-run meaningfulness silently degrade, and the harness's role as the collision tripwire is half-disarmed.
findings.evidence: packages/supabase/scripts/verify-account-purge.ts:301-317 (expectedPurged pins only 4 tables; comment at :302-306 states the cascade rationale), :336 (log_reactions asserted), §2 seed contains no log_reactions insert; cascade FKs: 20260730090000_achievements.sql:143, 20260421000002_log_reactions.sql:12, 20260629193636_wallet_balances.sql:5, 20260501000004_bounces_and_analytics_distribution.sql:34
findings.remediation: Extend expectedPurged to pin achievement_unlocks (>= 1, count captured from the check_achievements result), wallet_balances (1), and bounces (1); seed one log_reactions row via the service-role client (insert a throwaway published log or reuse an existing one) and pin its count too.

findings.title: delete_pebble, remove_connection, and the moderation takedown RPCs have no verification harness
findings.detail: Of the destructive operations on this surface, only account purge, drafts, and visibility have harnesses. delete_pebble (cascades pebble_cards/souls/domains/snaps/collection_pebbles and interacts with karma clawback), remove_connection (two-sided sever plus optional directed block insert, with not_found masking for non-members), and the moderation takedowns (reject_glyph, admin_delete_glyph, set_glyph_listed=false, which must change marketplace visibility without stranding buyers' entitlements) are exercised by no script — their correctness rests on reading the SQL. remove_connection is the more urgent of these: it carries the same in-body append marker as purge_account (M52/M53 will append seam/pair severing), and the decision log names it in 'the next likely collision' — but unlike purge_account it has no harness at all to turn a re-emission collision from silent into loud.
findings.evidence: ls packages/supabase/scripts/ shows five scripts, none covering these RPCs (grep for delete_pebble/remove_connection/reject_glyph/admin_delete_glyph in scripts/ returns nothing); remove_connection marker at packages/supabase/supabase/migrations/20260730070347_mutual_connections.sql:320-324; docs/decisions/log.md:378 names remove_connection in the next-collision warning
findings.remediation: Add a verify-connections-sever harness (anon-key pattern: connect two users, remove with and without p_block, assert connection gone for both, block row directionality, not_found for a third user) before M52/M53 land; add takedown coverage (seed a listed glyph with a buyer, delist/reject, assert market visibility and entitlement survival) and a delete_pebble cascade check to an existing or new harness.

findings.title: Dark-mode wiring is broken: media-query dark: utilities activate under OS dark while the class-based token block can never apply
findings.detail: The admin defines a full .dark token block but nothing ever sets the .dark class: no ThemeProvider is mounted and no toggle exists. Meanwhile globals.css is missing the @custom-variant dark override that apps/web has, so every dark: utility in the component library compiles to the prefers-color-scheme media query. An operator whose OS is in dark mode gets a hybrid render: page and tokens stay light while dark-tuned utilities activate on top, producing measurably broken pairs, e.g. analytics delta badges switch to emerald-400/rose-400 text on a still-light secondary background at roughly 1.8:1, inputs render dark:bg-input/30 translucent fills on white, and the sonner toaster (theme defaulting to system) shows dark toasts on the light app. Since OS-level dark preference is common among internal operators, this fires under completely ordinary conditions.
findings.evidence: app/globals.css:39-71 (.dark block, class-based) with no @custom-variant dark line (present in apps/web/app/globals.css:5); rg 'next-themes|ThemeProvider|setTheme' over apps/admin hits only components/ui/sonner.tsx:3; app/layout.tsx:11-19 mounts no provider; mismatch consumers at components/analytics/KpiCard.tsx:77-78, DomainShare.tsx:157-158, UserAverages.tsx:128-129, QualitySignalsTable.tsx:111-112, components/ui/input.tsx:12
findings.remediation: Pick one: commit to light-only by removing the dead .dark block and all dark: utilities (and pinning sonner theme='light'), or wire the theme properly by adding @custom-variant dark (&:is(.dark *)) plus the next-themes provider as apps/web does.

findings.title: Measured AA contrast failures: retention heatmap bucket 4 at 2.41:1 and chart series 1 and 2 at 1.48:1 and 2.68:1
findings.detail: Mechanically computed WCAG ratios show three concrete failures on the analytics surface. RetentionHeatmap's fourth bucket (40-49 percent retention) renders text-stone-50 on bg-stone-400 at 2.41:1 for text-xs cell values, far below the 4.5:1 minimum, so a common retention range becomes unreadable to low-vision operators. The grayscale chart ramp puts chart-1 at oklch(0.87 0 0), 1.48:1 against the white card, and chart-2 at 2.68:1, both below the 3:1 non-text minimum; chart-1 is the primary series color for DAU lines, bounce bars, domain bars and pebble volume, so the most important series in nearly every chart is a barely visible pale gray. The muted-foreground on muted hover pair also computes 4.39:1, a marginal miss. Nothing in the repo measures contrast and there is no CI to catch drift.
findings.evidence: components/analytics/RetentionHeatmap.tsx:14 (bg-stone-400 text-stone-50 bucket) and :9-18; app/globals.css:32-33 (chart-1/chart-2 values); consumers at components/analytics/ActiveUsersChart.tsx:38-39, PebbleVolumeChart.tsx:35-36, BounceDistributionChart.tsx:17, DomainShare.tsx:37; ratios computed by script over the token values (stone-400 #a8a29e vs stone-50 #fafaf9 = 2.41:1; oklch(0.87 0 0) vs white = 1.48:1; oklch(0.70 0 0) vs white = 2.68:1; muted-foreground on muted = 4.39:1)
findings.remediation: Darken the bucket-4 pair (e.g. keep stone-900 text through bucket 4) and rebase the chart ramp to start at chart-3 lightness or add hue; add a small token-contrast script to the workspace and run it in lint.

findings.title: No reduced-motion handling anywhere in the admin: every animation ignores the user preference
findings.detail: There is not a single occurrence of prefers-reduced-motion, useReducedMotion, or Tailwind's motion-reduce/motion-safe variants in the admin workspace, and the tw-animate-css library it imports ships no built-in gate. Consequently all motion plays unconditionally for users who have asked the OS to reduce it: zoom-and-slide enter/exit animations on every dialog, dropdown, select, tooltip and sheet; the looping skeleton pulse during analytics loading; the toast spinner; and recharts' default mount animations which redraw every line and bar on each analytics visit (isAnimationActive is never disabled). The motion vocabulary is small-scale so physical harm potential is modest, but the preference is ignored one hundred percent of the time for the users it exists to protect, and there is no shared helper to route future animations through.
findings.evidence: rg 'prefers-reduced-motion|useReducedMotion|motion-reduce|motion-safe' apps/admin/app apps/admin/components apps/admin/lib apps/admin/hooks returns zero hits; rg -l 'prefers-reduced-motion' node_modules/tw-animate-css/dist/ returns nothing; animation entry points at components/ui/dialog.tsx:34,56, dropdown-menu.tsx:44,138, select.tsx:86, tooltip.tsx:53, skeleton.tsx:7, sonner.tsx:28; rg 'isAnimationActive' apps/admin/components returns nothing
findings.remediation: Add a global @media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) block in globals.css that zeroes animation and transition durations, and pass isAnimationActive={false} (or a shared useReducedMotion hook value) to the recharts components.

findings.title: French strings default to masculine forms when addressing the user, with no inclusive-copy guideline in the repo
findings.detail: The French locale addresses the user with masculine participles in the connections and record flows: 'Te voila connecte avec %1$s', 'Tu es deja connecte avec %1$s', 'Tu dois etre connecte pour enregistrer'. For a product whose entire premise is emotional self-recording, defaulting every non-masculine French user to the wrong grammatical gender in core flows is an inclusion defect, and it will multiply as string count grows because no written inclusive-language guideline exists anywhere in docs/ to steer new copy or review. Epicene rewrites exist for all three strings (for example 'Te voila en connexion avec', 'Ta connexion avec %1$s existe deja', 'Connecte-toi pour enregistrer').
findings.evidence: apps/android/app/src/main/res/values-fr/strings.xml:432,433,534; rg -i 'inclusive|copy guideline|tone of voice' over docs/ returns only Kritik framework files
findings.remediation: Rewrite the three strings with epicene constructions, sweep values-fr for other user-addressing participles, and add a short inclusive-copy note to the repo docs so review can hold the line; apply the same sweep to the iOS and web French resources.

findings.title: Interactive targets below the 48dp Android minimum with no minimum-size enforcement anywhere
findings.detail: Several custom interactive elements have hit areas well under the 48dp Android guideline: the week-navigation chevrons are 24dp clickables (the primary way to move between weeks on the Path header), the Lab reaction button is roughly 24dp tall (16dp icon plus 4dp vertical padding), and the record-flow back and close buttons are 44dp (the iOS point value ported without conversion to the Android floor). No usage of minimumInteractiveComponentSize or LocalMinimumInteractiveComponentSize exists in the codebase, so nothing imposes a floor on custom clickables; the single explicit floor (ValenceFan's MinimumHitTarget) is also set to the iOS 44 rather than 48. Users with reduced dexterity will mis-tap the week chevrons and reactions routinely.
findings.evidence: apps/android/app/src/main/kotlin/app/pbbls/android/features/path/components/WeekHeader.kt:101-103 (24dp clickable chevron); features/lab/components/ReactionButton.kt:57-58,67 (icon 16dp, padding 6/4dp); features/path/record/RecordFlowChrome.kt:55,76 (44dp); features/path/valence/ValenceFan.kt:47 (MinimumHitTarget = 44.dp); rg 'minimumInteractiveComponentSize' over apps/android returns nothing
findings.remediation: Add Modifier.minimumInteractiveComponentSize() (or explicit 48dp size with centered glyph) to the chevron, reaction, and chrome buttons, and raise the shared MinimumHitTarget constant to 48dp on Android.

findings.title: Detail and store dates hardcode English field order for all locales
findings.detail: PebbleReadDateFormat formats the pebble detail title with the literal pattern 'EEE, MMM d, yyyy' and GlyphDetailDrawer uses 'MMM yyyy' and 'MMM d, yyyy'. The locale parameter localizes month and weekday names but keeps the English comma-and-order structure, so a French user reads 'mar., aout 26, 2026' instead of 'mar. 26 aout 2026' on every pebble they open. The codebase already contains the correct technique (WeekHeaderFormatting builds its pattern via DateTimeFormatterBuilder.getLocalizedDateTimePattern), so this is an inconsistency between sibling formatters rather than a missing capability; the iOS mirror should be checked for the same fixed order.
findings.evidence: apps/android/app/src/main/kotlin/app/pbbls/android/features/path/PebbleReadDateFormat.kt:24; features/glyph/store/GlyphDetailDrawer.kt:165,243; correct approach at features/path/WeekHeaderFormatting.kt:46
findings.remediation: Derive the skeleton per locale (DateTimeFormatterBuilder.getLocalizedDateTimePattern or ofLocalizedDate with FormatStyle) in PebbleReadDateFormat and GlyphDetailDrawer, and extend PebbleReadDateFormatTest with a French-locale assertion.

findings.title: Three user-facing error strings ship untranslated and the localization harness is built to miss them
findings.detail: 'Photo is still uploading.', 'Photo upload failed. Retry or remove it.', and 'You must be signed in to save.' have no localizations at all in Localizable.xcstrings, so French users see English errors at the exact moments things go wrong (save/upload failures in the create, edit, and record flows). Worse, two flows assign these as raw Swift String literals to saveError, bypassing the localization mechanism entirely rather than using String(localized:). The catalog coverage test cannot catch any of this: its guard 'guard let localizations = entry.localizations else { continue }' skips precisely the entries that have no localizations dict - i.e. brand-new untranslated strings - so the drift-detection harness has a hole shaped exactly like this bug class.
findings.evidence: apps/ios/Pebbles/Resources/Localizable.xcstrings (entries 'Photo is still uploading.', 'Photo upload failed. Retry or remove it.', 'You must be signed in to save.' carry only auto-comments, no localizations); apps/ios/Pebbles/Features/Path/CreatePebbleSheet.swift:163-174 and EditPebbleSheet.swift:204-218 (raw literals); RecordFlowView.swift:67-68,241 (String(localized:) but no catalog entry); PebblesTests/LocalizationTests.swift:293 (guard-continue hole)
findings.remediation: Add en+fr localizations for the three keys, convert the raw saveError literals to String(localized:), and change the test to fail on any non-empty key whose entry has no localizations dict (or no fr) instead of skipping it.

findings.title: The Rive cairn animation on the Path screen autoplays per week cell and ignores Reduce Motion
findings.detail: WeekRollCairnCell instantiates a RiveViewModel running the pbbls-cairn-states state machine, one per visible cell in the horizontal weeks roll on the primary Path screen. Nothing reads accessibilityReduceMotion in this file, there is no static-frame fallback, and the idle state machine has no pause or stop path - so a user who has asked the OS to reduce motion still gets multiple simultaneously-animating vector loops on the app's home screen. This is the one animation-runtime entry point in the app, and it is exactly the uncovered wrapper class the criterion's l2 anchor describes; the rest of the app's major motion (pebble settle render, welcome logo, valence scale) is properly gated, which makes the omission a drift, not a policy.
findings.evidence: apps/ios/Pebbles/Features/Path/Components/WeekRollCairnCell.swift:25-40 (RiveViewModel, rvm.view(), no reduceMotion read); grep 'reduceMotion' in that file = 0; gated comparators at PebbleAnimatedRenderView.swift:86,98,202 and HandcraftedLogoView.swift:91; used from WeekRollView.swift:33
findings.remediation: Read @Environment(\.accessibilityReduceMotion) in WeekRollCairnCell and render a static first/last frame (rvm.stop() or a static GlyphView-style fallback) when set; audit any future Rive call sites behind one shared wrapper view that owns the gate.

findings.title: French copy defaults to masculine forms when addressing the user, with no inclusive-language guideline to catch it
findings.detail: Three FR strings address the user with masculine-only participles/adjectives: 'Tu es déjà connecté avec %@.', 'Te voilà connecté avec %@.' (connection accept flow), and 'Toi seul peux voir celui-ci.' (privacy copy on secret pebbles). Every non-male French user is misgendered by their own private journal at emotionally salient moments (connecting with someone, being told a memory is theirs alone). The rest of the FR surface avoids the trap with epicene noun constructions - which shows the translation practice can do better and that these are unreviewed drift. No written inclusive-language or copy guideline exists in the repo, so nothing prevents the next gendered default from landing.
findings.evidence: apps/ios/Pebbles/Resources/Localizable.xcstrings FR values for 'You're already connected with %@.', 'You're connected with %@.', 'Only you can see this one.' (rendered from InviteAcceptSheet.swift:46-47 and the pebble read/privacy path); guideline search over docs/ and .claude/ for 'inclusive|épicène|écriture inclusive|copy guideline' = no policy doc
findings.remediation: Rewrite the three strings epicenely ('Te voilà en lien avec %@', 'Vous êtes déjà lié·es' or a noun construction; 'Il n'y a que toi pour voir celui-ci'), and add a short inclusive-copy guideline (FR epicene rules, deny-list) to docs/agents/ referenced from the localization sections of the surface CLAUDE.md files.

findings.title: Residual hardcoded English strings and an unlocalized date formatter leak through the otherwise complete i18n layer
findings.detail: Three concrete leaks: the gamification stat dialog's dismiss button is the literal 'Got it' (shown untranslated to French users every time they open a bounce/karma explainer from the Path header); the stats group carries a hardcoded aria-label 'Gamification stats' so screen readers get English inside a French UI; and WalletHistoryItem formats the karma event date with toLocaleDateString() with no locale argument, so the wallet shows browser-locale dates even when the user picked the other app language. Additionally app/layout.tsx renders lang='en' at SSR for all users, only corrected client-side after hydration, so assistive tech and search engines see an English-declared document on first paint of French sessions.
findings.evidence: apps/web/components/path/GamificationBlock.tsx:54 ('Got it'); apps/web/components/path/GamificationBlocks.tsx:29 (aria-label='Gamification stats'); apps/web/components/wallet/WalletHistoryItem.tsx:12 (bare toLocaleDateString()); apps/web/app/layout.tsx:76 (lang='en' hardcoded, corrected by LocaleProvider HtmlLangSync post-hydration).
findings.remediation: Move the three strings into the message files (both locales), format the wallet date via the existing useFormatDate hook, and derive the SSR lang attribute from the locale cookie/param where feasible or document the hydration-sync tradeoff.

findings.title: apps/admin has no test entry point at all, so an agent cannot prove any admin change beyond lint and build
findings.detail: apps/admin/package.json defines dev, build, start, and lint but no test script, and no test files exist for the workspace; the machine baseline marks admin tests as nonexistent. Admin carries real logic worth proving (analytics fetchers, fixture variants, is_admin-gated flows), and its own CLAUDE.md mandates playground fixtures precisely because states are hard to review, yet none of that is assertable by a command. Failure scenario: an agent refactors a fetcher's error mapping (the PostgrestError-is-not-an-Error rule) and has no loop that would catch the regression; the break surfaces as a blank ErrorBlock in production analytics.
findings.evidence: apps/admin/package.json scripts block (dev/build/start/lint only); docs/quality/audits/2026-08/baseline.md:14; apps/admin/CLAUDE.md:23-28 (fixture and error-mapping conventions with no test harness behind them)
findings.remediation: Add vitest to apps/admin mirroring the web setup, seed it with tests for the fetcher error mapping and fixture-driven component states, and wire npm run test.

findings.title: iOS has no CI workflow and no fail-soft wrapper, so no agent-runnable proof exists for any iOS change
findings.detail: apps/ios exposes build/lint/test only through xcodegen, xcodebuild, and swiftlint, which are absent in the Linux agent environment (baseline records exit 127), and .github/workflows contains no iOS job at all, so iOS lint and Swift Testing suites run only on the maintainer's machine. Unlike Android, which ships gradle-if-sdk.sh to no-op loudly, the iOS scripts fail hard, which means the root-level 'npm run lint' and 'npm run build' that CLAUDE.md mandates for Large tasks abort on any macOS-less host when turbo reaches @pbbls/ios. The failure scenario is routine: an agent edits shared iOS code (e.g. a mirrored contract change per the 1:1 rule), can run no check, and the regression ships unverified because nothing in CI would have caught it either. This makes the platform with the most intricate hazard rules the only one with zero automated verification.
findings.evidence: apps/ios/package.json:6-9 (build/lint/test scripts); ls .github/workflows/ shows only android.yml, android-release.yml, arkaik.yml, lab-note-reminder.yml; docs/quality/audits/2026-08/baseline.md:13; contrast apps/android/scripts/gradle-if-sdk.sh:26-28; CLAUDE.md:58 (Large: full root build/lint)
findings.remediation: Add a macos-latest workflow path-filtered on apps/ios/** running swiftlint and xcodebuild test (the same tasks package.json names), and wrap the npm scripts in an xcode-if-toolchain guard mirroring gradle-if-sdk.sh so root turbo loops degrade gracefully on Linux.

verification.note: Re-checked every citation at the audited tree. Confirmed: apps/ios/package.json:6-9 shells raw xcodegen/xcodebuild/swiftlint with no fail-soft wrapper (unlike apps/android/scripts/gradle-if-sdk.sh:22-24 which exits 0); .github/workflows has no iOS job at commit 10181916 or HEAD; baseline.md:13 records exit 127; root package.json runs unfiltered turbo build/lint over apps/*, so the CLAUDE.md Large-task mandate (full root build/lint) fails hard on any macOS-less host, and no agent-runnable iOS proof exists. That AGT-03 core is real. Overstated: the claims of "no iOS CI at all", "nothing in CI would have caught it", and "zero automated verification" are wrong. apps/ios/ci_scripts/ci_post_clone.sh (present in tree 10181916) configures Xcode Cloud hosted CI; apps/ios/README.md:72 and docs/superpowers/specs/2026-07-10-android-bootstrap-design.md:26 state iOS builds on Xcode Cloud; remote branch fix/246-xcode-cloud-spm-resolution shows it actively runs; and the auditor's own cited baseline line reads "lint/tests run locally/Xcode Cloud only", a qualifier the finding dropped. The repo's own criterion (docs/quality/criteria/tst-testing-verification.md:271) instructs auditors to count Xcode Cloud ci_scripts. So a compile-breaking mirrored contract change has an automated backstop; the genuinely uncovered residue is SwiftLint (not installed in ci_post_clone.sh) and behavior-level regressions if the Xcode Cloud workflow lacks a test action (unprovable from the repo since that config lives in App Store Connect). Likelihood 4 stands: any agent iOS edit on Linux hits the no-check condition. Impact drops 3 to 2: the narrated harm (regression ships with zero automated verification on the most hazardous surface) is contradicted by the existing hosted build gate plus the documented maintainer TestFlight verification loop; the residual impact is the broken root build/lint workflow and deferred, partial verification, not an absent one.

findings.title: The sanctioned dev loop writes to the production Supabase project, with only the logs table under an explicit no-write rule
findings.detail: By recorded decision, migrations, edge functions, and DB changes are tested against the remote (production) project rather than local containers: db:push applies migrations directly, and the service-role harnesses seed and purge throwaway users on the same database that holds real users' intimate data. The harnesses are carefully scoped (statements bound to run-minted user ids, cleanup on failure) and credentials are runtime-env only, but the only instruction-level ban on production writes from the dev loop covers the logs table; there is no staging project, no written boundary listing which production writes are sanctioned, and an agent handed SUPABASE_SERVICE_ROLE_KEY for a harness run holds full production write capability for the whole session. Failure scenario: a buggy backfill or a mis-scoped harness edit during routine dev deletes or mutates real user rows with no environment boundary to absorb the mistake.
findings.evidence: docs/decisions/log.md:52-60 (2026-05-26 remote-first decision: 'test edge functions, migrations, and DB changes against the remote Supabase project'); packages/supabase/scripts/verify-account-purge.ts:1-40 (service-role harness against the linked project, env-supplied key); CLAUDE.md:169 (the only ban: 'Never write to Supabase / logs from the dev loop'); CLAUDE.md:35 (harnesses 'run against the linked project')
findings.remediation: Stand up a staging project or Supabase branch database for harness runs and migration rehearsal, and add a standing rule naming exactly which operations may touch the production project and under whose hands; keep the service-role key out of routine agent sessions.

findings.title: 22 view/sheet files perform PostgREST queries inline, and nothing stops the pattern from growing
findings.detail: The documented boundary only forbids views from constructing SupabaseClient; query composition, decoding configuration, and write sequencing live directly inside SwiftUI view structs across the Profile, Path, and Connections features (multi-line select strings, .rpc calls, and in SettingsSheet a four-step write orchestration). Consequences: any schema or column rename becomes a hunt through view files; the data paths embedded in views are untestable without UI (directly feeding the TST-01 gaps on delete and settings); and two architectural eras now coexist, since the newest feature (Record flow) routes everything through an @Observable view model while older sheets keep inline IO — a new screen copies whichever pattern its author sees first. No SwiftLint custom rule or architecture test flags a new supabase.client reference in a View file.
findings.evidence: grep -rln 'supabase.client' apps/ios/Pebbles/Features/ = 26 files, 22 of them views/sheets; representative: Features/Path/PathView.swift:232-235,266-268; Features/Path/EditPebbleSheet.swift:164-178 (25-line select in the view); Features/Profile/Sheets/SettingsSheet.swift:455-500 (sequenced set_handle, update_profile, profiles update, auth.update in a view function); Features/Profile/ProfileView.swift:106,128; contrast with the boundary-respecting era at Features/Record/RecordFlowModel.swift:15-38 and Services/*.swift; stated (weaker) rule at apps/ios/CLAUDE.md:21-22; .swiftlint.yml is defaults-only with no custom rule.
findings.remediation: Adopt the Record-flow pattern as the stated target (view model or feature service owns queries), migrate the highest-churn sheets (Settings, EditPebble, detail views) first, and add a SwiftLint custom_rules regex flagging 'supabase.client' inside files whose primary type conforms to View.

findings.title: No incident-response runbook: an Art. 33 notification within 72 hours is not achievable from documented material
findings.detail: The repo contains no incident-response document of any kind: no roles, no severity assessment, no 72-hour notification flow to the CNIL (the controller's lead authority, already named in the policy for complaints), no Art. 34 user-communication criteria or template, and no processor notification chain for Supabase or Vercel. Combined with the missing audit trail, a breach discovered today would be handled entirely from improvisation by a single operator, with the deadline consumed by inventing process rather than scoping impact.
findings.evidence: grep -rilE 'incident.response|breach notification|72.hour|supervisory authority' over docs/, apps/, packages/ returns only the audit framework's own criteria files and the privacy policy's complaint section (apps/web/docs/privacy/en.md:266-272); docs/ directory listing contains no security or incident folder
findings.remediation: Author docs/security/incident-response.md covering detection sources, severity assessment, the CNIL Art. 33 flow with a notification template, Art. 34 user-communication criteria and channel, and the Supabase/Vercel processor chain; add a last-reviewed date and revisit it at milestone audits.

findings.title: No scheduled retention enforcement exists; policy lifetimes for auth logs and backups are claims with no backing mechanism
findings.detail: The policy states 12-month auth-log retention, a 90-day backup tail, and a 30-day post-deletion buffer, but the migrations contain zero pg_cron jobs or scheduled functions and no CI cron prunes anything, so every stated lifetime is either a platform default nobody verified or fiction. Deletion is the only reaper: purge_account fires at account deletion and nothing else expires. Rejected glyph submissions keep submitter identity and the operator's review_note forever. The policy also names data that does not exist (Cairns aggregates), evidence that the schedule document and the system have never been reconciled.
findings.evidence: grep -rniE 'pg_cron|cron\.schedule|schedule' over packages/supabase/supabase/migrations/*.sql: zero hits; .github/workflows contains no scheduled cleanup; apps/web/docs/privacy/en.md:197-223 (stated lifetimes incl. Cairns at :214-217, a feature absent from the schema); 20260630084718_admin_glyph_moderation.sql:11-12 (review_note retained indefinitely)
findings.remediation: Reconcile section 8 of the policy with reality (verify the Supabase project's actual auth-log and backup retention and correct the numbers), add pg_cron jobs or scheduled functions for any category with a stated lifetime (e.g. detach submitter identity from old rejected submissions), and document the mapping category-to-job in docs/.

findings.title: No incident-response runbook and no operator audit-log table to scope or notify a breach within 72 hours
findings.detail: There is no incident runbook in docs/ (grep -rnil breach/incident finds only unrelated specs and the quality framework), and there is no general audit-log table: privileged mutations write no actor+timestamp trail beyond reviewed_by/reviewed_at on glyph_submissions (20260630084718:72-73), while admin achievement/emotion/domain management RPCs (20260730150000, 20260717120000, 20260703000000) write no audit row, and scoping queries are not prewritten. Failure scenario: a personal-data breach involving the emotional-content tables occurs; the operator cannot enumerate affected users and records for a given table and window from any in-app audit trail, has no notification templates or processor-notification chain, and cannot demonstrate the Art.33 72-hour flow, so awareness-to-notification blows the deadline. Positive: service_role appears in zero client sources and admin RPCs enforce is_admin server-side, so the detection gap is documentation+audit-trail, not key leakage.
findings.evidence: grep breach/incident docs/ -> none; audit trail limited to 20260630084718_admin_glyph_moderation.sql:72-73; admin RPCs write no audit row (20260730150000_admin_achievement_management.sql, 20260717120000_admin_emotion_management.sql, 20260703000000_admin_domain_management.sql)
findings.remediation: Write the incident runbook (roles, Art.33 72-hour flow, Art.34 criteria/channel, notification templates, processor chain) and add an audit-log table that every admin/privileged RPC writes to with actor and timestamp; prewrite affected-user scoping queries and date-stamp one tabletop drill.

findings.title: No retention schedule and no scheduled pruning; append-only categories accumulate indefinitely
findings.detail: No retention document exists and no scheduled cleanup runs: grep for pg_cron/cron.schedule/pg_net across migrations returns nothing. karma_events is append-only (20260411000001:92-99), connection_invites retains expired/revoked rows forever (only revoked_at is set; 20260730070347:47-63), and pebble_drafts have no TTL (20260729213348:29-35). The only deletion is on-demand (account purge, single-media delete). Failure scenario: over months of normal use these tables grow without bound and superseded drafts and dead invite tokens (plaintext capabilities) persist far beyond their purpose, breaching storage limitation (Art.5(1)(e)); nothing breaks, so the accumulation is silent and unmonitored. Backup retention is also undocumented and unreconciled with the erasure story.
findings.evidence: grep pg_cron/cron.schedule -> none; 20260730070347_mutual_connections.sql:47-63; 20260729213348_pebble_drafts.sql:29-35; 20260411000001_core_tables.sql:92-99
findings.remediation: Write a per-category retention schedule and implement scheduled pruning (pg_cron or a scheduled edge function) for expired connection_invites, stale drafts, and any capped log/event categories; add a periodic oldest-row check so silent accumulation becomes a failing signal.

findings.title: Stated retention lifetimes are enforced by nothing: no scheduled cleanup exists and drafts never expire
findings.detail: The policy commits to a 30-day post-deletion erasure window (purge is actually immediate, an undisclosed over-delivery that still contradicts the text), 12-month auth-log retention, and 90-day backup expiry, but the repo contains no pg_cron job, scheduled edge function, or CI cron enforcing any lifetime; auth-log and backup windows ride unexamined platform defaults. pebble_drafts, which can hold sensitive part-written content indefinitely, have no TTL, and orphaned media relies on best-effort client-side cleanup that logs and continues on failure, with no server-side reaper. The policy's retention chapter is therefore aspirational text rather than enforced schedule.
findings.evidence: apps/web/docs/privacy/en.md:197-222; grep -ri 'pg_cron|cron' packages/supabase/supabase/migrations: zero; 20260729213348_pebble_drafts.sql (no expiry: grep expire/ttl zero); apps/web/lib/data/supabase-provider.ts:551 (best-effort storage cleanup warn); functions/delete-account (immediate purge vs stated 30 days)
findings.remediation: Add a scheduled job (pg_cron or scheduled function) reaping expired drafts and orphaned media; verify and document the platform's auth-log and backup retention against the policy numbers; align the policy's 30-day claim with the immediate purge.

findings.title: Admin deploys with zero security headers in any tracked config
findings.detail: apps/admin/next.config.ts is an empty config object with no headers() function, apps/admin has no vercel.json, and there is no middleware.ts. The deployed operator app therefore ships with Vercel's permissive defaults: no Content-Security-Policy, no frame-ancestors/X-Frame-Options, no X-Content-Type-Options, no Referrer-Policy, no Permissions-Policy. The missing frame-ancestors means the admin can be iframed from any origin, enabling clickjacking of destructive one-click operator actions (delete glyph, unlist glyph, publish log); the missing CSP means any future XSS (the app renders user-supplied glyph names, review notes, and markdown via @uiw/react-md-editor) runs completely unmitigated on a surface that exposes user emails through admin_find_user and admin_list_glyph_submissions. The sibling web app is equally bare (apps/web/vercel.json holds only a $schema key), so no baseline exists anywhere to inherit.
findings.evidence: apps/admin/next.config.ts:3 (empty NextConfig); repo-wide find for vercel.json returns only apps/web/vercel.json containing just a $schema key; find apps -name middleware.ts returns nothing; rg 'headers|Content-Security|X-Frame|Strict-Transport' over both next.config.ts files returns nothing
findings.remediation: Add a headers() block to apps/admin/next.config.ts with HSTS, X-Content-Type-Options nosniff, Referrer-Policy, Permissions-Policy, frame-ancestors 'none', and a CSP (report-only first, then enforced); mirror the same baseline in apps/web so the two apps stay consistent.

findings.title: Operator app and its preview deployments rely on application auth alone, with previews pointed at production Supabase
findings.detail: Nothing in the repo or docs records any platform-level protection (Vercel Deployment Protection, SSO, or IP allowlist) for the admin production deployment or its previews; the only gate is the requireAdmin layout check plus RLS. apps/admin/README.md explicitly instructs copying the production Supabase URL and publishable key from the apps/web Vercel project, so every preview deployment of every open PR is a publicly reachable copy of the back-office running unreviewed branch code against the production database. An attacker who finds a preview URL gets the full login surface plus whatever a buggy branch leaks; the criterion treats an unprotected operator preview as an exposure independent of application-code care.
findings.evidence: apps/admin/README.md:24-31 (Vercel defaults, env vars copied from the web production project, no protection step); rg 'deployment protection|password protect|vercel authentication|preview.*protect' over docs/ and apps/admin/ matches only docs/quality framework files; lib/supabase/admin-guard.ts:16-46 is the sole gate
findings.remediation: Enable Vercel Deployment Protection (at minimum Standard Protection covering previews) on the admin project, record the setting and rationale in apps/admin/README.md, and either point previews at a non-production Supabase project or record the accepted reason for sharing production.

findings.title: No developer contact information is reachable in-app
findings.detail: Apple 1.2 requires published contact information so users can reach the developer, and the criterion treats in-app contact info as one of the four UGC pillars. The iOS app has none: the settings sheet offers only Terms and Privacy Policy sheets, and no screen anywhere renders a support email, contact link, or feedback flow. A user who hits a moderation, billing (karma), or account problem has no path to a human from inside the app, and store review can flag the missing pillar together with the missing report mechanism.
findings.evidence: grep -rni 'mailto|support@|contact' apps/ios/Pebbles --include='*.swift' = 0 hits; apps/ios/Pebbles/Features/Profile/Sheets/SettingsSheet.swift:361-376 (legal section only)
findings.remediation: Add a 'Contact us' row to the settings legal section opening a support email or the web contact page; keep the same address in both store listings.

findings.title: No key inventory or rotation runbook: the service_role key is used from dev machines, CI, and edge functions with no documented map of where keys live
findings.detail: The service_role key is required on maintainer machines to run the contract harnesses against the linked production project (remote-first workflow), is auto-present in edge functions, and the anon/publishable key is baked into GitHub Actions secrets, Vercel env vars, the deployed web bundle, and Android APKs. No document enumerates the issued keys or the places each lives, and no rotation runbook exists (repo-wide grep for rotation guidance finds none). Naming drift compounds it: web and admin read NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_PUBLISHABLE_KEY whose example value is described as '<your-anon-key>', while scripts and CI call the same class of key SUPABASE_ANON_KEY, so during an incident it is not obvious which stored secrets are the same credential. Failure scenario: the service_role key leaks from a developer laptop or shell history; with no runbook naming every location (Actions secrets, Vercel, edge function env, local .env files), rotation is slow and partial, prolonging a window in which the leaked key bypasses all RLS on intimate emotional data.
findings.evidence: packages/supabase/scripts/verify-account-purge.ts:32-40 and scripts/backfill-renders.ts:16-23 (service_role from env on dev machines); packages/supabase/supabase/functions/_shared/supabase-client.ts:10,32-36; .github/workflows/android.yml:55-56 and android-release.yml:82-83 (SUPABASE_ANON_KEY secrets); apps/web/.env.local.example:3-4 (PUBLISHABLE_KEY named, '<your-anon-key>' value); grep 'rotat' across docs/ and packages/supabase found no key runbook
findings.remediation: Write a short key runbook in packages/supabase or docs/: list each issued key, every location it is stored (Actions, Vercel, edge functions, local env files, APK bake), the exact rotation steps per location, and verification steps; prefer migrating to the new publishable/secret key pairs which support zero-downtime rotation, and reconcile the env var naming.

findings.title: Sign-out flushes the signed-URL cache but never purges Coil's disk/memory caches, leaving private snap images on disk
findings.detail: RootScreen invalidates SnapURLCache when the session drops to null, but the decoded JPEG bytes of every private snap the user viewed remain in Coil's default disk cache (and memory cache until process death). Nothing in the app ever touches imageLoader.diskCache or memoryCache. After sign-out on a shared or handed-over device, and even after full account deletion through the delete-account flow in SettingsScreen, the photos persist in the app's cache directory until Coil evicts them by size pressure. The URL cache purge shows the sign-out-purge intent exists; the image-byte layer was simply missed, turning a performance cache into private-content residue.
findings.evidence: apps/android/app/src/main/kotlin/app/pbbls/android/RootScreen.kt:113-123 (only snapUrls?.invalidateAll() on userId == null); PebblesApp.kt:134-139 (Coil loader built with defaults, no cache config); grep -rn 'diskCache|memoryCache' apps/android/app/src = 0 hits; features/profile/SettingsScreen.kt:189-201 (account erasure path also ends in signOut() with no image-cache purge).
findings.remediation: In the same effect that flushes SnapURLCache on session loss, clear Coil's memory cache and disk cache (SingletonImageLoader.get(context).let { it.memoryCache?.clear(); it.diskCache?.clear() } on the IO dispatcher), mirroring whatever iOS does with URLCache for the 1:1 rule.

findings.title: path_pebbles fetches the user's entire pebble history, render SVGs included, on every Path load and after every mutation
findings.detail: The path_pebbles RPC has no limit and no pagination: it returns every pebble the user ever recorded, each row carrying its full render_svg text (a complete SVG document per pebble). PathView calls it on first appearance and re-calls it wholesale after every create, edit, delete, and draft-publish (four separate callback sites all invoke load()). At development volumes this is invisible; for a daily journaling user it grows without bound (a year of use is hundreds of rows times kilobytes of SVG each, refetched several times per session), taxing latency, egress, memory, and battery on the app's home screen. Collection and soul detail views repeat the unbounded pattern. Because Android mirrors iOS 1:1, the shape is duplicated on the sibling client.
findings.evidence: packages/supabase/supabase/migrations/20260519141000_path_pebbles_positiveness.sql:26-49 (select ... order by p.happened_at desc; no LIMIT), apps/ios/Pebbles/Features/Path/PathView.swift:230-236 (load), :74-109 and :269-271 (full reload after every mutation); apps/ios/Pebbles/Features/Profile/Views/CollectionDetailView.swift:166-173 and SoulDetailView.swift:166-173 (unbounded pebble fetches, no .limit).
findings.remediation: Add keyset pagination to path_pebbles (cursor on happened_at + id tiebreak) or at minimum a windowed variant the Path's week roll can page through; drop render_svg from rows outside the visible window or fetch it per-week; mirror the change on Android in the same milestone since the RPC is a shared contract.

findings.title: Per-session in-memory signing forces a full re-download of all visible media on every app launch
findings.detail: SnapURLCache holds signed URLs only in memory with a one-hour TTL, so every cold launch mints fresh signed URLs for every visible snap. Since the signature is part of the URL and AsyncImage's HTTP cache is keyed by URL, the device's URLCache can never serve a previously downloaded thumb across sessions: each launch of the Path re-downloads every thumbnail in view, and every detail open re-downloads its banner original. The upload path also leaves cacheControl to the SDK default rather than choosing one (FileOptions carries only contentType), and no bounded URLCache is configured for media, so within-session reuse rides whatever the shared session defaults to. The cost compounds with the PRF-05 finding as the timeline grows: bytes, launch latency, and storage egress all scale with history on every open.
findings.evidence: apps/ios/Pebbles/Services/SnapURLCache.swift:19-31 (in-memory dictionary, 3600s TTL, no persistence), apps/ios/Pebbles/Features/PebbleMedia/PebbleSnapRepository.swift:33 (signedUrlTTL 3600) and :49 (FileOptions(contentType:) with no cacheControl); grep for 'URLCache|URLSessionConfiguration' across apps/ios returns no configuration; render sites: Features/Path/Components/PathPebbleSnapThumb.swift:18-31, Features/Path/Read/PebbleReadBanner.swift:70-73.
findings.remediation: Either persist signed URLs alongside their expiry (so a URL valid from a previous session is reused and the HTTP cache hits), or add a small on-disk image cache keyed by storage_path independent of the signed query string; set an explicit cacheControl on upload aligned with the signing TTL; keep the sign-out purge covering whichever store is added.

findings.title: List thumbnails fetch 1024px originals into 32-64px slots while the uploaded thumb.jpg variant is never read, and per-mutation re-signing busts the image cache
findings.detail: The upload pipeline deliberately produces a 420px/<=300KB thumb.jpg next to each 1024px/<=1MB original.jpg, but the web read path signs and renders only original.jpg everywhere: the path timeline row puts the original into a size-16 (64px) slot and the compact pebble card into a size-8 (32px) slot, so every photo-bearing list row downloads up to ~1MB to paint a thumbnail. The lib/data/data-provider.ts interface comment even documents getDraftSnapUrl as returning the thumb while the implementation signs the original. Compounding this, signed URLs are re-minted in bulk on every loadFromSupabase, which runs after every mutation, so URLs (and therefore browser HTTP cache keys) change well inside their 1h TTL and previously downloaded images are re-fetched. Uploads also pass no explicit cacheControl. The result is a media egress and latency profile several times larger than the pipeline was built to deliver, on the app's most-viewed screen.
findings.evidence: apps/web/lib/data/supabase-provider.ts:160-163 (only original.jpg paths collected), 165-179 (re-signed per load), 611-620 (getDraftSnapUrl signs original) vs apps/web/lib/data/data-provider.ts:216 (comment says thumb), 527 (no cacheControl); apps/web/components/path/PathPebbleRow.tsx:112-118 (size-16 slot); apps/web/components/path/PebbleCard.tsx:120-127 (size-8 slot); apps/web/lib/utils/process-pebble-image.ts:14-21 (thumb variant produced)
findings.remediation: Sign and render thumb.jpg for list/thumbnail slots (original only in the detail view), memoize the signed-URL map in the provider keyed by storage_path with reuse until near-expiry instead of re-signing on every reload, and pass an explicit cacheControl on upload. Mirrors the iOS repository's TTL approach the comments already cite.

findings.title: EXIF/GPS stripping has no regression test; the privacy guarantee rests on a code comment
findings.detail: ImagePipeline.encodeJPEG deliberately passes only the lossy-compression key to CGImageDestination so no EXIF/GPS/TIFF dictionaries are written, and this is currently correct. But no test uploads a GPS-tagged fixture and asserts the processed output carries no location metadata - the test suite has ImageFormatValidator and ExifCaptureDate coverage (the latter tests reading the capture date, not stripping), and no ImagePipeline test at all. A future edit that starts copying source properties (a common change when preserving orientation or color-profile metadata) would silently reintroduce GPS coordinates of intimate moments into uploaded photos, and nothing on this surface or in CI would notice. For the product's highest-impact single asset, the invariant deserves a mechanical pin.
findings.evidence: apps/ios/Pebbles/Features/PebbleMedia/ImagePipeline.swift:95-115 (comment-only guarantee at 97-99); apps/ios/PebblesTests/ has no ImagePipeline test (ls | grep -i pipeline: empty); grep -rniE 'gps|exif|metadata' apps/ios/PebblesTests matches only ExifCaptureDateTests.swift; apps/ios/Pebbles/Features/PebbleMedia/ExifCaptureDate.swift:5-8 confirms the strip is load-bearing by design
findings.remediation: Add a Swift Testing case that builds or embeds a JPEG fixture carrying a GPS EXIF dictionary, runs ImagePipeline.process, and asserts CGImageSourceCopyPropertiesAtIndex on both outputs contains no kCGImagePropertyGPSDictionary and no kCGImagePropertyExifDictionary.

findings.title: The M51 privacy-grade reinterpretation backfilled pebbles but not pebble_drafts, so pre-M51 drafts publish as connections-visible without a fresh owner choice
findings.detail: M51 reinterpreted visibility 'private' from owner-only to connections-visible and backfilled every existing pebbles row to 'secret' precisely because letting old rows become connection-visible would be a silent privacy regression. But all three clients always write visibility into pebble_drafts.payload, and between drafts shipping (2026-07-29) and grade activation (2026-08-17) every draft was saved with the then-default 'private' — chosen when it meant owner-only. The migration touched only public.pebbles; no sweep or hydration mapping exists for drafts: web applyDraftPayload, iOS PebbleDraft(payload:known:), and Android toDraft all restore 'private' verbatim, and publishing passes it straight to create_pebble, producing a pebble visible to every mutual connection. The record flows do land a resumed draft on the privacy step with the value pre-selected, but it is prefilled — a user who remembers choosing 'private' as owner-only has no cue that its meaning changed underneath them. This recreates for the drafts store exactly the regression the pebbles backfill was written to prevent, on an intimate-content product where the exposed rows are emotional records.
findings.evidence: packages/supabase/supabase/migrations/20260817130000_pebble_visibility_grades.sql:30-36 (backfill updates public.pebbles only; no pebble_drafts statement anywhere in the migration); docs/decisions/log.md:386-389 (M51 entry: all three clients sent visibility 'private' explicitly; backfill rationale); apps/web/components/record/draft-payload.ts:44-46 + 155 ('private' restored verbatim); apps/ios/Pebbles/Features/Path/Models/PebbleDraftPayload.swift:207-209 (Visibility(rawValue:) keeps .private); apps/android/app/src/main/kotlin/app/pbbls/android/features/path/models/PebbleDraftPayload.kt:168 (visibility ?: defaults keeps PRIVATE); apps/android/app/src/main/kotlin/app/pbbls/android/features/path/record/RecordFlowModel.kt:238 (resume lands on PRIVACY step prefilled, not re-asked as a gap)
findings.remediation: Ship one migration sweeping stale drafts: update pebble_drafts set payload = jsonb_set(payload, '{visibility}', '"secret"') where updated_at < '2026-08-17' (activation time) and payload->>'visibility' = 'private' — same updated_at-trigger caution as the pebbles backfill if a trigger exists on the table. Optionally add the same guard for web localStorage autosave snapshots at hydration.

findings.title: Orphaned snap uploads accumulate in pebbles-media with no sweep despite an in-code claim that a server-side sweep handles them
findings.detail: Snaps are uploaded to storage before the pebble row exists (uploadSnap runs at photo-pick time), so abandoning the composer, re-picking a photo, or a failed publish strands original.jpg and thumb.jpg pairs in the private bucket. QuickPebbleEditor's comment asserts 'the server-side sweep handles them', but no periodic orphan sweep exists anywhere in the repo: the only storage cleanup is the delete-account function, which walks the user's prefix at account deletion. Orphaned intimate photos therefore persist indefinitely for active accounts (a retention/cost hazard), and deletePebbleMedia's best-effort storage removal after the DB delete adds more orphans on its console.warn path. The media quota guards bound per-pebble attachments but do nothing for unattached files, so a user cycling photos in the composer grows unreferenced storage without limit.
findings.evidence: apps/web/components/path/QuickPebbleEditor.tsx:103-108 (claim); apps/web/lib/data/supabase-provider.ts:522-535 (upload before row), 546-553 (best-effort remove with warn); grep of packages/supabase for sweep/orphan/cron finds only supabase/functions/delete-account/index.ts:69-89 (purge-time prefix walk); no scheduled function or cron migration exists
findings.remediation: Add a scheduled orphan sweep (edge function on a cron, or pg_cron) that lists pebbles-media prefixes older than N hours and deletes files whose snap id appears in no pebble's snaps and no draft payload; or defer upload to publish time. Update the in-code comment either way so it stops asserting a sweep that does not exist.

findings.title: Operator accounts cannot enroll MFA and destructive admin actions need only a live session cookie
findings.detail: config.toml disables TOTP MFA enrollment and verification outright and sets secure_password_change=false, so an admin account, whose compromise exposes every user's submitter email, all aggregate emotional analytics, and full moderation power, is protected by exactly one password. No admin action requires recent re-authentication: admin_delete_glyph permanently destroys a marketplace glyph and every buyer's entitlement, and log publishing pushes content to all users, each behind only a client-side confirm dialog. admin_list_glyph_submissions additionally returns the full submission history with emails in one unpaginated call, so a hijacked session exfiltrates the entire dataset in one request with no rate or size friction and no audit record.
findings.evidence: packages/supabase/supabase/config.toml:285-288 (totp enroll_enabled=false, verify_enabled=false), :211 (secure_password_change=false); 20260701102810_glyph_marketplace_curation.sql:119-129 (admin_delete_glyph preconditions: is_admin + existence only), :166-205 (unpaginated listing with emails); apps/admin/app/(authed)/pebblestore/glyphs/_components/SubmissionCard.tsx:141-177 (client-side dialogs); grep -rni 'mfa|totp' over apps/admin: zero hits
findings.remediation: Enable TOTP MFA and enforce enrollment for is_admin accounts (aal2 check inside is_admin or in the admin guard), turn on secure_password_change, add a server-verified recent-auth requirement to admin_delete_glyph and log deletion, and paginate admin_list_glyph_submissions.

findings.title: A hot session can purge the account and rotate the password with no re-authentication or notification
findings.detail: The two highest-harm actions reachable from iOS gate on nothing but a live token. Account deletion shows a client-side dialog and then calls the delete-account edge function, which requires only auth.getUser() to succeed; the purge is immediate and irreversible. Password change submits a new password with no current-password field (the currentPassword state variable exists but is never rendered), and the committed auth config has secure_password_change = false and the password-changed notification template commented out, so a session thief can silently take over the account or destroy an entire emotional history from an unlocked phone or a stolen refresh token. The public-profile flip, an exposure-widening action, is likewise a bare toggle. Refresh-token rotation and a one-hour JWT are the only ceiling.
findings.evidence: apps/ios/Pebbles/Features/Profile/Sheets/SettingsSheet.swift:155-166 (client-only dialog), 404-416 (deleteAccount), 23 and 344-359 (unused currentPassword; new-password-only form), 496-500 (auth.update), 488-494 (public_profile direct update); packages/supabase/supabase/functions/delete-account/index.ts:52-58; packages/supabase/supabase/config.toml:211 (secure_password_change = false), 236-240 (notification template commented out)
findings.remediation: Enable secure_password_change and the password-changed notification in the auth config, require a fresh password or provider re-auth in the delete-account function (verify a recent auth_time claim or a just-issued token), add the current-password field on iOS, and send a deletion-requested notification email before executing the purge.

findings.title: No session-refresh middleware: RSC token refreshes discard rotated refresh tokens, causing reuse-detection logouts
findings.detail: apps/admin has no middleware/proxy file, so the @supabase/ssr session is only ever written by the auth route handlers and server actions. When an admin returns after access-token expiry, requireAdmin's getUser() in the (authed) layout triggers a token refresh inside a Server Component, where cookie writes throw and are swallowed (the code comment acknowledges this). The rotated refresh token is therefore lost; subsequent RSC requests re-present the already-consumed refresh token. With Supabase's default refresh-token rotation and reuse detection, reuse outside the grace interval revokes the whole session family and force-logs the admin out, and until then every request pays an extra auth round trip. This is the exact footgun the @supabase/ssr documentation's middleware pattern exists to prevent. Consequence is operational friction and confusing auth behavior on an internal tool, not data exposure.
findings.evidence: find apps/admin -name 'middleware.*' returns nothing (also no proxy file in the app listing); apps/admin/lib/supabase/server.ts:23-31 (setAll catch with comment 'Server Component cookies are read-only'); apps/admin/lib/supabase/admin-guard.ts:22 (getUser in RSC layout path via app/(authed)/layout.tsx:7)
findings.remediation: Add the Supabase session-refresh middleware (Next 16: check node_modules/next/dist/docs for the current middleware/proxy convention) that calls getUser/getClaims and persists refreshed cookies on every matched request, per the @supabase/ssr SSR guide, and verify a stale-session page load lands one Set-Cookie.

findings.title: No wrong-role negative tests exist for the ~20 is_admin-gated admin RPCs
findings.detail: Every privileged admin RPC (approve_glyph, admin_find_user, admin_list_glyph_submissions, admin_attribute_glyph, admin_create_achievement, the analytics getters, etc.) is granted to all authenticated users and relies solely on a copy-pasted in-body is_admin(auth.uid()) guard. Nothing exercises the rejection path: no harness in packages/supabase/scripts/ calls any admin RPC as a non-admin and asserts 42501. The repo has already documented and lived the failure mode that makes this dangerous: create-or-replace re-emissions of a function body silently drop each other's changes (root CLAUDE.md standing rule; the purge_account union incident), so a future migration re-emitting one of these bodies without the guard would ship with zero signal. If that happens on admin_list_glyph_submissions or admin_find_user, any authenticated app user can dump submitter emails or resolve emails to user ids; on the mutation RPCs, any user can tamper with the catalog, prices, and moderation state.
findings.evidence: grep -rn 'not_admin|42501' packages/supabase/scripts/ matches only a comment (verify-account-purge.ts:159); verify-public-profile.ts covers only get_public_profile; grants at 20260630084718_admin_glyph_moderation.sql:178-182 and 20260701102810_glyph_marketplace_curation.sql:214-217 give execute to all authenticated; re-emission hazard documented in root CLAUDE.md 'Standing cross-surface rules' and migration 20260731090000_purge_account_union.sql
findings.remediation: Add a verify-admin-rpcs.ts harness (same style as verify-public-profile.ts) that signs up a throwaway non-admin user, calls every admin_* / analytics / moderation RPC, and asserts each fails with 42501; run it against the linked project after any migration batch touching those functions, and wire it into the audit signals.

findings.title: Auth session tokens and intimate draft content ride device backups: allowBackup=true with no extraction rules over unencrypted SharedPreferences
findings.detail: AndroidManifest.xml declares android:allowBackup="true" with no android:dataExtractionRules or android:fullBackupContent (grep across app/src returns nothing; res/xml contains only locales_config.xml). The Supabase session is persisted by supabase-kt's default session manager because install(Auth) sets no custom sessionManager, and that default writes the access and refresh tokens to plain SharedPreferences, not Keystore-backed storage. The composer crash snapshot (pebble name, description, emotion, souls) also lives in the pebbles_prefs SharedPreferences file. Under Auto Backup and device-to-device transfer, both files are eligible for inclusion: a restored backup on another device resurrects a live refresh token (account takeover surface) and intimate draft text outside the app's control. The failure scenario is a user's Google backup restored to a new or second-hand device, or backup-extraction tooling against a device without a strong lock, yielding a usable session token for an account holding mental-state records.
findings.evidence: apps/android/app/src/main/AndroidManifest.xml:12 (allowBackup="true"); apps/android/app/src/main/kotlin/app/pbbls/android/services/SupabaseService.kt:51-58 (no sessionManager override); grep for dataExtractionRules|fullBackupContent in apps/android/app/src/main returns nothing; grep for EncryptedSharedPreferences|Keystore in app/src returns nothing; ComposerSnapshotStore.kt:33-35, 75 (pebbles_prefs, MODE_PRIVATE plain prefs)
findings.remediation: Add android:dataExtractionRules (and fullBackupContent for the d2d path) excluding the supabase-kt session prefs file and pebbles_prefs, or set allowBackup=false outright; record the decision. Optionally supply a Keystore-backed SessionManager (EncryptedSharedPreferences) to supabase-kt and mirror the decision check on iOS/Keychain parity.

findings.title: Play service-account JSON and upload keystore exposed to a mutable-tag third-party action in the release workflow
findings.detail: android-release.yml mirrors KEYSTORE_BASE64 and PLAY_SERVICE_ACCOUNT_JSON into job-level env, making both visible to every step in the job, and then passes the service-account JSON in plaintext to r0adkll/upload-google-play@v1, a third-party action pinned only to a mutable major tag rather than a commit SHA. gradle/actions and the GitHub-owned actions are likewise tag-pinned. A compromised or hijacked tag update to any of these actions executes with the Play publishing credential and the signing keystore in scope, which is sufficient to publish a malicious build of an intimate-data app to the Play track. No dependabot or audit automation exists to surface a compromised or vulnerable action version. Fork PRs are safe (pull_request events carry no secrets) and the deploy-beta label gates PR builds, so the exposure is specifically the supply-chain trust in mutable action refs.
findings.evidence: .github/workflows/android-release.yml:50-54 (job-level env mirror of both secrets), 105-113 (r0adkll/upload-google-play@v1 with serviceAccountJsonPlainText), 57-68 (tag-pinned actions); .github/ contains no dependabot.yml or renovate config (checked)
findings.remediation: Pin all third-party actions to full commit SHAs (bot-updated), move the two secret mirrors from job env to the minimal steps that need them, and prefer passing the service account via a file with scoped permissions; add dependabot's github-actions ecosystem so action bumps arrive as reviewed PRs.

findings.title: Destructive moderation operations (admin_delete_glyph cascade, takedown, log delete) have no runnable harness
findings.detail: admin_delete_glyph issues a bare 'delete from public.glyphs' whose FK graph cascades to glyph_submissions and glyph_entitlements: a buyer who purchased the glyph but has not yet placed it on a pebble or soul loses the purchased item and the karma spent, silently and irreversibly. Whether the delete is instead blocked (pebbles.glyph_id has no on-delete action, souls.glyph_id is on delete restrict) depends on usage state, and the blocked path surfaces as an unmapped generic error (messageFor has no case for FK violations). None of this is exercised by anything runnable: the packages/supabase verify-* harnesses never call an admin RPC, and verify-account-purge.ts explicitly seeds submissions directly to avoid the admin gate. The only verification that ever existed is an 8-step manual checklist in the design doc. The repo's own bar for destructive operations (a seeded, asserting, re-runnable harness like verify-account-purge.ts) is established one directory over and simply not applied to the back-office's destructive surface.
findings.evidence: glyphs/actions.ts:112-122 (deleteGlyph, comment 'cascades to its submission + entitlements. Destructive.'); packages/supabase/supabase/migrations/20260701102810_glyph_marketplace_curation.sql:119-129 (function body); 20260630003348_glyph_marketplace.sql:13,33,44 (on delete cascade FKs); 20260411000001_core_tables.sql:61 and 20260426000000_add_glyph_to_souls.sql:31 (restricting FKs); grep 'admin_delete_glyph|approve_glyph|reject_glyph' over packages/supabase/scripts/ matches only verify-account-purge.ts:158 which bypasses the RPCs; moderation design doc section 9 (manual-only)
findings.remediation: Write verify-glyph-moderation.ts on the verify-account-purge.ts pattern: seed an admin, submitter, and buyer; drive approve/reject/delist/attribute/delete through the real RPCs; assert entitlement survival on delist, entitlement destruction plus karma ledger state on delete, and the blocked-delete path when a pebble or soul references the glyph; map the FK-violation error code in messageFor.

findings.title: Account-menu trigger in the top bar suppresses the focus outline with no focus-visible replacement
findings.detail: TopBar's DropdownMenuTrigger (the control that opens the sign-out menu) sets outline-none in its className without any focus-visible ring or border substitute, unlike every other control in the ui kit which pairs outline-none with focus-visible:ring styles. A keyboard user tabbing through the header gets no visible indication when this control has focus, violating WCAG 2.4.7 on the one control that reaches sign-out. The trigger also sets cursor-default, further masking its interactivity. Because Base UI's Menu.Trigger renders an unstyled element, the shadcn default styles do not apply here; the custom className is the only styling this control gets.
findings.evidence: apps/admin/components/layout/TopBar.tsx:30 (className with outline-none and no focus-visible: token, contrast with components/ui/button.tsx:7 which pairs outline-none with focus-visible:border-ring focus-visible:ring-3)
findings.remediation: Append focus-visible:border-ring focus-visible:ring-3 focus-visible:ring-ring/50 (the kit's standard pair) to the trigger's className, or render the trigger through the Button component.

findings.title: Rive logo autoplays and loops regardless of the reduce-motion setting, with no static fallback or pause
findings.detail: RiveLogo hands RiveAnimationView autoplay = true unconditionally. The Rive runtime drives its own render loop, so unlike Compose animations it is unaffected by the system animator-duration-scale that the app's rememberReduceMotion helpers read; under 'Remove animations' the Welcome screen still shows a continuously looping vector animation with no pause control, while the carousel beside it correctly stops. The reduce-motion helper is also deliberately duplicated as two private per-file copies (the ValenceFan comment records the copy), and each caches the setting with remember so a mid-session settings change is not picked up. Celebration surfaces (AchievementMomentOverlay, KarmaEarnedCapsule) carry no explicit gate either, relying entirely on the framework's animation-scale behavior.
findings.evidence: apps/android/app/src/main/kotlin/app/pbbls/android/rive/RiveLogo.kt:53 (setRiveResource(autoplay = true), no gate in file); features/path/valence/ValenceFan.kt:201-216 ('deliberately copied' helper, remember-cached read); features/welcome/WelcomeScreen.kt:283-291 (second copy); no reduce-motion reference in features/karma/AchievementMomentOverlay.kt or KarmaEarnedCapsule.kt (rg 'reduceMotion|ANIMATOR_DURATION_SCALE' listing)
findings.remediation: Hoist rememberReduceMotion into theme/ as the single shared helper, pass it to RiveLogo and render the placeholder/static first frame (autoplay = false) when set, and gate the celebration overlays explicitly.

findings.title: Fixed dp heights under sp-scaled text with no verification at large font scales
findings.detail: Multiple containers pin dp heights around sp-scaled text: the welcome carousel pager is a fixed 110dp, week-roll cells are fixed 96dp with two text lines inside, and the repo's own parity audit records that no font-scaling pass has ever been done on either platform. At Android's larger accessibility font scales (up to 2x on many devices) the sp text grows while the dp boxes do not, clipping or overlapping the copy on first-run and Path surfaces. No screenshot preview or test renders at an elevated fontScale, so regressions are invisible to the SDK-less maintainer loop that reviews UI exclusively through CI screenshots.
findings.evidence: apps/android/app/src/main/kotlin/app/pbbls/android/features/welcome/WelcomeCarousel.kt:60 (.height(110.dp)); features/path/components/WeekRoll.kt:92 (.height(96.dp)); docs/superpowers/specs/2026-07-16-android-parity-audit.md:147 ('several Android layouts pin dp heights ... no pass has been done'); rg 'fontScale' apps/android/app/src/screenshotTest returns nothing
findings.remediation: Add @Preview(fontScale = 2f) variants for the funnel, Path, and record-flow screenshot previews so clipping is visible in the CI artifact, then convert pinned heights to heightIn(min) or intrinsic sizing where the render shows loss.

findings.title: User snap photos are hidden from TalkBack (contentDescription = null on informative images)
findings.detail: The photo a user attaches to a pebble is core content of the memory, but every surface that renders it passes contentDescription = null: the Path row thumbnail, the detail-view snap frame, and the composer's attached-photo preview. TalkBack users get no indication a photo exists on a pebble at all, an information gap rather than a decoration correctly hidden. A generic localized description ('Your photo for this pebble') would restore presence even without image understanding; the merged row semantics do not mention the photo either.
findings.evidence: apps/android/app/src/main/kotlin/app/pbbls/android/features/path/components/PathSnapThumb.kt:43; features/path/read/PebbleSnapFrame.kt:60; features/pebblemedia/AttachedPhotoView.kt:125
findings.remediation: Add a pebble_snap_a11y string (en and fr) and pass it as contentDescription on the three image sites, mirroring the same fix on the iOS AsyncImage counterparts.

findings.title: Locale key drift between en.json and fr.json is mechanically undetectable: types check against en.json only and no parity gate exists
findings.detail: next-intl messages are typed via messages.d.ts against en.json alone, so any key added to en.json but forgotten in fr.json compiles cleanly, lints cleanly (web lint is green in the baseline), and silently renders the fallback or the raw key for French users at runtime. Parity is exact today (829 = 829 verified during this audit), but nothing in the repo or CI re-verifies it: .github/workflows contains no web job at all, and no vitest test diffs the key sets. On a bilingual EU-first product this is the exact drift class the criterion warns about, and it will regress on the first rushed copy change.
findings.evidence: apps/web/lib/i18n/messages.d.ts:1-8 (Messages: typeof en.json only); .github/workflows/ contains only android.yml, android-release.yml, arkaik.yml, lab-note-reminder.yml; no *.test.ts under apps/web touches lib/i18n (test file list checked); parity verified manually via recursive key diff of en.json and fr.json.
findings.remediation: Add a vitest test in apps/web/lib/i18n that flattens both message files and asserts identical key sets (runs in the existing npm test), and consider extending it to assert non-empty values; wire web lint/test into a CI workflow so the gate actually executes on PRs.

findings.title: apps/ios/CLAUDE.md bans if #available guards while three now exist in the codebase
findings.detail: The always-loaded iOS instruction file states in bold 'iOS 17 APIs only. No backports, no if #available guards', but the tree contains #available(iOS 26.0, *) in KarmaEarnedCapsule and GlyphTabBar and #available(iOS 18, *) in ValenceStoneStyle.
