The decision log entry for #727 already flags that the line 'is now contradicted by the codebase and needs rewording' to 'no availability guards around APIs that have an iOS 17 equivalent', but the reword is deferred to the next grooming pass, so every iOS agent session since 2026-08-24 loads a rule the code violates. Failure scenarios: an agent 'fixes' the existing guards by removing them (breaking iOS 26 styling), refuses a legitimately needed guard, or burns time reconciling the contradiction against the decision log.
findings.evidence: apps/ios/CLAUDE.md:12; apps/ios/Pebbles/Features/Karma/KarmaEarnedCapsule.swift:68; apps/ios/Pebbles/Features/Glyph/Views/GlyphTabBar.swift:67; apps/ios/Pebbles/Features/Path/Valence/ValenceStoneStyle.swift:168; docs/decisions/log.md:415-424 (2026-08-24 #727 entry, Consequences)
findings.remediation: Apply the reword the decision log already specifies (ban guards only around APIs with an iOS 17 equivalent, citing MeshGradient as the precedent) in apps/ios/CLAUDE.md now; the repo's no-per-PR-edit policy governs learnings, not corrections of a rule its own decision log declares wrong.

findings.title: packages/supabase lint is a placeholder that exits 0 while checking nothing, yet root guidance names it as the workspace proof
findings.detail: The lint script is literally an echo ('placeholder, no lint step yet') that always succeeds, and the root CLAUDE.md task-size triage tells agents to run 'npm run lint --workspace=packages/supabase' as the scoped check for small changes touching that workspace. An agent following instructions gets a green turbo summary and reasonably believes SQL and TypeScript in the package were checked; in reality nothing ran. This converts the documented verification loop into false assurance, which is worse than an absent loop because it terminates the agent's search for proof.
findings.evidence: packages/supabase/package.json ('lint': 'echo placeholder, no lint step yet'); docs/quality/audits/2026-08/baseline.md:11; CLAUDE.md:44 (workspace-scoped lint named for packages/supabase)
findings.remediation: Either wire a real check (eslint over scripts/ and src/, optionally sqlfluff over migrations) or make the script exit nonzero with a clear 'no lint exists, run build instead' message so it cannot pass as proof.

findings.title: The highest-impact DB standing rules have no mechanical backstop: purge coverage, catalog resync, and function re-emission are prose-only defenses
findings.detail: Three root standing rules guard silent-corruption hazards: purge_account table coverage must move in lockstep with verify-account-purge.ts, reference-table inserts must re-run sync_achievement_catalog in the same transaction, and batches re-emitting the same function body must be manually unioned. All three rely entirely on an agent having loaded and obeyed the rule; no CI check diffs the purge function's table list against the harness's zero-row assertions, no check pairs emotion/domain inserts with a resync call in the same migration file, and nothing detects two pending migrations re-emitting one function (5 migrations already re-emit purge_account, and #687 showed the failure is silent with no git conflict). Failure scenario: a milestone adds a user-owned table, the agent misses the rule, purge_account leaves intimate rows behind, and the harness passes because it never learned about the table, exactly the incident class the rules were written after.
findings.evidence: CLAUDE.md:81-83 (the three rules); grep -rln 'create or replace function public.purge_account' packages/supabase/supabase/migrations/ returns 5 files; grep of .github/workflows for purge_account returns nothing; docs/decisions/log.md:371 (#687 incident); packages/supabase/scripts/verify-account-purge.ts:25-27 (standing rule restated in the harness header)
findings.remediation: Add a small CI script on packages/supabase/** PRs that (a) extracts the table list from the latest purge_account body and diffs it against the tables asserted in verify-account-purge.ts, (b) fails when a migration inserts into emotions/domains without sync_achievement_catalog() in the same file, and (c) warns when a PR batch contains two re-emissions of one function name.

findings.title: No CI detects drift between migrations and the committed generated types/database.ts
findings.detail: AGENTS.md mandates regenerating and committing database.ts after any migration change, and the regen is scripted (db:types), but nothing verifies the committed file actually matches the schema: no workflow triggers on packages/supabase/** and no job regenerates types and runs git diff --exit-code (the criterion's own l4 example). The workspace has already been bitten by a corrupted database.ts (the documented TS1434 stderr-leak incident that broke every TypeScript consumer and Vercel deploys), which shows both that drift happens and that its blast radius spans web and admin. Failure scenario: a migration lands via a PR whose author skipped the regen; web code autocompletes against stale types, and a column rename becomes a runtime undefined instead of a compile error.
findings.evidence: AGENTS.md:2-9 (regen mandate); packages/supabase/package.json db:types; no workflow with a packages/supabase paths filter in .github/workflows/ (ls + grep); packages/supabase/CLAUDE.md:48 (TS1434 incident narrative)
findings.remediation: Add a CI job on packages/supabase/** that spins up supabase-cli, applies migrations, runs the committed db:types script, and fails on git diff --exit-code types/database.ts, so the same entry point runs locally and in CI.

findings.title: docs/arkaik/arkaik.json declares the map hosted while the file map is the one actually maintained, and the skill orders agents to stop editing it
findings.detail: The arkaik skill opens with a check-first rule: if docs/arkaik/arkaik.json exists the map is hosted, agents must not edit bundle.json, and 'if the MCP tools are unavailable, say so and stop rather than falling back to the file'. arkaik.json exists (added in 2d63805e), no arkaik-mcp configuration exists in the repo (no .mcp.json), yet bundle.json has received 13 commits since and is the artifact CI gates and root CLAUDE.md names. A strictly obedient agent invoking the skill would halt map maintenance entirely (causing silent map drift), while current practice violates the skill's letter on every update; either way the instruction chain contradicts itself at the exact decision point the skill says to check first. This is the 'two maps disagreeing' state the skill itself warns about.
findings.evidence: .claude/skills/arkaik/SKILL.md:46-61 (check-first box, 'say so and stop'); docs/arkaik/arkaik.json (project_id prj_5dDiZc-G6lseF3cb, remote https://arkaik.app); git log: arkaik.json added 2d63805e, 13 bundle.json commits since (git log --oneline --since=2026-07-30 -- docs/arkaik/bundle.json | wc -l); no .mcp.json at repo root; CLAUDE.md:57 directs edits to bundle.json
findings.remediation: Delete docs/arkaik/arkaik.json if the file map is authoritative, or if the hosted project is real, add a repo-local note (and a skill parameter) stating that this repo intentionally dual-runs the file map and which one wins, so the skill's stop rule does not fire.

findings.title: Logs boards render database failures as empty states, indistinguishable from 'no entries'
findings.detail: Four files in the logs family log a failed select to the server console and then render from 'data ?? []': the features board, the announcements drafts board, and both shipped/published sections. On any transient DB or auth failure the admin sees 'No features in progress.' / 'No planned features.' instead of an error, and may conclude entries were lost or recreate duplicates. The surface already owns two better patterns applied elsewhere by the same authors: analytics cards catch fetcher throws and render ErrorBlock, and the reference-data pages (domains, achievements, emotions) branch on the error and render a destructive-styled message. The inconsistency means error surfacing depends on which route you are on, which is the definition of an improvised rather than structural failure path.
findings.evidence: app/(authed)/logs/features/page.tsx:32-38 (error logged, page renders grouped empty sections); app/(authed)/logs/announcements/page.tsx:19-23; app/(authed)/logs/features/_components/FeaturesShippedSection.tsx:24-30; app/(authed)/logs/announcements/_components/AnnouncementsPublishedSection.tsx:15-19; contrast domains/page.tsx:25-28 and achievements/page.tsx:78 (error UI rendered) and components/analytics/ActiveUsersChartCard.tsx:11-20 (ErrorBlock pattern)
findings.remediation: In the four logs files, branch on the select error and render the existing ErrorBlock (or the reference-pages' inline destructive message) instead of falling through to the empty-state copy.

findings.title: Unchecked casts on Json-returning RPCs and hand-mirrored row types bypass the generated database contract
findings.detail: Where an RPC returns jsonb, admin asserts the shape blind: lib/pebblestore/fetchers.ts:13 casts Json to AdminSubmission[] with 'as unknown as', and achievements/actions.ts:47 casts an RPC result to string without a justification comment. Where the generated types do carry structured Returns, admin re-declares the rows by hand instead of importing them: lib/analytics/types.ts states it mirrors the SQL views, and its nullability already diverges from the generated contract (generated get_pebble_enrichment fields are non-null; the hand type marks every field nullable). The hand copies are currently the safe direction of divergence, but nothing detects the unsafe direction, and the casts mean a schema change to the submissions payload compiles clean and fails at runtime in the moderation queue. Only lib/logs/types.ts follows the intended pattern of deriving from Database generics.
findings.evidence: lib/pebblestore/fetchers.ts:13; app/(authed)/achievements/actions.ts:47; app/(authed)/achievements/page.tsx:31, app/(authed)/domains/page.tsx:13, app/(authed)/emotions/palettes/page.tsx:12 (as-casts on RPC data); lib/analytics/types.ts:1-9 and 51-60 vs packages/supabase/types/database.ts:2288-2296 (nullability divergence); packages/supabase/types/database.ts:2105-2108 (admin_list_glyph_submissions Returns: Json); counter-example lib/logs/types.ts:3-5
findings.remediation: Import structured RPC returns from the generated Database type where they exist (analytics, achievements, domains, emotions lists) and delete the hand mirrors; for the two genuinely-Json RPCs (admin_list_glyph_submissions, admin_find_user) either change the SQL to 'returns table' so types generate, or add a narrow runtime validator at the cast site.

findings.title: isLogPlatform and its platform value list are defined three times on the surface, beside a module that already owns the sibling guards
findings.detail: lib/logs/options.ts is the designated home for log enum options and derives isLogSpecies and isLogStatus from its option arrays, but the platform guard was never added there. Instead, three independent copies exist: app/(authed)/logs/actions.ts:9-19 (own PLATFORM_VALUES array plus guard), lib/logs/parse-lab-note.ts:7-17 (second array in a different order plus guard), and app/(authed)/logs/_components/LogSection.tsx:121 (third guard). When a platform value is added (a plausible event: the enum already grew to include 'project' and 'infra'), a contributor must find and update all three, and a missed copy silently rejects the new value: the Lab Note prefill drops the platform field, or the form validation refuses a legitimate submission, with no error pointing at the stale copy.
findings.evidence: app/(authed)/logs/actions.ts:9-19; lib/logs/parse-lab-note.ts:7-17; app/(authed)/logs/_components/LogSection.tsx:121; lib/logs/options.ts:8-15 (PLATFORM_OPTIONS) and 27-33 (the pattern the guard should follow)
findings.remediation: Export a single isLogPlatform from lib/logs/options.ts derived from PLATFORM_OPTIONS (same as isLogSpecies/isLogStatus) and delete the three local copies.

findings.title: SupabaseService exposes its raw client publicly and SettingsScreen already invokes an edge function through it from view code
findings.detail: SupabaseService.client is a public val, and SettingsScreen's deleteAccount handler calls supabase.client.functions.invoke("delete-account") directly from the view file, bypassing the service layer that mediates every other network operation on the surface. This is a faithful 1:1 mirror of iOS (SettingsSheet.swift does the same), so it is mirrored debt rather than Android drift, but it is still the one place where swapping or instrumenting the transport would require touching a view, and the public client property is an open invitation for future view code to grow direct queries; nothing mechanical (lint rule, architecture test, CI grep) would catch the next occurrence. Account deletion is also the surface's most destructive action, exactly where the log-and-surface discipline of a named service method matters most.
findings.evidence: apps/android/app/src/main/kotlin/app/pbbls/android/features/profile/SettingsScreen.kt:194-207 (raw client call at 199) and import at :63; apps/android/app/src/main/kotlin/app/pbbls/android/services/SupabaseService.kt:46 (public client); mirror: apps/ios/Pebbles/Features/Profile/Sheets/SettingsSheet.swift:408; grep 'supabase.client' outside services/ returns only this hit plus MainActivity deep-link plumbing (MainActivity.kt:48,83)
findings.remediation: Add SupabaseService.deleteAccount() (invoke the edge function, then signOut) and call it from SettingsScreen; mirror the same extraction on iOS per the 1:1 rule. Optionally add a CI grep or Konsist test asserting no file under features/ references supabase.client.

findings.title: Edge functions and the verification harnesses are type-checked by nothing in the repo
findings.detail: packages/supabase/tsconfig.json includes only ["src","types"], so the workspace build (tsc --noEmit, the baseline's green 'supabase typecheck' row) covers a one-line re-export plus the generated file — while the code that actually runs (four edge functions, the shared engine, and the five contract harnesses) is Deno code checked by no configured command. deno run does not type-check by default, so a type error introduced into verify-account-purge.ts or delete-account/index.ts surfaces only at invocation time — for the harnesses, that means at the exact moment they are needed as the proof after a purge-touching batch, and a broken harness that fails to run is easily mistaken for a transient environment problem. The deno-lint-ignore directives in the functions show deno tooling is used ad hoc, but no script or doc pins it.
findings.evidence: packages/supabase/tsconfig.json ('include': ['src','types']); packages/supabase/src/index.ts (single re-export line); package.json scripts contain no deno check/test entry; baseline.md:10 green row covers only this include set; deno-lint-ignore usage at supabase/functions/_shared/compose-and-write.ts:52,82
findings.remediation: Add package scripts 'check:functions' and 'check:scripts' running deno check over supabase/functions/**/index.ts and scripts/*.ts, fold them into the workspace build or lint task, and run them in the supabase CI workflow once it exists.

findings.title: Collection create/update are multi-table writes stitched client-side, breaching the written RPC-first rule; no collection RPC exists to call
findings.detail: createCollection (supabase-provider.ts:841-853) inserts into collections then collection_pebbles as two sequential client statements; updateCollection (:867-881) runs up to three (update collections, delete all collection_pebbles, re-insert the new set). Root AGENTS.md states that a multi-table or multi-statement operation with no existing RPC requires creating one rather than stitching client calls, and grep of packages/supabase/supabase/migrations for a collection function confirms none exists, so this flow is a standing breach of the convention on the surface where it was authored. The delete-then-reinsert shape in updateCollection means a failure between the two statements leaves the collection silently emptied of members (the runtime atomicity exposure itself is REL-03 territory; the convention breach and the divergence risk across the three clients is this finding). Every other write family on web complies (pebbles via compose edge functions, connections/karma/glyphs via RPCs), which makes collections the drift point future surfaces will copy.
findings.evidence: apps/web/lib/data/supabase-provider.ts:841-853 and :867-881; root AGENTS.md section 'Supabase - prefer RPCs for multi-table writes'; grep -rn 'function public.*collection' packages/supabase/supabase/migrations returns zero hits
findings.remediation: Add save_collection (or create_collection/update_collection sibling pair with symmetric payloads) as a security definer RPC owning the collections + collection_pebbles writes with an in-body auth.uid() ownership check, and port the web provider to .rpc; check iOS/Android for the same stitching in the same change per the mirror rule.

findings.title: Dead gamification logic: computeKarmaDelta and the bounce computation functions have zero production callers yet remain documented as the live business logic and green-tested
findings.detail: lib/data/karma.ts exports a single function, computeKarmaDelta, whose only importer is its own test file; the karma shown to users is server-computed (v_karma_summary, before/after store diff in usePebbles.ts:22-27). The module duplicates the SQL compute_karma_delta with an explicit 'keep the two in sync' instruction (karma.ts:13-15), so agents are told to maintain parity with a function nothing runs. Likewise computeBounceLevel and the window roll/prune functions in bounce-levels.ts:24-76 have no importer outside the module (only the BOUNCE_THRESHOLDS display table is used, GamificationBlocks.tsx:56), bounce being served by v_bounce. apps/web/CLAUDE.md:71 still names both files as where gamification business logic lives, actively misleading every agent context, and karma.test.ts's 87 lines contribute green checkmarks that protect nothing. A related dead remnant: eslint.config.mjs:25 still restricts imports of the deleted @/lib/data/local-provider module. No dead-export analyzer (knip/ts-prune) exists to catch this class.
findings.evidence: grep -rn 'computeKarmaDelta' apps/web excluding karma.ts/karma.test.ts returns zero hits; grep -rn 'computeBounceLevel' returns only in-module uses; apps/web/CLAUDE.md:71; apps/web/eslint.config.mjs:25; ls apps/web/lib/data shows no local-provider.ts; grep 'knip|ts-prune|jscpd' in package.json files returns nothing
findings.remediation: Delete karma.ts plus its test (or move the parity assertion into a supabase-side harness against the real RPC), prune the unused bounce functions, drop the local-provider lint pattern, correct apps/web/CLAUDE.md:71, and add knip or ts-prune to the milestone audit cadence.

findings.title: No DPIA exists despite expanding Art. 9 processing, and operator analytics lack minimum-cohort thresholds
findings.detail: The product self-qualifies moods and reflections as Art. 9 health data, and processing has widened materially since the policy date (public profiles, pebble sharing, connections, a marketplace joining auth emails), yet no data protection impact assessment or Art. 9 memo exists in the repo beyond the policy text itself; Art. 35(3)(b) makes a DPIA hard to avoid for large-scale special-category processing, and it should predate the shipped features. Separately, the operator emotion-share dashboard aggregates with no minimum cohort: for a week where one or two users were active (the reference tooltip in admin conventions cites 12 active users total), the weekly emotion mix is effectively one identifiable person's emotional record rendered to the operator.
findings.evidence: grep -riE 'DPIA|data protection impact' over docs/, apps/, packages/ returns only docs/quality framework files; apps/web/docs/privacy/en.md:113-128 (Art. 9 self-qualification, dated 2026-04-09) versus migrations 20260730120000/20260817130000/20260730070347 (July-August 2026 features); 20260501000003_analytics_meaning_share.sql:41-53 (group by week+emotion, no HAVING threshold); apps/admin/CLAUDE.md tooltip example ('the 12 active users')
findings.remediation: Write and date a DPIA in docs/ covering the current processing inventory and gate future Art.-9-enlarging features on updating it; add a minimum-cohort HAVING clause (e.g. suppress emotion/domain shares for weeks with fewer than N distinct active users) to the analytics views.

findings.title: Sign-out and account deletion leave the composer draft snapshot and photo disk cache on device, and the snapshot is offered to the next signed-in user
findings.detail: Signing out clears only the in-memory signed-URL cache. The composer crash snapshot - intimate draft content in SharedPreferences - is cleared solely on publish/save/discard, and it is keyed by nothing user-specific: ComposerDraftCoordinator.hydrate() loads whatever snapshot exists and raises the restore prompt. On a shared device, user A signing out mid-draft (or after process death) and user B signing in leads to B being offered A's unpublished emotional content verbatim; the snapshot equally survives A's full account deletion. Coil's disk cache of snap photos likewise persists after sign-out. This is a storage-limitation and confidentiality failure on the client store that the criterion's own anchor names ('client-side stores persist personal data after logout').
findings.evidence: apps/android/app/src/main/kotlin/app/pbbls/android/RootScreen.kt:120-122 (only snapUrls?.invalidateAll() on session null); services/ComposerSnapshotStore.kt:33,46-75 (unscoped pebbles_prefs snapshot); services/ComposerDraftCoordinator.kt:88-96 (hydrate offers any existing snapshot); clear() called only from draft flows (ComposerDraftCoordinator.kt:109,136,149; CreatePebbleScreen.kt:235,251,403); no Coil diskCache clear anywhere (grep diskCache over kotlin sources)
findings.remediation: On the session dropping to null (and in deleteAccount before signOut), clear the composer snapshot and Coil's disk/memory caches; additionally key the snapshot by user id so a mismatched snapshot is never offered.

findings.title: Processor inventory names a nonexistent Gemma flow while omitting the real processors Android's outbound traffic touches
findings.detail: The only written processor list (policy section 6) covers Supabase (accurately, EU region) and Google Gemma - an AI processing flow that exists nowhere in the code. Meanwhile the Android surface's actual outbound endpoints include www.pbbls.app (Vercel-hosted legal docs, invite links, share pages - Vercel is unlisted with no DPA reference or region), Google as OAuth identity provider, Google Play as distributor plus Auto Backup recipient of app data, and a hardcoded WhatsApp community invite reachable from the Lab screen. Post-Schrems II, undocumented non-EEA hops for an intimate-data product are enforcement surface, and the inventory cannot be reconciled because it was never derived from code.
findings.evidence: apps/web/docs/privacy/en.md:161-176 (Supabase + Gemma only); code-derived endpoints: apps/android/app/src/main/kotlin/app/pbbls/android/components/LegalDocs.kt:14-15, features/path/models/SharedPebbleLink.kt:9, features/profile/SettingsScreen.kt:131, features/lab/models/LabConfig.kt:12 (WhatsApp), services/SupabaseService.kt:183-190 (Google OAuth); AndroidManifest.xml:12 (backup to Google); no inventory doc in docs/ (grep processor|DPA)
findings.remediation: Write the inventory from a code-derived endpoint/dependency sweep per surface, attach DPA references and regions (Vercel, Google), remove Gemma, document the transfer mechanism for each non-EEA hop, and add a PR-checklist tie between new outbound hosts and the inventory.

findings.title: The composer crash snapshot survives logout on disk and is offered to the next account
findings.detail: ComposerSnapshotStore writes the in-progress pebble draft (name, description, valence, emotion, tagged souls) as JSON to the caches directory. Neither sign-out call site clears it, and the file carries no user scoping, so after logout the previous user's emotional draft remains on disk and the restore prompt can offer it to whoever signs in next on the same device. On a shared or family device this exposes intimate content across accounts; it also contradicts the storage-limitation posture the privacy policy claims. The fix is one call: clear the snapshot (and any pending autosave) in the sign-out path.
findings.evidence: apps/ios/Pebbles/Services/ComposerSnapshotStore.swift:29-33 (caches-directory file, no user key); sign-out sites with no clear: apps/ios/Pebbles/Services/SupabaseService.swift:190-196, apps/ios/Pebbles/Features/Profile/ProfileView.swift:58, apps/ios/Pebbles/Features/Profile/Sheets/SettingsSheet.swift:409; restore offer logic: apps/ios/Pebbles/Features/Path/ComposerDraftCoordinator.swift:95-115
findings.remediation: Clear ComposerSnapshotStore (and cancel the autosave debounce) on sign-out and on account deletion, or scope the snapshot filename by user id and drop snapshots whose owner does not match the active session at restore time.

findings.title: Logout leaves the in-progress pebble draft, including emotional content and soul names, in localStorage
findings.detail: The composer crash-insurance autosave writes the full draft payload (pebble name, description, valence, intensity, emotion, newly typed soul names) to localStorage under pbbls-composer-draft, debounced and flushed on tab hide. Logout only calls supabase.auth.signOut and clears nothing else, so a draft abandoned mid-composition survives the session and is offered for restore ('Pick up where you left off?') to whoever next uses the browser profile, including a different account holder on a shared or public device. For an intimate-journal product this is residual special-category data persisting past the session boundary.
findings.evidence: apps/web/lib/hooks/useComposerAutosave.ts:6,84-101 (payload persisted); apps/web/lib/data/useSupabaseAuth.ts:179-184 (logout = signOut only); grep removeItem over the auth path: no clearing on SIGNED_OUT; restore copy at lib/i18n/messages/en.json record.draft.restoreTitle
findings.remediation: Clear pbbls-composer-draft (and any future personal localStorage keys) in the SIGNED_OUT branch of the onAuthStateChange handler and in deleteAccount; optionally namespace the key by user id so a different signer-in never sees another user's draft.

findings.title: The account email address cannot be rectified from the web client
findings.detail: The settings Informations section renders the email read-only and no code path calls auth.updateUser with an email anywhere in the web app, so the primary contact identifier, a personal data field under Art. 16, cannot be corrected self-serve. A user who loses access to their mailbox or made a typo at signup is permanently bound to it or must abandon the account entirely (deletion is the only out). The store roadmap has acknowledged 'no password reset or email change' since July.
findings.evidence: apps/web/components/settings/InformationsSection.tsx:16,39 (read-only email); grep 'updateUser({ email|updateEmail' over apps/web: zero; docs/superpowers/specs/2026-07-28-store-launch-roadmap.md:25
findings.remediation: Add an email-change flow using Supabase's double-confirmation (double_confirm_changes is already true in config.toml:207) once SMTP is configured; pair it with the security-notification work from the SAF-07 finding.

findings.title: Account deletion executes with no re-authentication step
findings.detail: The delete path is a plain confirm dialog: tapping 'Delete account' then 'Delete forever' immediately invokes the delete-account edge function, which purges all data and destroys the auth user. There is no password or provider re-authentication and no typed confirmation, so anyone holding an unlocked phone (or a session on a shared device) can irreversibly destroy the account and every pebble in it in two taps. For an intimate-data journal the asymmetry is stark: the data is unrecoverable by design (purge plus auth delete in one call) while the gate in front of it is the weakest possible. The criterion checklist explicitly asks that the confirmation flow re-authenticate before deleting.
findings.evidence: apps/android/app/src/main/kotlin/app/pbbls/android/features/profile/SettingsScreen.kt:194-207 (deleteAccount invokes functions.invoke("delete-account") directly) and :588-599 (ConfirmDeleteDialog with only onConfirm); packages/supabase/supabase/functions/delete-account/index.ts:61 (purge_account) and auth admin delete
findings.remediation: Require fresh credentials before the destructive call: password re-entry for email accounts and a fresh OAuth round-trip for SSO accounts (or minimally a type-to-confirm phrase), on both Android and iOS in the same change.

findings.title: No repo-visible mechanism tracks the App Store toolchain floor; the Xcode version is pinned nowhere
findings.detail: The iOS app builds only on Xcode Cloud, whose Xcode version is chosen in the App Store Connect console and recorded nowhere in the repo; ci_post_clone.sh selects no Xcode, there is no iOS GitHub workflow, and no dependabot/renovate config or release checklist watches Apple's annual SDK submission floor. Today this is survivable because Xcode Cloud defaults tend to be current, but when Apple raises the floor (each April) nothing in the repo or CI will warn before an upload is refused, and nothing records which toolchain produced a given release for reproduction.
findings.evidence: apps/ios/ci_scripts/ci_post_clone.sh (no xcode-select/XCODE_VERSION); ls .github/workflows = android.yml, android-release.yml, arkaik.yml, lab-note-reminder.yml; no dependabot.yml or renovate.json in repo; docs/quality/audits/2026-08/baseline.md (iOS has no GitHub Actions workflow)
findings.remediation: Record the Xcode Cloud workflow's Xcode version in apps/ios/README.md or project.yml comments, add a release-checklist item comparing it to Apple's current submission minimum, and enable a dependency bot over project.yml SPM pins.

findings.title: Web app ships with zero security headers: no CSP, no frame-ancestors, no HSTS, no Referrer-Policy in any tracked config
findings.detail: apps/web/vercel.json contains only a $schema key and apps/web/next.config.ts defines no headers(); there is no middleware and a repo-wide grep for every baseline header name returns nothing. The deployed PWA therefore runs on permissive PaaS defaults. Missing frame-ancestors/X-Frame-Options means any site can embed pbbls.app in an iframe and clickjack a signed-in user (the app is cookie/localStorage session based and fully interactive in a frame); missing CSP removes the main mitigation layer if any XSS or dependency compromise lands in an app that renders user-supplied text and photos of intimate emotional content; missing Referrer-Policy leaks share URLs (/p/{uuid} capability links) to third-party destinations via the referrer header, and the uuid IS the access capability per app/p/[id]/page.tsx:16-19.
findings.evidence: apps/web/vercel.json:1-3 (only $schema); apps/web/next.config.ts:1-6 (no headers()); rg -i 'Content-Security-Policy|X-Frame-Options|Strict-Transport|Referrer-Policy|Permissions-Policy|X-Content-Type' apps/web --glob '!node_modules' returns zero hits; no middleware.ts/proxy.ts exists; app/p/[id]/page.tsx:16-19 documents the uuid-as-capability share link that a leaked referrer would expose.
findings.remediation: Add a headers() block in next.config.ts (or vercel.json headers) setting HSTS, X-Content-Type-Options, Referrer-Policy strict-origin-when-cross-origin, Permissions-Policy, and frame-ancestors 'none'; introduce CSP report-only, then enforce; mirror the same baseline in apps/admin; record Vercel deployment-protection posture for previews in a tracked doc.

verification.note: Re-verified all cited evidence at the repo: vercel.json has only $schema, next.config.ts defines no headers(), no middleware/proxy file exists, no http-equiv meta or referrerPolicy attribute anywhere, and the header-name grep hits only the audit's own docs. The uuid-as-capability comment is verbatim at app/p/[id]/page.tsx:16-19. The core defect (zero security headers in tracked config) is real. But all three headline attack scenarios are overstated. (1) HSTS: Vercel injects Strict-Transport-Security max-age=63072000 on every HTTPS deployment automatically, so the marginal harm is near zero. (2) Referrer leak of /p/{uuid}: evergreen browsers have defaulted to strict-origin-when-cross-origin since ~2020, so cross-origin navigations send only the origin, never the uuid path; the capability does not leak under any modern browser default. (3) Clickjacking a signed-in user: the finding says the app is 'cookie/localStorage session based and fully interactive in a frame', but the session is cookie-based via @supabase/ssr 0.10.2 with DEFAULT_COOKIE_OPTIONS sameSite:'lax' (verified in the installed package; apps/web/lib/supabase/client.ts and server.ts pass no cookieOptions override). SameSite=Lax cookies are neither sent with a cross-site iframe's document request nor exposed to document.cookie in that context, so a framed pbbls.app renders signed out in modern browsers and the described authenticated clickjacking fails. The honest residual is the missing CSP as defense-in-depth, which is meaningful here: real DB-fed injection sinks exist (dangerouslySetInnerHTML on pebble.render_svg in components/shared-pebble/SharedPebbleView.tsx:56 and components/connections/ConnectionPebbleTile.tsx:41), and the app holds intimate personal content. But exploiting it requires a separate primary XSS or supply-chain compromise, and the standalone attack paths cited are blocked by platform/browser defaults. Adjusted to impact 3 x likelihood 2 = 6.

findings.title: Composer autosave draft in localStorage survives sign-out, exposing one user's in-progress pebble to the next account on a shared browser
findings.detail: useComposerAutosave persists the record-flow draft under the fixed key pbbls-composer-draft, and logout only calls supabase.auth.signOut() without clearing it (deleteAccount likewise only clears the auth session). On a shared or family device, user B signing in after user A sees A's unsent pebble draft (emotion, valence, description text of a potentially intimate moment) prefilled in the composer. The service worker side is handled correctly (Supabase responses are NetworkOnly, never cached), which makes this localStorage remnant the one user-scoped store that outlives the session, directly against the criterion's sign-out clearing requirement.
findings.evidence: apps/web/lib/hooks/useComposerAutosave.ts:6 (fixed STORAGE_KEY, not user-scoped) and :89 (setItem); apps/web/lib/data/useSupabaseAuth.ts:179-184 (logout body, no storage clearing) and :186-202 (deleteAccount, local signOut only); rg 'caches\.|localStorage\.removeItem|localStorage\.clear' over lib/components/app shows no clearing tied to auth state.
findings.remediation: Clear pbbls-composer-draft (and any other user-scoped keys such as pending invite state) in logout and deleteAccount, or key the autosave entry by user id and drop entries whose id does not match the active session on hydrate.

findings.title: The Play-declared account deletion URL is tracked nowhere in the repo, so declaration drift against the web deletion page is invisible
findings.detail: The web deletion flow exists and works (Settings > Delete account invoking the delete-account edge function), and Play policy requires that flow's URL to be declared in the Play Console Data safety section. No file in the repo records which URL was declared: docs/android-play-deploy.md, the decision log, and the arkaik bundle carry no deletion-URL entry. If the settings route moves or the declaration was entered differently (deep link vs page anchor), the mismatch would only surface as a Play policy rejection or removal, with no review-time signal. The deletion confirm also performs no re-authentication, a step both store review guidelines expect for destructive account actions.
findings.evidence: Deletion flow: apps/web/components/settings/DeleteAccountSection.tsx:36-82, apps/web/lib/data/useSupabaseAuth.ts:186-202. Absence: rg -i 'data.?safety|deletion url|account-deletion' over docs/ matches only quality templates and the decision log narrative; docs/android-play-deploy.md contains zero lines matching 'deletion'.
findings.remediation: Record the declared deletion URL in docs/android-play-deploy.md (or a store-metadata file), add a scheduled or CI HTTP probe asserting it returns 200 and renders the deletion entry point, and consider a password/OAuth re-auth step before invoking delete-account.

findings.title: Unbounded wildcard reads: logs boards fetch full markdown bodies, moderation RPC returns every submission with full strokes
findings.detail: No list read in the surface carries a limit. The four logs board queries use select('*') so every row's body_md_en and body_md_fr markdown bodies travel to the server component even though LogSection renders only title, platform, and one date; payload grows with every authored log and doubles per language. Worse, admin_list_glyph_submissions aggregates all submissions for a status into a single jsonb including each glyph's full strokes array; the 'approved' tab is the entire community market catalog and grows monotonically with users, so the moderation page's payload and RPC time grow without bound, with no pagination affordance in the RPC or the UI. Detail routes also over-fetch: achievements/[id] and domains/[id] pull the entire catalog to find one row.
findings.evidence: select('*') with no .limit: apps/admin/app/(authed)/logs/features/page.tsx:21-26, features/_components/FeaturesShippedSection.tsx:13-18, announcements/page.tsx:12-17, announcements/_components/AnnouncementsPublishedSection.tsx:8-13; rendered columns: LogSection.tsx:174-183. Unbounded jsonb_agg with strokes: packages/supabase/supabase/migrations/20260630084718_admin_glyph_moderation.sql:26-47; caller: apps/admin/lib/pebblestore/fetchers.ts:4-14, page apps/admin/app/(authed)/pebblestore/glyphs/page.tsx:21. Whole-catalog single-row fetches: achievements/[id]/page.tsx:15-20, domains/[id]/page.tsx:15-21. Grep for limit(|range( in apps/admin: zero hits.
findings.remediation: Project named columns for the boards (id, species, platform, status, title_en, updated_at, released_at, published, published_at) and add a sane .limit with a 'show all' escape; add p_limit/p_offset (or keyset on created_at) to admin_list_glyph_submissions and paginate the approved tab; fetch single rows by id for the detail editors.

findings.title: Cover images are stored and served as uncompressed originals with no cache-control
findings.detail: The cover-image upload performs no downscaling or recompression, only a 5 MB ceiling and MIME allowlist, and passes no cacheControl to the storage upload, so the object gets whatever default the SDK applies rather than a deliberate CDN/browser lifetime. The admin preview then fetches the stored original through a raw into a 160px-tall slot. Because the logs table drives the iOS Lab tab, every end user's Lab feed downloads whatever original the admin happened to pick, up to 5 MB per cover, multiplied across the user base for each published log; the fix point is this upload pipeline, not the readers. No storage transform parameters are used anywhere in the surface.
findings.evidence: apps/admin/app/(authed)/logs/_components/CoverImageInput.tsx:11 (MAX_BYTES 5 MB), :27-34 (type/size gates only, no canvas/createImageBitmap resize), :43-45 (upload with contentType but no cacheControl), :78-83 (raw with the lint rule disabled inline, fetching the original). User-facing consumer: packages/supabase/supabase/migrations/20260421000001_logs_table.sql:1-5,24. Grep for next/image and transform params (width=|quality=) in apps/admin: zero hits.
findings.remediation: Downscale client-side before upload (createImageBitmap + canvas to a bounded long edge, re-encode to webp/jpeg ~80), pass an explicit cacheControl (e.g. '31536000' since paths are content-addressed by uuid), and render the admin preview through next/image or a storage transform URL sized to the slot.

findings.title: The Path screen fetches the user's entire pebble history, render SVGs included, on every load and after every mutation
findings.detail: path_pebbles() returns every pebble the user has ever recorded in one response with no limit, and each row carries its render_svg markup string. PathScreen calls it on first composition, again after every create, edit, and delete (reload and reloadFocusing), and the record flow triggers it behind the success step. Payload size and decode time therefore grow linearly with account age on the app's most-visited screen, and every publish costs a full-history refetch plus a stats refresh. The no-pagination choice is documented and mirrors iOS, so this is a deliberate v1 tradeoff, but nothing bounds it and the UI already pages by week, so a week-windowed or keyset-paginated read would fit the existing rendering model.
findings.evidence: apps/android/app/src/main/kotlin/app/pbbls/android/services/PathService.kt:19-27 ('every pebble in one response ... no pagination'); features/path/models/Pebble.kt:28-29 (render_svg per row); features/path/PathScreen.kt:101-114 (initial load), :137-171 (full reload after delete/create/edit plus stats.refresh()).
findings.remediation: Add a keyset-paginated or week-windowed variant of path_pebbles (cursor on happened_at desc, id tiebreak) and fetch incrementally as the pager approaches older weeks; after a mutation, refresh only the affected week or apply the returned row locally. Contract change: mirror on iOS and web.

findings.title: The composer autosave snapshot survives sign-out in localStorage and is offered to the next account on the device
findings.detail: useComposerAutosave persists the in-progress pebble payload (name, description, emotion, and any other composed intimate content) under the fixed key pbbls-composer-draft with no user binding. Sign-out clears only Supabase auth state and the in-memory store; no code path removes the snapshot (clear() runs only on publish or server-draft save). On a shared or family device, user A signs out mid-compose, user B signs in, opens the composer, and the restore prompt offers user A's private journal text for adoption into user B's account. This is exactly the PRF-07 checklist item 'anything holding private content and not purged at sign-out is a finding', and it also cuts against the product's privacy-first posture.
findings.evidence: apps/web/lib/hooks/useComposerAutosave.ts:6 (fixed key), 84-91 (write), 66-74 (clear only via publish/save path in useComposerDrafts); apps/web/lib/data/useSupabaseAuth.ts:179-184 (logout clears nothing local); apps/web/app/profile/page.tsx:36-39; grep for localStorage.removeItem on any sign-out path returns nothing
findings.remediation: Clear the composer snapshot (and any other private localStorage keys) on the SIGNED_OUT branch of onAuthStateChange in useSupabaseAuth, or namespace the storage key by user id and discard snapshots whose owner does not match the active session.

findings.title: No bundle discipline tooling, zero dynamic imports, and two unused heavy dependencies declared (@rive-app/react-canvas, esbuild-wasm)
findings.detail: The web workspace has no bundle analyzer, no size gate, and no CI at all, so client JS growth is invisible. Not a single dynamic import exists in the codebase: framer-motion is statically imported in 8 files and modal/sheet-only UI ships eagerly; 25 of 33 routes are client components rendered behind a fully client provider tree. Meanwhile package.json declares @rive-app/react-canvas and esbuild-wasm as production dependencies with zero import sites anywhere in app/, components/, lib/ or scripts/, contradicting the workspace CLAUDE.md which still lists Rive as the canvas layer. Unused deps inflate install/audit surface and mislead agents reading the manifest; the absent tooling means the first-load JS of the main routes is unknown and unguarded, and a heavy dependency added tomorrow would ship unnoticed.
findings.evidence: apps/web/package.json:19 (@rive-app/react-canvas), 26 (esbuild-wasm); grep -rn 'rive-app|esbuild' over apps/web app/, components/, lib/, scripts/ returns nothing; grep for next/dynamic|React.lazy|import( across the same tree returns nothing; 25/33 page.tsx files carry "use client"; .github/workflows has no web workflow; apps/web/CLAUDE.md:22 still documents Rive
findings.remediation: Remove the two unused dependencies and fix the CLAUDE.md stack table; add @next/bundle-analyzer plus a first-load-JS budget check to a web CI workflow; dynamically import modal-only and below-the-fold motion-heavy components.

findings.title: No Core Web Vitals measurement or budget exists while the primary route's LCP is gated on the unbounded full-store fetch
findings.detail: There is no field RUM hook, no analytics or speed-insights package, no Lighthouse configuration, and no written numeric target for any route anywhere in the repo or docs. At the same time /path, the app's home, renders its primary content strictly client-side behind DataProvider's full-history load, so its LCP is a function of account size and network and grows over a user's lifetime with the product; nobody can currently observe that degradation because nothing measures it. A vitals regression introduced by any future change (or simply by users accumulating pebbles) will be discovered by users, not by the team, which is the exact failure mode this criterion exists to prevent.
findings.evidence: apps/web/package.json:14-60 (no vitals/analytics dep); grep for onLCP|onINP|onCLS|reportWebVitals|SpeedInsights across apps/web returns nothing; no lighthouserc*/budget file repo-wide; grep -rin 'lighthouse|LCP|INP' over docs/ yields no vitals content; apps/web/app/path/page.tsx:8-13 with components/layout/DataProvider.tsx:20-41 (client-fetch-gated primary content)
findings.remediation: Add @vercel/speed-insights (one component in the root layout) or a web-vitals reporting hook, write p75 budgets for /path, /record and /u/[handle] into docs, and review the field numbers at milestone boundaries; a Lighthouse CI assertion can follow once a web CI workflow exists.

findings.title: No PII inventory exists, so the operator surface's personal-data exposures (submitter emails) have no documented purpose mapping
findings.detail: The repo contains no personal-data inventory anywhere in docs/. The admin surface reads real PII: admin_list_glyph_submissions joins auth.users to return submitter_email and owner_email to the moderation queue, and admin_find_user resolves arbitrary emails to user ids. The purposes are only reconstructable from decisions-log prose, not from any field-to-purpose map, so nothing distinguishes a justified email exposure from scope creep in review, and a future widened projection would not be flagged against anything. Per the criterion checklist the missing inventory also caps the score for every surface. GDPR mapping is the GDP domain's concern; this finding is the engineering artifact gap.
findings.evidence: grep -rli 'PII|ROPA|data map|data inventory' docs/ matches only the Kritik criteria files and unrelated plans; email projections at packages/supabase/supabase/migrations/20260701102810_glyph_marketplace_curation.sql:189-191 and 132-143; rendered at apps/admin/app/(authed)/pebblestore/glyphs/_components/SubmissionCard.tsx:101
findings.remediation: Author docs/privacy/pii-inventory.md mapping every personal-data column and RPC projection (including admin-facing emails) to purpose and exposure surface; require the file to be updated in the same change that adds a personal-data field.

findings.title: No PII inventory exists, so the minimization practice on this surface is unverifiable against any stated purpose
findings.detail: Searched docs/ for PII, personal data, ROPA, data map, and inventory (case-insensitive): the only hit is the quality framework's own criteria file. No document maps the personal-data fields the Android client reads and writes (display name, handle, pebble free text, emotion/valence values, soul names, media paths, consent timestamps) to collection points, storage, and display. The client's column-level discipline is genuinely good, but without an inventory no reviewer can distinguish a purposeful field from an accreted one, and GDPR Art. 30 record-keeping has nothing to point at. This is a repo-wide gap surfacing in every cell; it caps this criterion at level 1 by the framework's own checklist rule. Failure scenario: a new column lands on profiles or pebbles with no recorded purpose, every surface dutifully fetches it, and nobody can later say why it exists or whether it may be dropped.
findings.evidence: grep -rli 'PII|personal data|ROPA|data map|data inventory' docs/ returns only docs/quality/criteria/prv-privacy-data-protection.md; find docs -iname '*pii*' -o -iname '*inventory*' -o -iname '*ropa*' returns the same single file; contrast with the field surface actually read at services/ProfileService.kt:34 and services/PathStatsService.kt:90-99
findings.remediation: Author the inventory once from packages/supabase/types/database.ts (one row per personal-data field: purpose, where collected, stored, transmitted, displayed per surface), commit it under docs/, and adopt the rule that a migration adding a personal-data column updates the inventory in the same change; a CI diff between generated types and the inventory can come later.

findings.title: Sign-up consent record carries no policy version and is stranded in auth user metadata
findings.detail: Android captures terms_accepted_at and privacy_accepted_at at sign-up and passes them through the sign-up data block into auth.users.raw_user_meta_data. Two defects: the record is a bare pair of timestamps with no policy version, so when the terms or privacy policy change there is no way to show which text a user accepted; and the code itself documents that the handle_new_user trigger does not copy these values into public.profiles, leaving the only demonstration-of-consent record buried in auth metadata where no product query or export path reads it. GDPR Art. 7(1) puts the burden of demonstrating consent on the controller. Failure scenario: a policy revision ships, a user disputes what they agreed to, and the stored record cannot answer which version was accepted or be surfaced without raw auth-schema access. Google OAuth sign-ups also never pass through consentMetadata at all (signInWithGoogle carries no data block), so OAuth users have no consent timestamps anywhere.
findings.evidence: apps/android/app/src/main/kotlin/app/pbbls/android/services/SupabaseService.kt:153-173 (signUp with consentMetadata; doc comment 'the current handle_new_user trigger does not copy them into public.profiles — a separate fix(db) issue'), 183-190 (signInWithGoogle passes no consent data), 249-253 (consentMetadata: two timestamps, no version field); ConsentMetadataTest.kt asserts exactly this shape
findings.remediation: Add a policy_version (or accepted document hash) key to consentMetadata on all clients simultaneously, fix handle_new_user to copy the consent fields into profiles (the already-acknowledged fix(db) issue), and record consent for OAuth sign-ups at first-session onboarding where no sign-up data block exists.

findings.title: AsyncImage's shared URLCache persists private photo bytes on disk beyond the signed-URL grant and beyond sign-out
findings.detail: SnapImageView and the other snap renderers load signed URLs with SwiftUI AsyncImage, which uses the shared URLSession and its default disk-backed URLCache. Photo responses are cached keyed by the full signed URL and evicted per HTTP headers, not per the app's 1h grant, so image bytes remain in the app container's Cache.db/fsCachedData after the signed URL expires and after sign-out - the sign-out path invalidates only the SnapURLCache dictionary of URL strings, not the cached responses. The app's carefully bounded access-grant model (TTL 3600s, cache eviction at TTL-60s) therefore does not bound the actual pixel data at rest, and a device backup or filesystem inspection recovers photos of a signed-out account. Because signed URLs differ per signing, entries also accumulate as duplicates.
findings.evidence: apps/ios/Pebbles/Features/PebbleMedia/SnapImageView.swift:22 (AsyncImage on signed URL); same pattern in Features/Path/Components/PathPebbleSnapThumb.swift and Features/Path/Read/PebbleReadBanner.swift; apps/ios/Pebbles/RootView.swift:161-164 (invalidateAll only); apps/ios/Pebbles/Services/SnapURLCache.swift:77-79 (removeAll clears the dictionary of URLs, not response data); no URLCache configuration anywhere (grep 'URLCache' over Pebbles: no hits)
findings.remediation: Call URLCache.shared.removeAllCachedResponses() from the sign-out/deletion clear-all routine, or load snaps through a dedicated URLSession with an ephemeral or memory-only cache configuration keyed by storage path.

findings.title: Account deletion does not clear web client-side stores, leaving intimate draft content on the device after erasure
findings.detail: The server-side purge is complete and harnessed (purge_account covers all user-owned tables; delete-account also empties the storage prefix and deletes the auth user, idempotently). But the web deleteAccount only performs signOut({scope:'local'}) and clears no browser storage, so after a user exercises their right to erasure the localStorage composer draft (`pbbls-composer-draft`, containing name/description free text) and the pending-invite token persist on the device. Erasure that leaves personal content in a world-readable-on-the-origin store is incomplete for the surface, and on a shared device it is directly recoverable by the next user.
findings.evidence: apps/web/lib/data/useSupabaseAuth.ts:186-202 (deleteAccount, local signOut only, no store clear); apps/web/lib/hooks/useComposerAutosave.ts:6,89; packages/supabase/supabase/functions/delete-account/index.ts:60-101 (server purge, no client-cache concern); packages/supabase/scripts/verify-account-purge.ts (server harness only)
findings.remediation: Invoke the same clear-all-local-stores routine (see PRV-06 fix) inside deleteAccount after the edge function returns, before the local signOut. Extend the acceptance criteria for account deletion to include client-store emptiness on web.

findings.title: Logs boards render database failures as the empty state
findings.detail: All four logs board fetch sites log the error and then fall through to `data ?? []`, so a failed select renders the dashed 'No features in progress.' / 'No drafts.' empty visual instead of an error. An admin hitting a transient Supabase outage, an expired session edge case, or an RLS regression sees a confidently empty board and can reasonably conclude drafts or shipped entries were lost or deleted, and may re-create entries (producing duplicates once the read path recovers). This directly contradicts the surface's own documented ErrorBlock pattern, which the analytics cards follow.
findings.evidence: apps/admin/app/(authed)/logs/features/page.tsx:32-38 (error -> console.error -> `const active: LogRow[] = data ?? []`); apps/admin/app/(authed)/logs/features/_components/FeaturesShippedSection.tsx:24-30; apps/admin/app/(authed)/logs/announcements/page.tsx:19-23; apps/admin/app/(authed)/logs/announcements/_components/AnnouncementsPublishedSection.tsx:15-19. Empty rendering: LogSection.tsx:146-149. Contrast with the compliant analytics pattern at components/analytics/KpiStrip.tsx:11-27.
findings.remediation: In each of the four sites, return the shared ErrorBlock (components/analytics/ErrorBlock.tsx) when `error` is non-null, as the analytics cards do, keeping the empty branch for a genuinely zero-row result.

findings.title: No error.tsx boundary anywhere; a failed log delete or moderation-queue load crashes the whole app
findings.detail: apps/admin/app contains no error.tsx, global-error.tsx, or not-found.tsx (verified by find). Two production paths throw where nothing catches: (a) deleteLog throws on a failed delete and DeleteLogButton awaits it inside startTransition with no try/catch, so any delete failure (network blip, RLS denial) escapes to React with no boundary and produces Next's generic production crash screen, discarding the admin's open form; (b) listSubmissions rethrows RPC errors and GlyphModerationPage awaits it with no try/catch, so any failure of admin_list_glyph_submissions crashes the whole moderation route instead of rendering a labeled, retryable error.
findings.evidence: find apps/admin/app -name error.tsx -o -name global-error.tsx -o -name not-found.tsx returns nothing. Throwing action: apps/admin/app/(authed)/logs/actions.ts:155-158; unguarded call: apps/admin/app/(authed)/logs/_components/DeleteLogButton.tsx:43-47. Throwing fetcher: apps/admin/lib/pebblestore/fetchers.ts:9-12; unguarded page: apps/admin/app/(authed)/pebblestore/glyphs/page.tsx:21.
findings.remediation: Add an app/(authed)/error.tsx (and a root global-error.tsx) rendering the ErrorBlock pattern with a reset() retry; change deleteLog to return an ActionResult like every sibling action instead of throwing, and surface it in DeleteLogButton; wrap the moderation page fetch in try/catch rendering ErrorBlock.

findings.title: Cover-image storage objects and the logs row have no consistency story
findings.detail: The lab-assets cover image is a file-plus-row pair with three unmanaged failure paths. (1) CoverImageInput uploads the object before any logs row references it; abandoning the form (or a failed createLog) strands the object forever. (2) deleteLog deletes only the row, leaving the referenced object in the public bucket indefinitely. (3) The Remove button deletes the object from storage immediately, before the form is saved; if the admin then navigates away without saving, the saved row still holds cover_image_path pointing at a deleted object, and the iOS Lab tab (the logs table 'drives the iOS Lab tab' per the migration header) renders a broken cover for end users. There is no cleanup job, no fail-safe ordering, and no orphan sweep.
findings.evidence: Upload-before-row: apps/admin/app/(authed)/logs/_components/CoverImageInput.tsx:39-53; immediate best-effort remove of a possibly-referenced object: CoverImageInput.tsx:59-69; row-only delete: apps/admin/app/(authed)/logs/actions.ts:151-162; user-facing consumer: packages/supabase/supabase/migrations/20260421000001_logs_table.sql:1-5,24 (cover_image_path, 'Drives the iOS Lab tab').
findings.remediation: Defer the storage delete to save time (mark for removal in form state, delete in updateLog after the row update succeeds); make deleteLog remove the referenced object after the row delete; add a periodic orphan sweep (list covers/ not referenced by any logs.cover_image_path) or fold lab-assets into an existing cleanup harness.

findings.title: A failed reference-data or palette load silently bricks the record flow for the whole session
findings.detail: ReferenceDataService.load() and EmotionPaletteService.load() each fire exactly once per session from RootScreen with no retry and no user-visible error; a failure leaves empty lists by documented design. The record flow then breaks silently in three ways. First, the DOMAIN and EMOTION steps are mandatory tile steps with no action button (RecordFlowScreen.actionFor returns null for them), and with zero tiles rendered and no empty-state message the user cannot advance and is given no reason. Second, ComposerDraftCoordinator.hydrate is gated on refs.hasLoaded, which stays false forever after a failed load, so resuming a server draft opens a blank composer instead (the tapped draft never hydrates), and a subsequent save-as-draft creates a duplicate row because serverDraftId was never bound. Third, the crash-restore prompt never fires for the same reason. One transient network error at app open degrades the app's core loop for the rest of the session with no error and no recovery short of process restart.
findings.evidence: apps/android/app/src/main/kotlin/app/pbbls/android/services/ReferenceDataService.kt:42-57 (hasLoaded stays false on failure, log-only catch, 'pickers empty until next launch'); services/EmotionPaletteService.kt:37-58 (same one-shot pattern); RootScreen.kt:98,129-133 (single fire per Unit/userId); services/ComposerDraftCoordinator.kt:78-95 (hydrate returns null while !refsLoaded, decides at most once); record/RecordFlowScreen.kt:181-191 (hydrate gate), :527 (EMOTION/DOMAIN get no action button); record/steps/RecordDomainStep.kt:13-25 plus create/pickers/DomainPickerContent.kt (no empty/error branch); RecordFlowModel.kt:73-87 (DOMAIN/EMOTION mandatory).
findings.remediation: Give the composer an explicit failed-refs state: retry the reference and palette loads on composer open when hasLoaded is false, and render an error-with-retry branch in the mandatory pickers instead of an empty grid. Distinguish hasLoaded from didFail in both services.

findings.title: Edit save treats any HTTP 5xx as success, so an infrastructure 5xx silently discards the user's edit
findings.detail: PebbleWriteService.update() maps every status >= 500 to SoftSuccess by design (iOS parity), on the assumption that a 500 means the edge function committed the write but failed during render composition. But a 502/503/504 from the gateway or a cold-start failure means the function never ran and nothing was written. EditPebbleScreen's SoftSuccess branch calls onSaved(), dismissing the editor and reloading; the user sees success while their changed fields are gone. The create path is protected against exactly this (it requires a pebble_id in the 5xx body before advancing, PebbleWriteService.softSuccessPebbleId), so the update path's blanket >= 500 rule is a known-weaker heuristic that converts a backend outage into silent data loss of edits.
findings.evidence: apps/android/app/src/main/kotlin/app/pbbls/android/services/PebbleWriteService.kt:94-104 ('Edit soft-success = any status >= 500 advances (iOS parity)') versus :76-85 (create demands pebble_id in the body); features/path/EditPebbleScreen.kt:207-210 (SoftSuccess -> onSaved(), editor dismissed, no message); record flow analog RecordFlowScreen.kt:285-293.
findings.remediation: Require a function-emitted marker in the 5xx body (as create does) before advancing the update path, treating body-less or gateway-shaped 5xx as Failure so the form stays open with the user's edits intact. This is a cross-surface policy change; fix it on the contract and mirror on iOS.

findings.title: Pebble create has no idempotency key; a retry after a lost response duplicates the pebble and double-credits karma
findings.detail: PebbleCreatePayload carries no client-generated id or idempotency key, and the transport helper returns a generic failure whenever the response cannot be read (timeout, connection reset), including the case where the server already committed. The record flow keeps the composer open on Failure precisely so the user retries, and the retry runs create_pebble again: a second pebble row, a second pebble_created karma credit, and a second achievement-count bump. The snap id is client-generated (SnapUploadCoordinator UUIDs) so the machinery for client ids already exists; the pebble itself is the one unguarded high-frequency create. Client pending-guards cannot help here because the duplicate comes from a legitimate second request, not a double-tap.
findings.evidence: apps/android/app/src/main/kotlin/app/pbbls/android/features/path/models/PebbleCreatePayload.kt:22-42 (no id field in the wire payload); services/PebbleWriteService.kt:121-144 (post() returns null on any transport exception, indistinguishable from never-sent) and :70-85 (null -> failGeneric); record/RecordFlowScreen.kt:294-299 (Failure keeps the flow on the privacy step for retry); packages/supabase/supabase/functions/compose-pebble/index.ts has no idempotency handling (grep -iE 'idempoten|client_id|dedupe|on conflict' = 0 hits).
findings.remediation: Add a client-generated pebble id (or idempotency key) to the create payload, honored by create_pebble via on-conflict or a precheck, and send it from all three clients. Extend the drafts-style verify harness with a replay-twice assertion (one row, one karma event).

findings.title: No explicit timeout configuration exists on either HTTP stack; all blocking calls ride unlabeled library defaults
findings.detail: Neither the supabase-kt client nor PebbleWriteService's second raw Ktor/OkHttp client configures connect, read, write, or call timeouts, and no withTimeout-style wrapper exists (the repo's timeout discipline in docs/agents/data-and-async.md is web-only). Every render-blocking call (path load, detail load, publish, uploads, signing) is bounded only by OkHttp's incidental 10s per-phase defaults, with no overall call deadline, so a slow-drip response can hold a spinner well past any deliberate budget, and a timeout surfaces as a generic exception with no operation label to diagnose. The absence is uniform: grep for timeout across app/src/main returns zero hits, meaning no future call site has a convention to follow either.
findings.evidence: grep -riE 'timeout|withTimeout|HttpTimeout|connectTimeout|readTimeout' apps/android/app/src/main = 0 hits; apps/android/app/src/main/kotlin/app/pbbls/android/services/PebbleWriteService.kt:63 (HttpClient(OkHttp) with no engine config); services/SupabaseService.kt:46-67 (createSupabaseClient with no httpEngine/timeout block); docs/agents/data-and-async.md (withTimeout documented for web only).
findings.remediation: Install Ktor's HttpTimeout (or configure the OkHttp engine) once per client with a stated default request timeout, and route blocking calls through a small labeled wrapper mirroring the web withTimeout convention so timeout failures log their operation.

findings.title: The Path landing screen's failure state has no retry; recovery requires killing the app
findings.detail: When the initial path_pebbles() load fails, PathScreen renders a static error line with no retry affordance, and the load effect is keyed on Unit so it never re-runs. Unlike every other data screen in the app (detail, edit, souls, collections, lab, connections, drafts all carry a retry token), the app's landing surface dead-ends: a user who opened the app in a dead zone stays on the error text after connectivity returns until they force-kill the process or happen to trigger a write. This is the screen where a failed load most resembles data loss to the user, which is exactly the trust failure REL-01 exists to prevent.
findings.evidence: apps/android/app/src/main/kotlin/app/pbbls/android/features/path/PathScreen.kt:101-114 (LaunchedEffect(Unit), single-shot), :210-216 (didLoadFail branch renders PebblesText only, no button); contrast PebbleDetailScreen.kt:213 and profile/SoulsListScreen.kt:136-141 which pair the same error text with a Retry TextButton.
findings.remediation: Adopt the existing retry-token idiom on PathScreen: key the load effect on a reloadToken and add the standard Retry button to the failure branch, mirroring the iOS PathView error treatment if it has one (1:1 rule).

findings.title: Publishing a pebble has no server-side idempotence guard, so a lost response plus user retry duplicates the pebble and its karma
findings.detail: create_pebble inserts unconditionally and the compose-pebble request carries no client-generated pebble id or idempotency key. The client's defenses are a disabled-while-loading button and the soft-success path, but soft-success only recovers the case where a 5xx response body carrying pebble_id actually arrives; when the request lands server-side and the response is lost to a network drop or timeout (the ordinary flaky-mobile case), the client shows a failure, re-enables Publish, and the user's natural retry inserts a second pebble plus a second pebble_created karma event. The duplicate row is user-visible and deletable, but the karma ledger keeps both credits, and the draft-consumption logic (which exists precisely because the team identified duplicate publishing as the worst outcome, PebblePublisher.swift:20-22) cannot help here. Drafts, glyph purchases, reactions, connections, and achievements all have server-side guards; the product's single most important mutation is the one without.
findings.evidence: packages/supabase/supabase/migrations/20260415000000_pebble_rpc_collections.sql:99-183 (unconditional inserts, no on conflict, no idempotency parameter); apps/ios/Pebbles/Features/Path/Models/PebbleCreatePayload.swift:8-46 (no pebble id field); apps/ios/Pebbles/Features/Path/PebblePublisher.swift:60-63 (recovery requires an error body with pebble_id, unreachable on transport-level failure); RecordFlowModel.swift:213-217 (failure re-enables the flow for retry).
findings.remediation: Let the client generate the pebble UUID and pass it through compose-pebble into create_pebble as an insert-with-id guarded by on conflict do nothing returning the existing id (mirroring how drafts already use a stable client UUID); apply the same key to the karma_events ref so replay cannot double-credit; mirror on web and Android since the RPC contract changes.

findings.title: A failed initial Path load is a dead end: the error state has no retry and the screen never reloads until app restart
findings.detail: PathView.load() runs from a .task that fires once per view identity. When the first timeline fetch fails (airplane mode, a network blip at launch, backend hiccup), the view renders 'Couldn't load your pebbles.' as plain text with no retry button, no pull-to-refresh, and no connectivity-recovery hook. The only paths that re-invoke load() are callbacks from create/edit/delete sheets, which are unreachable from the error state (the + button is part of the content branch, not the error branch). The user of a journaling app opening it in a dead zone therefore sees what reads as their data being gone and has no in-app recovery except backgrounding until iOS kills the process. Sibling screens (PebbleDetailSheet, DraftsListSheet, EditPebbleSheet) already ship Retry buttons, so the pattern exists in the codebase and simply was not applied to the primary screen; Collection and Soul detail error states share the same gap.
findings.evidence: apps/ios/Pebbles/Features/Path/PathView.swift:152-155 (error branch is a bare Text), :64-67 (one-shot .task), :230-261 (load() only re-called from sheet callbacks); contrast with PebbleDetailSheet.swift:74 ('Retry' button) and DraftsListSheet.swift:64 ('Try again'); CollectionDetailView.swift and SoulDetailView.swift error branches likewise lack retry.
findings.remediation: Add a retry button to PathView's error branch invoking load() (and stats.refresh()), and apply the same affordance to CollectionDetailView and SoulDetailView; optionally re-attempt automatically when the app returns to foreground from the error state.

findings.title: All Supabase calls ride the 60-second URLSession default with no explicit or labeled timeouts
findings.detail: The SupabaseClient is constructed with no options, so every RPC, PostgREST, Storage, and edge-function call inherits URLSession's 60s request timeout. On a stalled connection (the classic one-bar cellular case where packets trickle rather than fail), publish, save-as-draft, and the initial timeline load can hold their spinner or disabled button for a full minute before failing, with no operation label in the resulting error to aid diagnosis. The web surface documents and uses a 10s labeled withTimeout wrapper for exactly these paths; iOS has no analog, and the single explicit timeout in the app (30s on the read-banner photo fetch) shows the need was felt at least once. The 8s launch watchdog protects only the splash, not in-app interactions.
findings.evidence: apps/ios/Pebbles/Services/SupabaseService.swift:30-35 (SupabaseClient(supabaseURL:supabaseKey:) with no options/session config); grep for 'timeoutInterval|withTimeout|URLSessionConfiguration' across apps/ios yields only Features/Path/Read/PebbleReadBanner.swift:72; blocking call sites: RecordFlowView.swift:246-249 (publish), PathView.swift:230-236 (timeline), EditPebbleSheet.swift:228-233 (update); web-side convention at docs/agents/data-and-async.md:15,21.
findings.remediation: Pass a URLSession configured with timeoutIntervalForRequest around 15-20s into SupabaseClientOptions (or add a small labeled with-timeout async wrapper mirroring the web util) and adopt it on user-blocking call sites; log the label on timeout so hangs become diagnosable.

findings.title: create_pebble has no idempotency guard, so a retried or double-fired compose-pebble call duplicates the pebble and double-credits karma
findings.detail: create_pebble mints a fresh pebble id server-side and unconditionally emits a pebble_created karma event; pebbles has no unique constraint beyond the PK and the RPC accepts no idempotency key. A timeout-then-retry or a double submit therefore creates two pebbles and credits karma twice (the wallet and bounce triggers fire per event). When the payload carries snaps with client-generated ids, the retry instead fails on the snaps PK after the second pebble insert and rolls that transaction back, which accidentally protects photo-bearing pebbles but proves the mechanism exists and is simply unused for the pebble row itself. Every newer mutation on this surface names its guard (connections on-conflict, achievement PK, wallet lock, entitlement unique), making the top-volume mutation the outlier. Client-side pending guards are the only current protection, which the criterion explicitly discounts.
findings.evidence: Latest create_pebble emission: packages/supabase/supabase/migrations/20260817130000_pebble_visibility_grades.sql:144-333 (server-minted id at insert :235-251, unconditional karma insert :328-329, client-supplied snap ids accepted :306-313); no unique constraints on pebbles (20260411000001_core_tables.sql:51-64); edge function forwards any POST straight to the RPC (supabase/functions/compose-pebble/index.ts:55-57)
findings.remediation: Accept an optional client-generated pebble id in the payload (the pattern snaps[].id already uses), insert with on conflict (id) do nothing and return the existing id on replay; add a replay-twice assertion to a verify harness proving one row and one karma event. Keep sibling symmetry by documenting the same key on update_pebble.

findings.title: Collection writes are client-stitched across two tables; updateCollection deletes all memberships before re-inserting, so a mid-sequence failure permanently drops them
findings.detail: createCollection inserts the collections row, then separately inserts collection_pebbles rows; a failure between the two leaves a collection stripped of the pebbles the user selected. Worse, updateCollection first deletes every collection_pebbles row for the collection and then inserts the new set; if the insert fails (network drop, RLS hiccup, tab closed) the user's entire membership set is gone with no error recovery path, and nothing on the server can restore it. This directly violates the repo's own standing rule in AGENTS.md that multi-table writes must be RPCs because PostgREST offers no client-side transactions, and no create/update_collection function exists in the migrations to route through. Every other multi-table flow on this surface (pebbles, connections, wallet, marketplace) complies, which makes collections the one unprotected write family.
findings.evidence: apps/web/lib/data/supabase-provider.ts:841-865 (createCollection two-step), 867-893 (updateCollection delete at 875 then insert at 877); AGENTS.md 'Supabase — prefer RPCs for multi-table writes'; DB function inventory grep of packages/supabase/supabase/migrations shows no collection RPC
findings.remediation: Add upsert_collection(payload jsonb) as a transactional security-definer RPC handling the row plus membership diff in one transaction (create_pebble's collections handling is the in-schema template), switch the web provider to it, and check whether iOS/Android stitch the same shape.

findings.title: Pebble creation has no idempotency guard: a retry after an ambiguous compose-pebble failure duplicates the pebble and double-credits karma
findings.detail: compose-pebble calls create_pebble, which inserts the pebbles row and a karma_events credit with no idempotency key, unique constraint, or dedupe. If the edge-function response is lost after the RPC commits (function timeout, network drop, browser abandon), the web client throws, RecordFlow re-enables the publish button in its finally block, and the natural user action of pressing publish again inserts a second identical pebble and a second karma credit. The client sends no idempotency key the server could use to detect the replay. The ledger flows that spend karma are properly guarded (buy_glyph already_owned + unique index, spend_karma FOR UPDATE), which makes the earn side the asymmetric gap: the product's only karma emitter is the one unguarded mutation, and it is also the most frequently invoked.
findings.evidence: packages/supabase/supabase/functions/compose-pebble/index.ts:55-62 (RPC then response, no key); packages/supabase/supabase/migrations/20260817130000_pebble_visibility_grades.sql create_pebble body (insert into pebbles ~line 235, insert into karma_events ~line 328, no on conflict); apps/web/lib/data/supabase-provider.ts:451-473 (payload has no client key); apps/web/components/record/flow/RecordFlow.tsx:299-306 (catch re-enables publish)
findings.remediation: Add a client-generated idempotency uuid to the compose payload, store it on pebbles under a unique (user_id, idempotency_key) index, and make create_pebble return the existing id on conflict instead of inserting. All three clients pass the key; the karma insert rides the same transaction so double-credit disappears with the double-insert.

findings.title: The render-blocking initial store load and all provider mutations bypass withTimeout, so a hung request leaves the home screen spinning forever
findings.detail: The repo's own rule (docs/agents/data-and-async.md) says to wrap any Supabase call that blocks rendering or interaction in withTimeout with a 10s default, and the wrapper exists with labels. Adoption stops at the auth and reference-data hooks: the nine-query loadFromSupabase that gates every authenticated screen is raw awaits, the browser client configures no transport timeout, and every SupabaseProvider mutation including the functions.invoke publish call is unwrapped. A single hung connection during initial load leaves DataProvider in loading=true indefinitely and /path shows a spinner with no timeout, no message, and no escape short of a manual reload; a hung publish leaves the composer pinned in its pending state. The dev-only auth watchdog demonstrates the team knows the hazard, but nothing bounds it in production.
