findings.evidence: docs/agents/data-and-async.md:15 (the rule); apps/web/lib/utils/with-timeout.ts:7-21; grep shows only 8 withTimeout call sites, none in supabase-provider.ts; apps/web/lib/data/supabase-provider.ts:113-126 (raw awaits), 746-749 (unwrapped invoke); apps/web/components/layout/DataProvider.tsx:20-41; apps/web/lib/supabase/client.ts:14 (no transport timeout)
findings.remediation: Wrap loadFromSupabase's Promise.all and the invokeCompose/functions.invoke calls in withTimeout with operation labels (30s for publish, 15s for load), or set a global fetch timeout on the browser client; surface the timeout error through the (to-be-wired) DataProvider error state so it lands on the REL-01 retry UI.

findings.title: Operators have no anti-harassment enforcement tooling: no admin block, connection severance, or account suspension exists
findings.detail: The block primitive is user-initiated only: connection_blocks rows are written exclusively by remove_connection, which requires the caller to be a member of the connection. An operator handling an abuse escalation (for example a harassment report arriving by email, the only channel that exists) cannot place a block between the parties, sever their connection, revoke a harasser's invite token, or suspend the account; every one of those is manual SQL against production. The SAF-04 checklist expects operator blocks to flow through the same server-side primitive as user blocks, and no such path exists, so escalated enforcement is slower and error-prone exactly when it matters.
findings.evidence: packages/supabase/supabase/migrations/20260730070347_mutual_connections.sql:301-332 (remove_connection is the only connection_blocks write path, membership check at :313); admin RPC inventory (grep rpc( over apps/admin) contains no block/connection/suspension capability; no admin_ban/suspend function in any migration (grep -rniE 'admin_(block|ban|suspend)' over migrations: zero)
findings.remediation: Add an is_admin-gated RPC that inserts into connection_blocks (and deletes the pair's connection row) using the same table the user path writes, so operator blocks inherit the existing enforcement; pair it with a minimal admin escalation page and audit-log the action.

findings.title: display_name is unconstrained and unmoderated while served to anonymous visitors and invite recipients
findings.detail: profiles.display_name is bare 'text not null' with no length cap, charset rule, or reserved-name guard, unlike handles which get a format CHECK plus a trigger-enforced reserved list. It is projected to anonymous callers via get_public_profile and to invite recipients via preview_connection_invite before any relationship exists, so a display name like 'Pebbles Support' or a multi-kilobyte abuse string reaches strangers unfiltered. There is no admin tooling to reset or moderate a display name, so remediation of an impersonation or abuse case is manual SQL. The reserved-handles work shows the team identified the impersonation class and guarded only one of the two identity fields.
findings.evidence: packages/supabase/supabase/migrations/20260411000001_core_tables.sql:23 (display_name text not null, no CHECK); contrast 20260730120000_public_profiles.sql:35-37 and :89-106 (handle format CHECK + reserved trigger); exposure paths 20260730120000:242-243 (get_public_profile) and 20260730070347:186-194 (preview_connection_invite, anon-granted); admin RPC inventory has no profile moderation call
findings.remediation: Add a length and control-character CHECK on display_name, reuse the reserved-word trigger for impersonation-prone values, and add an is_admin RPC to reset a display name (audit-logged).

findings.title: Block state is inferable through the block-unaware invite preview, giving a blocked harasser a confirmation oracle
findings.detail: The accept path deliberately returns invite_expired for blocks so a blocked peer is never told directly, but the migration documents that preview_connection_invite is block-unaware by design: a blocked user previewing the same token sees the inviter's live card (name, glyph) while their accept fails as 'expired', and third parties keep succeeding on that token. Comparing those outcomes (or comparing notes with any third party) confirms the block. In this product's threat model - where the blocked party may be an abuser named in the victim's entries - a block oracle is exactly the signal the silence design exists to deny, and it can escalate real-world risk for someone leaving an abusive relationship. Android faithfully surfaces both shapes (preview then accept) in AcceptInviteScreen, so the oracle is user-reachable on this surface.
findings.evidence: packages/supabase/supabase/migrations/20260730070347_mutual_connections.sql:226-236 (comment: 'Not fully hidden: preview is block-unaware by design (D4) ... a blocked peer can infer the block'); apps/android/app/src/main/kotlin/app/pbbls/android/services/ConnectionsService.kt:53-73 (preview never raises, accept maps block to invite_expired); features/connections/AcceptInviteScreen.kt (renders preview then accept outcome)
findings.remediation: Make preview block-aware in the direction blocked-viewer -> blocker, returning the same unusable-token status shape as expiry (blocker -> blocked direction can stay live to avoid the reverse oracle); add both directions to a future block-matrix harness.

findings.title: iOS renders cross-user display names and user-carved glyph strokes with no moderation state behind them
findings.detail: The invite preview, accept confirmation, and connections list all display the peer's free-text display name and raw carved glyph geometry. Unlike marketplace glyphs, which pass a pending/approved/rejected pipeline, profile glyphs and display names have no moderation status anywhere in the schema, and the anon-callable invite preview shows them to recipients before any relationship exists. An abusive user can put an offensive drawing or name in front of anyone they can hand a link to, and takedown would be manual SQL; iOS offers no report affordance on these surfaces (control presence is PLT-04's row, but the absent enforcement depth behind these types lands here). Public pebbles' free-text name and description served to anonymous visitors share the same gap.
findings.evidence: packages/supabase/supabase/migrations/20260730070347_mutual_connections.sql:186-196 (anon preview projects display_name + glyph strokes), 277-287, 347-362 (accept and get_connections); no status column on profiles.display_name or glyphs outside glyph_submissions (20260630003348_glyph_marketplace.sql:15-28 covers marketplace only); 20260817130000_pebble_visibility_grades.sql:106-127 (anon pebble projection, no moderation state); iOS render sites: apps/ios/Pebbles/Features/Connections/InviteAcceptSheet.swift, ConnectionsListView.swift
findings.remediation: Add a moderation/takedown state to profiles (display name, glyph) and public pebbles, gate the cross-user projections on it, extend the admin definer-RPC pattern already used for the glyph market, and add report affordances on the client surfaces that render foreign content.

findings.title: emotion_first achievements condition the unlock and its karma reward on which emotion the user records
findings.detail: SAF-02 forbids rewards conditioned on emotion choice. check_achievements() qualifies the emotion_first family by matching the badge's emotion_id against the user's pebbles.emotion_id (20260730090000:219-221) and then pays each unlocked badge's karma_reward (lines 240-246), so recording a pebble tagged with a specific emotion (including negative ones like sadness, anger, fear, grief) mints a badge and pays karma. This gamifies emotional disclosure by emotion type and fails the criterion's l4 signal that a grep of achievement trigger bodies for emotion column names returns nothing. Failure scenario: a user records emotions they are not genuinely feeling to complete the emotion collection and earn karma, converting a reflective tool into a collect-the-emotions loop. Impact is bounded because there is no loss framing and no inactivity penalty, and the karma catalog rewards for these rows default to 0 unless an admin prices them.
findings.evidence: 20260730090000_achievements.sql:219-221 (emotion_first reads emotion_id), 240-246 (karma paid on unlock); neutral karma helper by contrast 20260411000005_security_hardening.sql:13-42
findings.remediation: Either drop the emotion_first family or re-key it off neutral activity, or document an explicit, reviewed exemption in the design record explaining why per-emotion first-time awareness is safe; encode a test that fails when an achievement/karma trigger references emotion/valence/intensity columns.

findings.title: No documented removal channel for recorded third parties and no owner warning before free text goes public
findings.detail: Structured third-party identifiers (souls) are engineered out of every outbound projection, but free-text pebble names and descriptions, which the policy itself acknowledges may contain real people's names, are served verbatim to mutual connections and to anonymous visitors of public share links. The visibility step tells the owner who can see the pebble but never flags that mentions of other people are leaving private scope, and the privacy policy documents no procedure by which a named third party can request removal (section 2.5 only states that Pebbles never contacts them; section 12.3 shifts responsibility to the owner). Publication to an audience removes the household exemption, so the controller needs a stated recourse path it currently lacks.
findings.evidence: apps/web/docs/privacy/en.md:74-77 and 337-339; get_shared_pebble serves name/description to anon (20260817130000:106-113); visibility copy record.flow.privacy.* in apps/web/lib/i18n/messages/en.json has no third-party warning
findings.remediation: Add a removal-request paragraph (channel + expected handling) for named third parties to the privacy policy, and a one-line caution on the public/private visibility options noting that text mentioning other people becomes visible to that audience.

findings.title: lab-note-reminder workflow runs a third-party reusable workflow pinned to mutable @main with a pull-requests:write token
findings.detail: lab-note-reminder.yml delegates the whole job to alexisbohns/ariko/.github/workflows/lab-note-reminder.yml@main. A branch ref is mutable: whoever can push to that repo's main can change what executes in this repo's PR context on the next event, receiving the GITHUB_TOKEN with contents:read and pull-requests:write. The ariko repo appears to belong to the same maintainer, which lowers but does not remove the risk (single compromised account or force-push propagates instantly, with no review gate in pbbls). The workflow correctly uses pull_request (not pull_request_target) and needs no extra secrets, so blast radius is limited to token scope: PR comments, labels, and read access. Still, it is the one non-version-pinned action reference in the repo and the only cross-repo execution path.
findings.evidence: .github/workflows/lab-note-reminder.yml:18 (uses: alexisbohns/ariko/.github/workflows/lab-note-reminder.yml@main) with permissions at lines 12-14; all other workflow uses: references are @v4/@v1 tags (grep 'uses:' .github/workflows)
findings.remediation: Pin the reusable workflow to a tag or commit SHA in the ariko repo and bump deliberately; optionally mirror the workflow into this repo.

findings.title: No secret-scanning gate in CI and no recorded git-history scan
findings.detail: Secret placement discipline currently holds (only publishable keys under apps/admin, env files gitignored), but nothing detects regression: no gitleaks/trufflehog job exists in any workflow, and there is no record in docs/decisions/log.md of a one-time history scan. Whether GitHub push protection is enabled is not verifiable from the repo. The admin workspace is exactly where a service-role key is most likely to be introduced by accident (back-office scripts, analytics experiments), and a NEXT_PUBLIC_-prefixed privileged variable would ship straight into the client bundle. Today the only guard is reviewer attention.
findings.evidence: grep -rn 'gitleaks|trufflehog|secret' .github/workflows/*.yml shows only legitimate secrets-context references in the Android workflows; no scan/rotation entry in docs/decisions/log.md (grep 'rotat|leak|scan'); positive posture evidence at apps/admin/.gitignore:3-5 and .env.local.example
findings.remediation: Add a gitleaks workflow (push + PR) with a one-time full-history run recorded in the decisions log; assert in the same job that 'service_role' never appears under apps/* directories.

findings.title: SwiftPM lockfile is deliberately gitignored, so release builds float dependency versions with no vulnerability monitoring
findings.detail: apps/ios/.gitignore explicitly ignores Package.resolved and project.yml pins only lower bounds (from: 2.0.0 / 1.0.4 / 6.0.0) for supabase-swift, SVGView, and RiveRuntime. The Xcode Cloud release lane regenerates the project and resolves packages fresh on every build, and installs xcodegen via unpinned brew. Consequently two builds of the same commit can ship different third-party code, a compromised or broken upstream release is adopted automatically into the next App Store build with no review step, and no Dependabot/Renovate or audit job watches the Swift ecosystem for known CVEs. This is the l0 anchor of the criterion for this surface.
findings.evidence: apps/ios/.gitignore (Package.resolved under '# SwiftPM'); apps/ios/project.yml:27-36 (from: ranges); apps/ios/ci_scripts/ci_post_clone.sh:4 (brew install xcodegen unpinned), 20-27 (fresh xcodebuild -resolvePackageDependencies per build); git ls-files apps/ios shows no *.resolved tracked; .github/dependabot.yml absent; no audit workflow in .github/workflows/
findings.remediation: Remove Package.resolved from apps/ios/.gitignore and commit it (xcodegen keeps it stable next to the generated project via -clonedSourcePackagesDirPath or the xcshareddata path); have ci_post_clone.sh fail if the committed resolved file is missing; enable Dependabot for the swift ecosystem (and pin xcodegen via a version-locked install).

findings.title: Client-facing edge functions use wildcard CORS and parse unbounded request bodies with no size cap or rate limiting
findings.detail: compose-pebble, compose-pebble-update and delete-account all set Access-Control-Allow-Origin: '*' and call await req.json() with no content-length or byte-size guard before parsing, and no per-user/per-IP rate limiting on the expensive compose/purge paths. Failure scenario: a caller posts a multi-megabyte JSON body (or a deeply nested payload / a huge snaps array) to compose-pebble; the function buffers and parses it fully before any DB-side quota (the 1.5MB bucket cap and snap-count guard live in create_pebble, after the body is already parsed), giving a cheap memory/compute amplification vector; repeated calls have no throttle beyond platform defaults. The wildcard CORS is lower-risk here because these endpoints authenticate via an Authorization bearer rather than cookies (so classic CSRF does not apply), but it still permits any origin to drive the credentialed endpoint from a victim's browser session if a token is present. No negative-path (413 oversized, 401 missing token) tests exist.
findings.evidence: packages/supabase/supabase/functions/compose-pebble/index.ts:26-30 (CORS '*'), :42-47 (req.json() with no size guard); compose-pebble-update/index.ts:33-37,47-53; delete-account/index.ts:29-33,50-56; snap quota enforced only later in create_pebble (20260817130000:293-302).
findings.remediation: Add a shared body-size guard constant (reject when content-length or the read byte count exceeds a small bound) applied before req.json() in every client-facing function; replace wildcard CORS with an allowlist of the known app origins; add per-user rate limiting (or document reliance on platform abuse protection) on compose and delete-account; add 401/413 rejection tests.

findings.title: No dependency vulnerability monitoring, a mutable @main action ref, and edge functions with no deno lockfile
findings.detail: The repo has no dependency vulnerability monitoring: no .github/dependabot.yml, no renovate.json, and no npm audit / osv-scanner gate in any workflow, so a newly disclosed CVE in a pinned dependency is never surfaced. A reusable workflow is pinned to a MUTABLE branch ref (alexisbohns/ariko/.github/workflows/lab-note-reminder.yml@main), meaning its code can change under the pipeline without review. The Supabase edge functions import remote modules (deno.land/std@0.224.0, esm.sh/@supabase/supabase-js@2) with no committed deno.lock, so the @2 major-range and transitive resolution are not integrity-pinned and can drift between deploys. Failure scenario: an upstream compromise or breaking change in the @main reusable workflow or the unpinned esm.sh graph reaches CI/edge deploys with no lockfile or scanner to catch it.
findings.evidence: .github/workflows/lab-note-reminder.yml (uses: alexisbohns/ariko/...@main); no .github/dependabot.yml or renovate.json (ls confirmed absent); packages/supabase/supabase/functions/*/index.ts import deno.land/std@0.224.0 and esm.sh/@supabase/supabase-js@2; no deno.lock found under packages/supabase (find returned none).
findings.remediation: Add dependabot or renovate for npm + GitHub Actions; SHA-pin third-party and reusable-workflow actions (replace @main); commit a deno.lock for the edge functions and pin supabase-js to an exact version; optionally add an npm audit / osv-scanner CI gate that fails on high-severity advisories.

findings.title: compose-pebble parses an unbounded request body, expensive edge paths have no rate limit, and raw RPC error messages are returned to the client
findings.detail: compose-pebble calls await req.json() with no content-length or byte guard before parsing, so an oversized body is a cheap resource-consumption lever against the function (CWE-770). The expensive paths — compose (engine composition per call) and delete-account (a full transactional account purge) — carry no per-user or per-IP rate limiting and rely entirely on unstated platform protection. On failure, compose-pebble returns the raw RPC error string to the caller (`rpcError?.message`), which for a Postgres/PostgREST error can surface constraint names, column names, or SQLSTATE detail. None of these are catastrophic alone, but together they are the API-hardening gaps the criterion targets, and there are no negative-path tests exercising 400/401/413 behavior.
findings.evidence: packages/supabase/supabase/functions/compose-pebble/index.ts:43,61 (unbounded req.json, raw error passthrough); packages/supabase/supabase/functions/delete-account/index.ts (no rate limit on purge); grep for rate/throttle/maxBody across packages/supabase/supabase/functions returns nothing
findings.remediation: Add a shared body-size guard (reject bodies over a small constant before JSON.parse) used by every function that reads a body; add per-user rate limiting to compose and delete-account (or document the platform control that covers them); map RPC failures to opaque codes for the client and keep the detailed message server-side; add negative-path tests (oversized body -> 413, missing token -> 401).

findings.title: No secret scanning or history scan in CI; web has no CI gate at all
findings.detail: Secret placement is disciplined today (no service_role in the client, gitignored env files, publishable-only NEXT_PUBLIC vars), but nothing prevents regression. There is no gitleaks/trufflehog job and no GitHub push-protection config, no recorded full-history scan or rotation note in the decisions log, and no web CI workflow exists to run even lint/test — the only workflows are android, arkaik, and lab-note. A future PR that accidentally prefixes a privileged value with NEXT_PUBLIC_, or commits a local .env, would ship to the client bundle undetected.
findings.evidence: .github/workflows/ contains only android-release.yml, android.yml, arkaik.yml, lab-note-reminder.yml; grep for service_role/SERVICE_ROLE over apps/web returns nothing (current state clean); .gitignore:42; no gitleaks/dependabot config in git ls-files
findings.remediation: Enable GitHub secret scanning + push protection and add a gitleaks (or trufflehog) job to a web CI workflow that also runs lint/test; add a cheap CI grep asserting privileged key names (service_role, sk_, whsec_, PEM headers) never appear under apps/web; record a one-time full-history scan result in docs/decisions/log.md.

findings.title: No dependency vulnerability monitoring and a mutable third-party workflow ref
findings.detail: package-lock.json is committed so builds are reproducible, but there is no Dependabot/Renovate config and no npm-audit/osv gate, so known-vulnerable dependencies accumulate silently with no alerting. Additionally, lab-note-reminder.yml consumes a third-party reusable workflow at a mutable @main ref, meaning a change on that upstream branch executes in this repo's CI without review. Actions elsewhere are tag-pinned (@v4) rather than SHA-pinned.
findings.evidence: .github/workflows/lab-note-reminder.yml:18 (alexisbohns/ariko/...@main); no .github/dependabot.yml or renovate.json in git ls-files; no audit/osv step in any workflow; android/arkaik workflows pin actions to @v4 tags
findings.remediation: Add Dependabot or Renovate across the npm workspace, add a severity-gated `npm audit`/osv-scanner job that fails on high findings, pin the reusable workflow to a tag or SHA instead of @main, and prefer SHA pinning for third-party actions.

findings.title: Cross-surface shapes admin handles (glyph strokes jsonb, logs rows, Lab Note YAML) have zero contract tests, against the repo's own standing rule
findings.detail: The decision log's 2026-07-29 entry, promoted into root CLAUDE.md as a standing cross-surface rule, mandates that any shape shared by more than one client is tested against verbatim payloads produced by the other surfaces. Admin sits on three such shapes and tests none: (1) the strokes jsonb produced by web's carving flow is decoded through a blind double cast with no runtime validation, so a web-side change to the stroke shape lands as a moderation-queue crash or silent geometry corruption instead of a test failure; (2) logs rows written by admin are read by web, iOS, and Android Lab screens, and web's rowToLog silently returns null on rows missing fields admin could start emitting differently; (3) the Lab Note YAML parser consumes PR-authored text whose canonical schema lives in the lab-note skill, with no fixture pinning the two to each other. The precedent that motivated the rule (iOS drafts silently losing timestamps while all same-surface tests passed) is exactly the failure mode these three shapes are open to.
findings.evidence: docs/decisions/log.md:320-323 (the standing rule and its motivating incident); lib/pebblestore/fetchers.ts:13 ('as unknown as AdminSubmission[]' on a Returns: Json RPC, packages/supabase/types/database.ts:2105-2108); apps/web/lib/data/logs-api.ts:10-35 (cross-surface logs reader, 'Mirrors apps/ios ... LogsService.swift'); lib/logs/parse-lab-note.ts (no fixture from the skill's schema); no fixture or serialization test exists anywhere under apps/admin (find for *.test.* empty; only UI playground fixtures under components/analytics/__fixtures__/)
findings.remediation: Once the Vitest setup lands, add decoder tests fed verbatim captures: a real admin_list_glyph_submissions payload from the linked project, real strokes emitted by web carving, and the lab-note skill's own skeleton YAML as the parse-lab-note fixture; assert the explicit-null and absent-key variants the standing rule names.

findings.title: The destructive pebble-delete path and the auth session state machine have no automated tests
findings.detail: PebbleWriteService.delete is the only client-side code for the destructive core path: it invokes the delete_pebble RPC with the hand-typed parameter name p_pebble_id and rethrows. No test asserts this call, its parameter contract, or the surrounding PathScreen long-press flow, so a typo'd RPC name/param, a signature change server-side, or a regression that swallows the error would only be caught by a user watching a pebble fail to disappear (server-side karma clawback also silently stops firing). Likewise SupabaseService.start, the collector that owns session, isInitializing, the RefreshFailure keep-last-session policy, and the once-per-process OAuth display-name patch, has no test; this is also the code path guarded by the documented supabase-kt deadlock rule, which today is enforced only by a comment. The repo already demonstrates the needed pattern (SnapUploadCoordinatorTest fakes a repository interface per the extract-a-Servicing-interface-when-needed rule), so the gap is unforced, and it is not tracked as an issue anywhere I found.
findings.evidence: apps/android/app/src/main/kotlin/app/pbbls/android/services/PebbleWriteService.kt:107-117; apps/android/app/src/main/kotlin/app/pbbls/android/services/SupabaseService.kt:100-135; grep 'delete_pebble|deletePebble|sessionStatus|signIn' over apps/android/app/src/test returns only SnapUploadCoordinatorTest media-repo fakes and AuthLogic/InviteLink/consent hits; contrast apps/android/app/src/test/kotlin/app/pbbls/android/features/pebblemedia/SnapUploadCoordinatorTest.kt:35-66 (the existing fake pattern)
findings.remediation: Extract the minimal Servicing seam (or accept a JSON-building pure helper) so a test can assert delete() targets delete_pebble with p_pebble_id and propagates failure; model the session collector's transitions (Authenticated/NotAuthenticated/RefreshFailure/Initializing, isNew name-patch guard) behind a testable status stream and add JUnit cases; track the remaining UI-flow gap as an issue.

findings.title: verify-account-purge.ts oracles are vacuous for five purge tables: log_reactions is never seeded, and only four tables' purge counts are pinned while zero-row checks run after the auth cascade
findings.detail: The harness's own comment (lines 302-306) states the section-(4) tables cascade from auth.users, so post-deleteUser zero-row assertions cannot catch a dropped purge delete line — only the RPC's returned counts can. Yet expectedPurged pins counts for just pebble_drafts, connections, connection_invites and connection_blocks. The deletes for achievement_unlocks, wallet_balances, bounces and log_reactions are seeded (or trigger-seeded) but count-unpinned, and log_reactions violates the standing rule outright: it appears only in the zero-row assertion list and is never seeded, making that check pass unconditionally. Consequence: if the next create-or-replace clobber of purge_account (M52/M53 are explicitly forecast as the next collision, decision 2026-07-31) drops any of those five delete lines, the harness stays green. The dropped line matters whenever the delete-account flow stops before deleteUser (storage failure, expired JWT — the documented resume matrix), leaving those personal rows in place while the purge response reports success, and it falsifies the purge counts the edge function returns as erasure evidence.
findings.evidence: packages/supabase/scripts/verify-account-purge.ts:302-317 (only four tables pinned; comment admitting cascade makes later checks blind), :336 (log_reactions assertion with no seed anywhere in the file — grep 'log_reactions' matches only this line), :341-344 (zero-row loop runs after deleteUser at :296); packages/supabase/supabase/migrations/20260731090000_purge_account_union.sql:164-182 (the five section-(4) deletes at risk); docs/decisions/log.md:376-378 (standing rule: seed AND assertion in the same change; M52/M53 named as next likely collision)
findings.remediation: Seed one log_reactions row for the seller (requires one published logs fixture row or a service-role insert), and extend expectedPurged to pin the counts of every section-(4) table the seed creates (achievement_unlocks from check_achievements' return length, wallet_balances 1, bounces 1, log_reactions 1) so a dropped delete line fails loudly before the cascade hides it.

findings.title: Read-model decode tests build their own decoder and use whole-second-only fixtures, so production decoder drift on those shapes is invisible
findings.detail: PebbleDecodingTests (and the sibling read-model suites for PebbleDetail, RippleSummary, ProfileEngagement) construct a tolerant JSONDecoder inside the test file and feed it hand-written fixtures whose timestamps are whole seconds. Production decodes these shapes through the supabase-swift PostgREST pipeline's decoder, and real timestamptz output carries microseconds. Two failure modes escape the suite: a change to the production decode path's date strategy (e.g. a call site pinning .iso8601 the way EditPebbleSheet.save() already does for its edge-function response) would reject real fractional-second payloads while every test stays green; and the fixtures are not verbatim captures, so a field the server actually emits differently (numeric rendering, explicit null vs absent) can diverge from the fixture unnoticed. The drafts shape shows the house standard (attributed verbatim foreign payloads, precision variants, emit-side literal assertions); the read models fall short of it.
findings.evidence: apps/ios/PebblesTests/PebbleDecodingTests.swift:8-20 (test-local decoder with its own fallback 'return formatter.date(from: raw) ?? Date()'), fixtures at :28-29,50-51 whole-second only; production decode goes through supabase.client.rpc('path_pebbles').execute().value at apps/ios/Pebbles/Features/Path/PathView.swift:232-235 (SDK decoder, not the test's); precision-variant discipline exists elsewhere: PebblesTests/DraftCrossSurfaceDecodingTests.swift:15-40, PebblesTests/AchievementsDecodingTests.swift:61-62; grep 'T[0-9:]*Z"' over PebblesTests = 73 whole-second stamps vs 8 fractional across three suites.
findings.remediation: Capture one real path_pebbles and one real PebbleDetail payload from the linked project (microsecond timestamps, real nulls), check them in as attributed fixtures, and decode them in tests using the same decoder configuration the production call path uses (expose or mirror the SDK decoder in a shared test helper).

findings.title: Cross-surface read projections (get_connections, path_pebbles, get_profile_engagement) have no contract test at the database surface
findings.detail: The write-side shapes (draft payload, create payload) and two anon projections (get_public_profile, get_shared_pebble) are contract-tested end to end, but the jsonb projections that three hand-written clients decode on every screen open — get_connections (connection_id/connected_at/peer{display_name,glyph{strokes,view_box}}), path_pebbles rows, and get_profile_engagement — are asserted nowhere at this surface. A future re-emission that renames a key, changes connected_at precision, or nulls the peer object differently would type-check cleanly (jsonb returns are untyped in database.ts) and break iOS/Android/web decoding at runtime with no test failing anywhere. The repo's own standing rule ('any data shape shared by more than one client is tested on each surface against real payloads... a committed end-to-end harness is the proof') names the harness as the proof mechanism, so the gap is a rule-compliance gap, not just a nice-to-have.
findings.evidence: grep of packages/supabase/scripts/ for get_connections/path_pebbles/get_profile_engagement returns nothing; projection shapes at packages/supabase/supabase/migrations/20260730070347_mutual_connections.sql:338-366 (get_connections), 20260519141000_path_pebbles_positiveness.sql, 20260516104231_profile_glyph_and_engagement.sql; standing rule at docs/decisions/log.md:321 and root CLAUDE.md
findings.remediation: Extend verify-pebble-visibility (or a new verify-projections harness) to call get_connections and path_pebbles as a seeded user and assert the exact key sets and timestamp forms, mirroring the PROFILE_KEYS allowlist pattern from verify-public-profile.ts.

findings.title: The harness suite has no aggregate entry point — packages/supabase defines no test script
findings.detail: Five verify/smoke scripts are the surface's entire test suite, yet package.json has no test script and no doc lists a single command that runs them all; each script is invoked by hand with its own env-var incantation copied from its header. After a migration batch there is no one command that answers 'do all contract proofs still pass', so partial runs are the default (a contributor re-runs the harness their change obviously touches and skips the rest), and a new harness can be added without becoming part of any runnable whole. The uniform anon-key design of four of the five scripts means an aggregate runner is nearly free to build.
findings.evidence: packages/supabase/package.json scripts block (build/lint/db:* only, no test); root CLAUDE.md commands table notes no supabase test task; each script documents only its own run line (e.g. scripts/verify-pebble-drafts.ts:19-21)
findings.remediation: Add a scripts/run-all.ts (or npm 'test' script) that executes the four anon-key harnesses plus smoke-test-engine sequentially against SUPABASE_URL/ANON_KEY and aggregates exit codes; document it in packages/supabase/CLAUDE.md as the post-batch command.

findings.title: Web emits millisecond-precision timestamps into cross-surface payloads against the standing whole-seconds rule, and no web test guards either emit precision or foreign-payload decode of DB shapes
findings.detail: The hardened root CLAUDE.md rule (from decision #651) says timestamps crossing a surface boundary are emitted at the narrowest precision every reader accepts, whole seconds. Web still emits ambient new Date().toISOString() milliseconds into happened_at wherever the record flow writes it (RecordWhenStep.tsx:29,35,43; composerDefaults at draft-payload.ts:36), and that value travels verbatim inside the pebble_drafts jsonb payload that iOS and Android read back. Today's readers are tolerant (iOS ISO8601Flexible, Android OffsetDateTime), so nothing is currently broken, but the emit side of the standing rule is unimplemented on web and untested: no web test asserts encoder output precision, and no web decode test feeds verbatim iOS- or Postgres-produced payloads (all test fixtures carry web's own .000Z form, flow.test.ts:247-264). The proof of cross-surface fidelity lives solely in the manually run packages/supabase harness, which never executes web code. The failure mode returns the day a stricter reader or a changed SDK date default appears, exactly the silent-nil decode #651 documented.
findings.evidence: apps/web/components/record/flow/steps/RecordWhenStep.tsx:29,35,43; apps/web/components/record/draft-payload.ts:36; docs/decisions/log.md:316-323; root CLAUDE.md standing rule 'Timestamps crossing a surface boundary'; grep of apps/web/lib/**/*.test.ts shows only .000Z fixtures and no attributed foreign payloads for DB shapes; packages/supabase/scripts/verify-pebble-drafts.ts:222-223 explicitly checks that web's toISOString carries milliseconds
findings.remediation: Add a small emitTimestamp helper truncating to whole seconds, route RecordWhenStep and draft/composer emission through it, and add web decode tests over verbatim iOS-captured and PostgREST-captured payload fixtures (whole-second, microsecond, and explicit-null variants) with provenance headers.

findings.title: scripts/test-week-roll.ts is a hand-run ad-hoc test harness outside Vitest discovery; the Path week-grouping logic it covers is unprotected by the standard suite
findings.detail: The 175-line script implements its own eq() assertion and failure counter and tests lib/utils/week-roll-entries.ts, the ISO-week grouping the Path timeline depends on (isoWeekStart, weekIndex, buildWeekRollEntries). It runs only via the separate 'npm run test:week-roll' command; 'npm run test' (vitest run, include glob lib/**/*.test.ts) never executes it, and no CI runs either command. A regression in week-roll-entries therefore keeps the standard suite green while the covering assertions silently stop being run, which is the exact fragmentation TST-07 exists to prevent. The port is mechanical since the expectations are already literal, and it would also remove the script's 'as unknown as Pebble' double-cast fixture shortcut (scripts/test-week-roll.ts:33).
findings.evidence: apps/web/scripts/test-week-roll.ts:11-33 (hand-rolled eq harness); apps/web/package.json:11 (separate test:week-roll script); apps/web/vitest.config.ts:19 (include glob excludes scripts/); no workflow in .github/workflows invokes either command
findings.remediation: Port the script's cases to lib/utils/week-roll-entries.test.ts under Vitest, delete the script and the package.json entry, so the single documented command discovers every test.

findings.title: ActiveUsersChart metric switcher claims role=tablist without the APG tabs keyboard model, and LogSection hides platform from assistive tech
findings.detail: The DAU/WAU/MAU switcher marks a row of plain buttons with role=tablist and role=tab plus aria-selected, but implements none of the APG tabs contract: no roving tabindex, no arrow-key navigation, no aria-controls, and no tabpanel counterpart. A screen reader announces tab semantics that then behave like buttons, which is more confusing than plain buttons would be. Separately, LogSection conveys each log row's platform exclusively through an aria-hidden icon tile, so assistive-technology users get no platform information at all in the features and announcements lists. Both are semantics defects on real operator flows, though each control remains reachable and operable.
findings.evidence: apps/admin/components/analytics/ActiveUsersChart.tsx:77-89 (role=tablist, role=tab, aria-selected on Button elements, no keyboard handlers or panels); apps/admin/app/(authed)/logs/_components/LogSection.tsx:163-171 (platform icon container marked aria-hidden with no textual alternative in the row)
findings.remediation: Drop the tab roles in favor of a group with aria-pressed toggle buttons (or implement the full APG tabs pattern), and add an sr-only platform label or aria-label on the LogSection row link.

findings.title: Forced-colors and increased-contrast modes are unhandled anywhere on the web surface
findings.detail: rg for forced-colors and forced-color-adjust over apps/web returns zero hits. The product's signature visuals draw their own fills and boundaries with CSS custom properties and inline SVG (valence stones, pebble silhouettes via .pbbls-visual and .path-stone-fill currentColor fills, the carve drawing canvas, selection states expressed as opacity dimming in ValenceFanPicker), and under Windows High Contrast / forced-colors these custom fills are forcibly replaced or flattened, so selected-vs-dimmed stones and stone boundaries can become indistinguishable while nothing in the code opts critical indicators back in. Users who depend on system contrast settings lose the selection state of the core input control.
findings.evidence: rg -n 'forced-colors|forced-color-adjust' apps/web/app apps/web/components apps/web/lib returns nothing; self-drawn control surfaces at apps/web/app/globals.css:514-556 (.pbbls-visual, .path-stone-fill currentColor fills) and components/record/valence/ValenceFanPicker.tsx:160-166 (selection conveyed by opacity/scale on custom-painted stones).
findings.remediation: Add a forced-colors media block giving custom controls system-color borders and a non-color selection indicator (e.g. a visible ring using Highlight/CanvasText keywords), and verify the valence picker and carve canvas in a forced-colors session; record the pass.

findings.title: Overlay enter/exit animations from tw-animate-css ignore the reduce-motion preference on all five overlay primitives
findings.detail: dialog, alert-dialog, sheet, popover, and dropdown-menu apply animate-in/animate-out utilities (fade, zoom, and for the sheet a full-height slide-in-from-bottom) unconditionally; tw-animate-css ships no prefers-reduced-motion gating and none of the five components adds motion-reduce: variants. Every other animation layer in the app (all framer-motion call sites, CSS transitions) is gated, so users who set reduce motion still get moving overlays on every dialog and sheet open/close, with the mobile sheet translation being the largest offender. Low harm per event but it fires on core flows (pebble peek uses its own gated path, but pickers, confirms, and menus all animate).
findings.evidence: apps/web/components/ui/dialog.tsx:47 and the animate-in/out classNames in components/ui/sheet.tsx, popover.tsx, dropdown-menu.tsx, alert-dialog.tsx (grep counts: 8 usages across 5 files); rg 'prefers-reduced-motion' node_modules/tw-animate-css/dist/tw-animate.css returns nothing; contrast with gated sites like components/path/PathPolaroid.tsx:29.
findings.remediation: Append motion-reduce:animate-none (or motion-safe: prefixes on the animate utilities) to the five overlay primitives' class strings, matching the convention already used elsewhere in the codebase.

findings.title: Root CLAUDE.md and the PR template still name lab-note.yml, a workflow deleted when the GitHub App webhook took over
findings.detail: CLAUDE.md's CI-gates line says 'lab-note.yml posts the note at merge' and the PR template comment says 'On merge, lab-note.yml posts it to the Ariko changelog vault automatically', but that workflow was retired in commit 8d22e405 (#705, 2026-08-17); merge-time delivery now happens via the Arkaik GitHub App webhook, as the Lab Note contract section of the same CLAUDE.md correctly describes 100 lines later. The always-loaded file is internally inconsistent about the delivery mechanism. Failure scenario: an agent debugging a missing changelog entry greps for lab-note.yml, finds nothing, and either concludes CI is broken or wastes a search cycle; or it trusts a merge-time gate that does not exist as a workflow.
findings.evidence: CLAUDE.md:71 vs CLAUDE.md:169 (webhook description); .github/PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE.md:12; git log shows 8d22e405 deleted .github/workflows/lab-note.yml and was also the last commit touching CLAUDE.md, so the line was missed in the same change
findings.remediation: Fix the CI-gates sentence in CLAUDE.md:71 and the PR template comment to name the Arkaik GitHub App webhook as the merge-time destination.

findings.title: arkaik.yml declares no permissions block and lab-note-reminder.yml delegates pull-requests:write to a reusable workflow pinned to a mutable branch
findings.detail: Three of four workflows declare least-privilege token scopes, but arkaik.yml has no permissions block at all, so it runs with the repository's default token scope (potentially read/write depending on org settings) for a job that only needs contents: read. Separately, lab-note-reminder.yml grants pull-requests: write and then delegates execution to alexisbohns/ariko/.github/workflows/lab-note-reminder.yml@main, a mutable ref in another repository; any change on that branch immediately executes here with comment-write capability on PRs. Same-owner repos lower the practical risk, but the pattern defeats the review boundary: this repo's CI behavior can change without any commit here.
findings.evidence: grep -c 'permissions:' across .github/workflows/*.yml: arkaik.yml returns 0, others 1; .github/workflows/lab-note-reminder.yml:13-19 (permissions pull-requests: write; uses ...@main)
findings.remediation: Add permissions: contents: read to arkaik.yml, and pin the ariko reusable workflow to a tag or commit SHA instead of @main.

findings.title: CoverImageInput performs storage IO and owns upload business rules inside a client view component, with no lint guard on the data boundary
findings.detail: CoverImageInput is the one view component on the surface that constructs a Supabase client and talks to the backend directly: it uploads to and removes from the lab-assets bucket from inside the component, and the business rules for uploads (accepted MIME types, 5 MB cap, bucket name, object path scheme) live inline in the render module rather than in a lib module the rest of the surface could reuse or a test could import. Because eslint.config.mjs has no no-restricted-imports rule fencing lib/supabase/browser off from components, nothing prevents the next contributor from copying this pattern into other client components, eroding the otherwise clean fetchers-and-actions boundary the surface follows.
findings.evidence: app/(authed)/logs/_components/CoverImageInput.tsx:7 (imports createClient from lib/supabase/browser), :19 (client construction in a view), :43-45 (storage upload), :65 (storage remove), :9-11 (BUCKET/ACCEPT/MAX_BYTES rules inline); eslint.config.mjs:5-21 (no no-restricted-imports rule); grep 'createClient(' over components/ and app/ returns this file as the only view-layer hit
findings.remediation: Extract the upload/remove/publicUrl logic and its constants into lib/logs/cover-image.ts (or a server action), leave the component as state plus rendering, and add an ESLint no-restricted-imports rule blocking lib/supabase/browser imports outside lib/.

findings.title: The M47 draft lifecycle is implemented twice, inline in CreatePebbleScreen and in ComposerDraftCoordinator
findings.detail: CreatePebbleScreen carries its own inline copy of the draft lifecycle (hydrate-or-restore, can_use_glyph verification, save-as-draft, consume-after-publish, roughly lines 113-260) while RecordFlowScreen drives the extracted ComposerDraftCoordinator. The decisions log records this as a deliberate two-copies-today state with the migration as the named follow-up, and warns that any fix to the lifecycle must land in both copies until then. That is precisely the silent-drift failure mode the iOS extraction was written to prevent; the risk is real but bounded because the duplication is documented in both the decisions log and the workspace CLAUDE.md, so an agent reading the standard context will find the warning. Included as a finding so the follow-up does not silently age out: the longer both copies live, the more likely a draft-lifecycle fix lands in only one composer.
findings.evidence: apps/android/app/src/main/kotlin/app/pbbls/android/features/path/create/CreatePebbleScreen.kt:113-260 (inline hydrate/autosave/saveAsDraft/consumeDraftAfterPublish); apps/android/app/src/main/kotlin/app/pbbls/android/services/ComposerDraftCoordinator.kt; docs/decisions/log.md 2026-08-24 entry for #725 ('CreatePebbleScreen and RecordFlowScreen both implement the M47 draft lifecycle, so a fix ... must land in both'); apps/android/CLAUDE.md:253-265
findings.remediation: Execute the recorded follow-up: migrate CreatePebbleScreen onto ComposerDraftCoordinator (the worked pattern already exists in RecordFlowScreen), delete the inline copy, and cover the coordinator's lifecycle with the existing ComposerAutosaveTest-style JVM tests.

findings.title: Post-await force unwraps in GlyphsListView.commitRename can crash after a concurrent tab reload
findings.detail: commitRename guards itemsByTab[.mine] before its first force unwraps, but the catch branch reuses the pre-await 'index' and force-unwraps 'itemsByTab[.mine]![index] = original' after the 'await glyphService.updateName' suspension point. During that suspension a tab switch retriggers '.task(id: tab) { await load(tab) }', which can replace or nil the .mine array (onSwapped already sets itemsByTab[.owned] = nil, proving entries do get nilled). If the array shrank, the write traps on index-out-of-range; if it was nilled, the force unwrap traps — a crash of the Glyphs screen triggered by an ordinary rename-plus-network-failure race. The success branch defensively re-finds its index; the failure branch does not, and none of the four unwraps carries a justification comment.
findings.evidence: apps/ios/Pebbles/Features/Glyph/Views/GlyphsListView.swift:180 (let original = itemsByTab[.mine]![index]), :184, :195 (guarded re-lookup, safe), :202 (itemsByTab[.mine]![index] = original in catch, after await at :193); reload path at :43 (.task(id: tab)); array nulling precedent at :172 (itemsByTab[.owned] = nil).
findings.remediation: In the catch branch, re-find the item by glyph id (as the success branch does) and use optional-chained subscript assignment; drop the remaining force unwraps in favor of 'guard let' bindings.

findings.title: The 3x3 valence mapping is implemented three times and the copies must drift-check by hand
findings.detail: The (positiveness, intensity) -> Valence mapping — the rule that decides how every pebble renders — exists as Valence.from(positiveness:intensity:), as Pebble.valence, and as PebbleDetail.valence. The copies deliberately differ in fallback behavior (nil vs logged .neutralMedium), each carries a comment naming the others, and Valence.swift itself says 'worth collapsing into this one day'. Until collapsed, a change to the grid (e.g. a fourth intensity) must be applied in three places, and only one copy (Valence.from, plus the 9-case tables asserted in PebbleDecodingTests.swift:86-106) is directly pinned by tests; a partial edit would make the timeline, the detail sheet, and draft hydration disagree about the same row's valence.
findings.evidence: apps/ios/Pebbles/Features/Path/Models/Valence.swift:55-68 (canonical Valence.from with 'worth collapsing into this one day' at :52-53); apps/ios/Pebbles/Features/Path/Models/Pebble.swift:27-48 ('Mirrors PebbleDetail.valence' comment at :23-26); apps/ios/Pebbles/Features/Path/Models/PebbleDetail.swift:72-92 (third copy with its own logging fallback).
findings.remediation: Collapse Pebble.valence and PebbleDetail.valence onto Valence.from with an explicit '?? .neutralMedium (logged)' at the two non-optional call sites, keeping the differing fallback semantics as one-liners over the single mapping.

findings.title: Failure-kind branching relies on substring matching of server error text instead of stable codes
findings.detail: Two boundary mappings discriminate error kinds by searching free text: userMessageForPebbleSaveError matches 'media_quota_exceeded' or 'P0001' inside the edge-function body's error/message strings, and ConnectionsError.from matches token strings inside error.localizedDescription. Both work today because the DB raises stable message slugs, but the contract is implicit: a reworded raise message, a localization of localizedDescription, or an edge function wrapping the Postgres error differently silently degrades every branch to the generic fallback ('unknown' / 'Couldn't save your pebble'), losing the quota message and the invite-specific errors without any test or type failing. The mapping is at least centralized and unit-tested against today's strings (PebblePublisherTests quota cases), which is why this is Low rather than Medium.
findings.evidence: apps/ios/Pebbles/Features/Path/PebblePublisher.swift:80-86 (substring match on 'media_quota_exceeded' and 'P0001'); apps/ios/Pebbles/Services/ConnectionsService.swift:125-134 (ConnectionsError.from matching error.localizedDescription.lowercased() for 'cannot_accept_own_invite', 'invite_expired', 'invite_not_found', 'not_authenticated'); tests pinning current strings at PebblesTests/Features/Record/PebblePublisherTests.swift:37-50.
findings.remediation: Have the edge functions and connection RPCs return a stable machine field (e.g. {code: 'media_quota_exceeded'}) alongside the human message, branch on the code on all clients (iOS and Android mirror), and keep the substring match only as a fallback for older servers.

findings.title: Four view files reach through useDataProvider to call provider methods directly, sidestepping the documented hooks-only rule and the lint guard
findings.detail: apps/web/CLAUDE.md:69 states components never call the provider directly and always go through hooks, and the ESLint no-restricted-imports rule enforces it for the concrete provider modules. But the rule does not cover lib/data/provider-context, and four view files use it to invoke provider methods inline: app/record/page.tsx:44 calls provider.getPebbleDraft, components/record/flow/RecordFlow.tsx:179 and components/path/QuickPebbleEditor.tsx:215 call provider.getDraftSnapUrl, with components/record/GlyphPickerTabs.tsx also importing the context. Each call is small, but the escape hatch is unguarded, so the boundary erodes one convenience call at a time and the equivalent data hooks (usePebbleDrafts) stop being the single seam for these operations.
findings.evidence: grep -rln 'provider-context' apps/web/app apps/web/components lists app/record/page.tsx, components/record/flow/RecordFlow.tsx, components/record/GlyphPickerTabs.tsx, components/path/QuickPebbleEditor.tsx (plus the exempt DataProvider.tsx); direct calls at RecordFlow.tsx:179, QuickPebbleEditor.tsx:215, app/record/page.tsx:44; rule text at apps/web/CLAUDE.md:69; lint gap at eslint.config.mjs:22-33
findings.remediation: Add getDraftSnapUrl/getPebbleDraft accessors to the drafts data hook, migrate the four call sites, and extend no-restricted-imports to bar provider-context imports outside lib/data and DataProvider.tsx.

findings.title: lab-assets bucket is created public with no file_size_limit and no allowed_mime_types, unlike the deliberately constrained pebbles-media bucket
findings.detail: The lab-assets bucket insert sets only (id, name, public) and inherits no per-bucket size or MIME constraints, so any object an admin uploads (of any type and any size up to the global cap) is publicly readable. The sibling pebbles-media migration shows the intended pattern (private, 1.5 MB cap, image/jpeg only), so the omission is inconsistency rather than a decision. Writes are gated on is_admin, which keeps likelihood low, but the failure scenario is real: an admin session (or a compromised admin account, or a future widening of the insert policy) uploads an oversized file or an HTML/SVG document; the bucket serves it publicly, enabling hosted-content abuse (e.g. serving scripts or phishing pages from the product's storage domain) or storage-cost surprise. Since bucket rows are config-as-migration, the fix is cheap and reviewable.
findings.evidence: packages/supabase/supabase/migrations/20260421000003_lab_assets_bucket.sql:9-11 (insert with no limits) and :19-25 (public read, admin insert); contrast packages/supabase/supabase/migrations/20260426000001_pebbles_pictures.sql:22-33 (private, 1572864 bytes, array['image/jpeg'])
findings.remediation: Add a migration upserting lab-assets with an explicit file_size_limit and an image-only allowed_mime_types array (matching what announcement covers actually need), using the on conflict do update pattern from the pebbles-media migration.

findings.title: No bundle analyzer or size gate exists for the admin surface
findings.detail: Despite disciplined server/client boundaries, nothing measures or bounds shipped client JavaScript: there is no @next/bundle-analyzer or size-limit dependency, next.config.ts is empty, and no CI workflow builds admin at all, so a dependency regression (recharts major bump, a wholesale lodash import, the md-editor losing its dynamic import) would land invisibly. The surface already carries two heavyweight client dependencies (recharts, @uiw/react-md-editor) whose cost is currently managed only by convention; growth is not a visible decision for anyone reviewing a PR.
findings.evidence: apps/admin/package.json:11-38 (no analyzer/size tooling; recharts ^3.8.0 and @uiw/react-md-editor ^4.1.0 present); apps/admin/next.config.ts:1-5 (empty config); .github/workflows/ contains no admin build or size job (android-release.yml, android.yml, arkaik.yml, lab-note-reminder.yml, lab-note.yml).
findings.remediation: Wire @next/bundle-analyzer behind an ANALYZE env flag in next.config.ts and record the current first-load-JS route table as the baseline; optionally add a size-limit budget file and a CI job asserting it on apps/admin/** changes.

findings.title: Cover images upload verbatim to the public lab-assets bucket with no re-encode or EXIF strip
findings.detail: CoverImageInput uploads the picked File object directly to the public lab-assets bucket after only client-side type and size checks. No re-encode or metadata strip happens on any side, and the object is then served forever from a permanent public URL embedded in the changelog consumed by all app clients. If the maintainer ever uses a phone photo as a cover, its EXIF block (GPS, capture time, device) publishes with it. Exposure is limited to the operator's own metadata, not app users', and typical covers are designed graphics, so both impact and likelihood are low; but the gap is structural and the fix is cheap.
findings.evidence: apps/admin/app/(authed)/logs/_components/CoverImageInput.tsx:24-53 (raw file upload, client-only validation); bucket is public with no processing pipeline (packages/supabase/supabase/migrations/20260421000003_lab_assets_bucket.sql:9-11); no EXIF handling anywhere under apps/admin (grep 'exif|EXIF' empty)
findings.remediation: Re-encode the image in the browser before upload (canvas/createImageBitmap to WebP/JPEG drops all metadata) or add a server-side transform; also set allowed_mime_types and file_size_limit on the bucket while touching it.

findings.title: No Content-Security-Policy or security headers on the admin surface
findings.detail: next.config.ts is an empty object: no CSP, no connect-src/script-src allowlist, no frame-ancestors, no referrer policy. The app's egress posture is currently perfect (only the Supabase origin), which is exactly when a CSP is cheapest to adopt and most valuable, because it converts today's clean posture into an enforced invariant: any future dependency or copy-pasted snippet that phones home would be blocked and visible instead of silent. For an authenticated operator tool whose session cookies are JS-readable by SDK design, script-src restriction is also meaningful XSS blast-radius containment. Absence today is a hardening gap, not an active exposure.
findings.evidence: apps/admin/next.config.ts:3 (empty config, no headers()); no vercel.json or middleware anywhere under apps/admin; observed egress is Supabase-only (grep of https:// literals and package.json dependency review)
findings.remediation: Add a headers() block in next.config.ts with a CSP pinning default-src 'self', connect-src 'self' plus the Supabase project origin, img-src 'self' plus the storage origin, frame-ancestors 'none', and X-Content-Type-Options nosniff.

findings.title: Valence integers are logged with privacy .public in the decode-drift fallback
findings.detail: Both Pebble.valence and PebbleDetail.valence log the (positiveness, intensity) pair with privacy: .public when the pair falls outside the nine valid combinations. The branch is reachable only for invalid pairs (DB CHECKs guarantee valid ones), so today it can only emit corrupt values rather than a user's actual emotional state; but the log line establishes the precedent of emitting emotion-domain field values publicly into the unified log, and a future contract change (e.g. widening the valence range server-side before the client updates) would make real user values flow through the same public interpolation. Everywhere else the codebase marks payload-adjacent values .private, so these two sites are also an inconsistency in an otherwise uniform discipline.
findings.evidence: apps/ios/Pebbles/Features/Path/Models/Pebble.swift:39-45 (privacy: .public on positiveness/intensity); apps/ios/Pebbles/Features/Path/Models/PebbleDetail.swift:83-91 (same); contrast with the .private convention at e.g. SupabaseService.swift:61 and PebbleDraftsService.swift:123
findings.remediation: Switch the two interpolations to privacy: .private (the debugging value survives via log-level access on-device), and record the ID-and-code-only logging convention in apps/ios/CLAUDE.md so new call sites inherit it.

findings.title: No Content-Security-Policy and no third-party egress inventory on the web surface
findings.detail: Automatic egress is genuinely minimal (fonts self-hosted, Supabase first-party), which is good, but nothing pins or records it. next.config.ts is empty and vercel.json carries only a $schema, so no CSP with connect-src/font-src/script-src allowlists constrains where the app may talk, and there is no committed inventory of external destinations with a purpose per host. A dependency or code change that opens a new egress (an SDK phoning home, a remote font) would not be caught, and for an intimate-data product every third-party recipient is a data recipient under GDPR. A public Supabase asset host is hardcoded rather than derived from config.
findings.evidence: apps/web/next.config.ts:4 (empty config, no headers); apps/web/vercel.json (only $schema); apps/web/components/record/ValenceIntensityGrid.tsx:41 (hardcoded external host); apps/web/lib/config/lab.ts:5 (WhatsApp link); no egress inventory doc under docs/
findings.remediation: Add a CSP (via next.config headers or vercel.json) with explicit connect-src/font-src/script-src allowlists covering the Supabase project and self; commit a third-party destination inventory with a purpose per host; add a CI grep that diffs external hostnames in source against the inventory.

findings.title: No PII inventory exists and personal-data tables are read with select('*')
findings.detail: There is no data-minimization inventory anywhere in the repo mapping personal-data fields to purposes, so per the criterion the surface caps at l1. Compounding this, the web data layer reads whole rows of personal-data tables with select('*') (profiles, souls, collections, glyphs, and the v_pebbles_full view). These reads are owner-scoped so they are not a cross-user leak, but they carry every column regardless of what the consuming feature needs, there is no purpose record for those columns, and nothing (lint or CI diff of generated types vs an inventory) prevents a new personal-data column from landing undocumented and over-fetched.
findings.evidence: No inventory: grep of docs/ for inventory|PII|ROPA|data-map hits only plan files; over-wide reads at apps/web/lib/data/supabase-provider.ts:114,119,120,122 and apps/web/lib/data/useSupabaseAuth.ts:113
findings.remediation: Author a PII inventory from packages/supabase/types/database.ts (one row per personal-data field with purpose and flows); narrow the owner-side select('*') calls to explicit column lists; add a CI diff between generated types and the inventory so a new personal-data field cannot land undocumented.

findings.title: No app lock and no recorded ambient-exposure decision for the installable PWA
findings.detail: Pebbles ships as an installable, standalone-display PWA holding mental-state data, but there is no optional app lock (biometric/WebAuthn/passcode re-auth with an auto-lock timeout) and no recorded decision on the app-switcher/recents snapshot exposure that the criterion explicitly asks installable web surfaces to make. The lock-screen notification vector is absent (web uses in-app toasts, a recorded choice), but the shoulder-surfing and shared-device vectors that a journaling app faces are unaddressed on web, and the session simply stays open until it expires.
findings.evidence: apps/web/public/manifest.webmanifest (display:standalone); grep for app.?lock|biometric|passcode|WebAuthn|auto.?lock over apps/web returns nothing; docs/decisions/log.md 2026-06-29 records in-app toasts (no OS push) but no ambient/app-lock decision
findings.remediation: Record a deliberate decision on PWA ambient exposure in docs/decisions/log.md, and ship an optional re-auth app lock (WebAuthn/passcode) with an auto-lock timeout for users who share or hand over their device.

findings.title: Detail pages convert transient DB errors into 404 not-found responses
findings.detail: Three detail routes treat a failed read identically to a missing row: on error the data is coalesced to null/empty and the code falls into notFound(). A transient RPC or select failure therefore renders a 404 for a record that exists, telling the admin an achievement, domain, or log has vanished. For the logs editor this is the entry point to editing published, user-visible Lab content, so a spurious 404 during an incident window reads as data loss. The failure is logged server-side but the rendered state is indistinguishable from genuine absence.
findings.evidence: apps/admin/app/(authed)/logs/[id]/page.tsx:23-26 (`if (error || !data) { ... notFound() }`); apps/admin/app/(authed)/achievements/[id]/page.tsx:17-21 (error -> `data ?? []` -> find fails -> notFound()); apps/admin/app/(authed)/domains/[id]/page.tsx:17-21 (same shape).
findings.remediation: Branch on `error` before the notFound() check: render ErrorBlock (or rethrow into a new error.tsx boundary) for read failures, and reserve notFound() for a successful read that returned no row.

findings.title: No network call in the admin surface carries an explicit timeout
findings.detail: The surface has no timeout utility, no AbortSignal usage, and no configured client-level timeout anywhere: every Supabase RPC, table read, auth call, and storage upload relies on library defaults. A hung upstream leaves an RSC card suspended on its skeleton until the hosting platform's function deadline converts it into an opaque 5xx, and leaves the browser-side storage upload in CoverImageInput pending indefinitely with the file input disabled. The web workspace already has a documented withTimeout convention (docs/agents/data-and-async.md) that was never ported, so this is a known-pattern gap, not an unknown one. No retry loops exist, so there is no unbounded-retry hazard, but no flow can distinguish 'slow' from 'dead'.
findings.evidence: Case-insensitive grep for withTimeout|AbortSignal|AbortController|timeout across apps/admin/app, components, lib, hooks: zero hits. Representative unprotected call sites: apps/admin/lib/analytics/fetchers.ts:30 (rpc), apps/admin/lib/supabase/admin-guard.ts:22,32 (auth + rpc on every authed navigation), apps/admin/app/(authed)/logs/_components/CoverImageInput.tsx:43-45 (browser storage upload).
findings.remediation: Port the web workspace's withTimeout(label) wrapper into apps/admin/lib and wrap the fetchers, admin-guard calls, and the storage upload; alternatively pass a global fetch with AbortSignal.timeout into createServerClient/createBrowserClient so every SDK call inherits a deadline.

findings.title: Log creation and admin glyph publish have no server-side duplicate guard
findings.detail: createLog inserts into logs with no unique constraint beyond the primary key, and publish_admin_glyph inserts a new glyph unconditionally, so any double-fire that gets past the client pending guard (two tabs, a replayed POST, a future retry wrapper) creates duplicate rows; a duplicate published log is user-visible in the iOS Lab feed. Additionally, updateLog's read-then-write (fetch published/status, compute stamps, then update) makes concurrent edits by two admin sessions last-write-wins with stamp decisions based on stale reads, and no concurrency model is documented anywhere in docs/decisions/log.md. Client-side guards are consistently present, and the moderation RPCs' invalid_state preconditions are a good server-side model that these two flows lack.
findings.evidence: No unique constraints: packages/supabase/supabase/migrations/20260421000001_logs_table.sql:11-32 (grep for 'unique' in logs migrations: zero hits). Unguarded insert: apps/admin/app/(authed)/logs/actions.ts:78-82; unconditional glyph insert: packages/supabase/supabase/migrations/20260630084718_admin_glyph_moderation.sql:159-166. Read-then-write: apps/admin/app/(authed)/logs/actions.ts:106-139. Contrast server guards: same migration lines 67, 95, 124.
findings.remediation: Add a scoped uniqueness or idempotency guard for log creation (e.g. unique (species, title_en) where published, or an idempotency key column checked on insert); give publish_admin_glyph a dedupe key or unique (user_id, name) partial index; document the last-write-wins model for log edits in docs/decisions/log.md or add updated_at optimistic checking to updateLog.

findings.title: Snap upload retry is non-idempotent after a partial success: the surviving rendition blocks every retry
findings.detail: uploadProcessed uploads original.jpg and thumb.jpg in parallel and throws if either fails. On a flaky network one rendition can land while the other fails; the coordinator's auto-retry (and the user's manual retry) then re-uploads both to the same paths without upsert, and the pebbles-media bucket deliberately has no UPDATE policy, so the already-stored object makes the retry fail permanently (duplicate/permission error). The chip sits in FAILED forever under retry taps; the only recovery is removing the photo (which deletes the stored files) and re-picking it, which nothing tells the user to do. The retry path exists precisely for flaky networks, which is the one condition under which it cannot converge.
findings.evidence: apps/android/app/src/main/kotlin/app/pbbls/android/services/PebbleSnapRepository.kt:69-92 (parallel uploads, upload { contentType = ... } with no upsert), :46-48 (doc: 'The bucket has no UPDATE policy, replace is delete + re-upload'); features/pebblemedia/SnapUploadCoordinator.kt:153-177 (retry re-runs the same uploadProcessed to the same prefix), :97-102 (retryCurrent same id).
findings.remediation: Make the retry idempotent: best-effort delete both objects before re-uploading (deleteFiles already exists and is best-effort), or treat an already-exists response on a rendition as success for that half. Mirror on iOS since the coordinator is ported verbatim.

findings.title: No outbound call in any edge function carries an explicit deadline or abort signal
findings.detail: The supabase-js clients are constructed without a fetch override or signal, and no call site passes AbortSignal.timeout. delete-account chains an unbounded-latency sequence (auth.getUser, purge RPC, a BFS storage walk of list/remove batches, deleteUser); one hung storage call holds the whole function until the platform wall-clock kill, surfacing to the deleting user as an opaque gateway timeout mid-erasure rather than a labeled, diagnosable failure. The documented resume matrix makes retry safe, so the consequence is degraded diagnosability and slower failure rather than corruption, which bounds the severity.
findings.evidence: packages/supabase/supabase/functions/_shared/supabase-client.ts:20-36 (no fetch/signal configuration); delete-account/index.ts:50-99 and :105-126 (chained calls, storage BFS, no deadlines); grep 'AbortSignal|AbortController' over supabase/functions = 0 hits
findings.remediation: Add a small labeled withDeadline helper in _shared (AbortSignal.timeout passed through the clients' global fetch, or wrapping each awaited call) with a stated per-operation default, and apply it to the storage walk and RPC calls; log the label on timeout.

findings.title: No documented removal channel or operator procedure exists for a named third party (a soul) to request erasure
findings.detail: The privacy policy acknowledges that users store third-party names as souls but documents rights only for the account holder; a person who learns they are named in someone's Pebbles account has no stated channel to request removal, and operators have no procedure or tooling to locate and remove a soul by name across accounts if such a request arrives. Because public sharing now exists, the household exemption does not shield published paths, so the controller carries this obligation directly. The gap is recourse and procedure, not exposure: no third-party name currently leaves the owner's scope on any traced outbound path.
findings.evidence: apps/web/docs/privacy/en.md:74-77 (souls acknowledged, no recourse), :226-272 (rights section addresses only 'your' data); grep -rilE 'removal|third.party.*request' over docs/ finds no channel; admin surface has no soul lookup capability (RPC inventory)
findings.remediation: Add a paragraph to the privacy policy naming the contact channel for recorded third parties, and a short operator procedure in docs/ (verify the requester, locate matching souls via a service-role query, remove or pseudonymize with owner notification where required).

findings.title: is_admin(uuid) is an admin-status oracle callable by anon with any user id
findings.detail: public.is_admin(p_user_id uuid) is security definer and granted to anon and authenticated, and it returns the is_admin flag for whatever uuid the caller supplies rather than deriving the subject from auth.uid(). Any client can therefore probe whether a given user id belongs to an operator, which helps an attacker identify the account worth phishing or credential-stuffing. Exploitation requires knowing user uuids, which the schema is otherwise careful not to leak (get_public_profile excludes user_id), so likelihood is low; but submitter_id does travel to admin clients and uuids appear in logs and support contexts over time. The parameterized shape is needed by RLS policies, but those policies always pass auth.uid(), so constraining the argument costs nothing.
findings.evidence: packages/supabase/supabase/migrations/20260421000000_profiles_is_admin.sql:21-29 (definer function with caller-supplied p_user_id, grant execute to anon, authenticated); all in-repo call sites pass auth.uid() (e.g. 20260421000001_logs_table.sql:46-56, 20260421000003_lab_assets_bucket.sql:24)
findings.remediation: Re-emit is_admin to return false when p_user_id is distinct from auth.uid() (all existing policy and RPC call sites already pass auth.uid()), or revoke from anon and add a self-only wrapper for client use.

findings.title: lab-assets bucket enforces no server-side content-type or size limits; upload validation is client-only
findings.detail: The bucket insert in the migration sets only id, name and public; storage-level allowed_mime_types and file_size_limit are absent, so the server accepts whatever content type and size an admin-authenticated client sends, including SVG or multi-hundred-MB blobs, into a public bucket. The 5 MB and PNG/JPEG/WebP checks live only in CoverImageInput and can be bypassed by any direct storage API call holding an admin session. The trust boundary is soft because writers must already be admins, so this is a hardening gap rather than an open hole; the main practical risks are a scripted mistake filling the public bucket and script-bearing SVG served from the storage origin.
findings.evidence: packages/supabase/supabase/migrations/20260421000003_lab_assets_bucket.sql:9-11 (no file_size_limit/allowed_mime_types columns set); apps/admin/app/(authed)/logs/_components/CoverImageInput.tsx:27-33 (client-only ACCEPT and MAX_BYTES checks), 43-45 (contentType taken from the client file)
findings.remediation: Alter storage.buckets for lab-assets to set allowed_mime_types = image/png,image/jpeg,image/webp and file_size_limit = 5MB so the server enforces the same contract the client promises.

findings.title: createLog/updateLog throw an unhandled RangeError on a malformed released_at instead of returning a form error
findings.detail: readLogFields converts the raw released_at string with new Date(raw).toISOString() before any validity check. A string that Date cannot parse yields an Invalid Date, and toISOString() then throws RangeError, escaping the action as a 500 with a Next error digest instead of the structured { error } result every other invalid field produces. The normal datetime-local input never emits such a value, so this surfaces only via hand-crafted POSTs (which any authenticated user can send at the action endpoint) or a browser quirk; there is no data or security consequence because the throw happens before any DB call and RLS still gates writes. It is an input-boundary robustness defect on an operator endpoint.
findings.evidence: apps/admin/app/(authed)/logs/actions.ts:36-40 (new Date(released_at_raw).toISOString() with no isNaN/validity guard, upstream of the field validations at lines 42-46)
findings.remediation: Parse defensively: const d = new Date(raw); if (Number.isNaN(d.getTime())) return { error: 'Release date is invalid.' }; then call toISOString().

findings.title: snaps.storage_path is stored as unvalidated free text with no check that its prefix matches the caller
findings.detail: create_pebble and update_pebble insert snaps.storage_path directly from the client payload (v_snap.value->>'storage_path') with no validation that the path begins with the caller's auth.uid() prefix, even though the storage RLS policy and the whole media layout assume {user_id}/{snap_id}/... A caller can therefore persist a snaps row whose storage_path points at an arbitrary prefix (e.g. another user's uid). This does not leak data today because the storage.objects owner-prefix SELECT policy (20260426000001:43-47) scopes signed-URL generation to the caller's own prefix, so a forged path yields a broken image rather than a foreign read; it is a defense-in-depth gap and a data-integrity hazard (dangling/foreign path rows), not a confirmed exposure. Worth closing because the DB row is the record of truth for cleanup and a future code path that trusts storage_path without re-checking ownership would turn this into a real cross-user reference.
findings.evidence: packages/supabase/supabase/migrations/20260817130000_pebble_visibility_grades.sql:304-315 (create_pebble snaps insert, storage_path unvalidated); 20260729140000_media_quota_profile_lookup.sql:264-275 (update_pebble same); storage policy at 20260426000001_pebbles_pictures.sql:43-61.
findings.remediation: In create_pebble/update_pebble, validate that each snap storage_path starts with v_user_id::text || '/' (raise on mismatch), or derive the path server-side from v_user_id + snap id rather than trusting the client string; keep the two RPCs symmetric.

findings.title: No written or automated regression-test requirement on fix PRs
findings.detail: Both merged iOS fix commits happen to include pinning tests, but nothing makes that repeatable: no contributor doc, PR checklist item, or CLAUDE.md rule requires a fix to land with a test failing on the parent commit, and no CI or bot check inspects fix-labelled PRs for test changes. Pre-squash branch history already shows the habit lapsing when unenforced (the draft-hydration fix ce50014e and the #727 behavior fixes touched no test files). With a solo-maintainer, agent-heavy workflow, an agent producing a quick fix has no encoded instruction to add the pinning test, so the current 2-for-2 record is luck plus culture, not a system.
findings.evidence: grep -rn -i 'regression test|failing test|pinning|test first' over CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md, apps/ios/CLAUDE.md, docs/agents/, .claude/skills/ = zero hits; root CLAUDE.md 'PR checklist' items 1-7 contain no test requirement; .github/workflows/ has no check inspecting fix PRs; counter-examples on branches: commit ce50014e (1 file changed, view only), e2b449fa, 567e9fe5 (production files only); compliant merged sample: 6bf3f160, 6bacf149.
findings.remediation: Add one line to the root PR checklist and apps/ios/CLAUDE.md: a fix PR includes a test that fails on the parent commit, referencing the issue; optionally add a workflow step that warns on fix-labelled PRs with no test-file diff.

findings.title: apps/web/CLAUDE.md pins Next.js 16.2.0 while the workspace runs 16.3.0
findings.detail: The web instruction file states the Next.js version twice (the version warning and the tech-stack table) as 16.2.0, but package.json requires ^16.3.0 and the installed copy is 16.3.0 (bumped in #703). The file's own premise is that this Next.js differs from training data and version-specific docs must be read, so a wrong pinned version undercuts the very warning it anchors; an agent may consult changelogs or docs for the wrong minor. Low stakes, but it is exactly the class of drift the repo's doc-accuracy grooming is meant to catch.
findings.evidence: apps/web/CLAUDE.md:7 and :13 (16.2.0); apps/web/package.json dependencies next ^16.3.0; node resolution of next/package.json prints 16.3.0; bump commit bc1ffa59 (#703) did not touch apps/web/CLAUDE.md
findings.remediation: State the version as 16.x with a pointer to package.json as the source of truth, or update the pin in both places when bumping (add it to the bump checklist).
